docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
In Android development, themes are a powerful way to define the overall look and feel of your application. A theme is a collection of attributes that can be applied to an entire app, an activity, or a view hierarchy – allowing you to maintain a consistent design throughout your application.

Themes are typically defined in XML files located in the res/values directory of your Android project. They can include attributes such as colors, fonts, styles, and dimensions.

The Droid framework includes AppCompat and Material Design 3 themes that you can easily apply to your app or activities.

docs.title: Applying Themes
docs.text:
You can set a theme for your entire application in the app manifest:

import Droid

@main
public final class App: DroidApp {
    @AppBuilder public override var body: Content {
        Manifest
            .theme(.material3DayNightNoActionBar)
    }
}

You can also set a theme for individual activities by overriding the theme property in your activity class:

final class MainActivity: AppCompatActivity {
    override class var theme: Style? { .material3DayNightNoActionBar }
    /// ...
}

docs.title: Custom Theme
docs.text:
If you use a custom theme, it is probably named AppTheme, so it can be used via the predefined constant 

.theme(.appTheme)

Otherwise, simply use your own style reference as a string, such as:

.theme("@style/MyOwnTheme")

docs.title: Dimension Units
docs.text:
Android supports several dimension units for specifying sizes, margins, paddings, and other measurements in your app's UI.

All the methods that expect dimension values in Droid framework assume dp (density-independent pixels) by default:

.width(16) // 16dp
.padding(8) // 8dp
.padding(h: 8, v: 16) // 8dp, 16dp

However, you can specify other units explicitly:

.width(16, .px) // 16 pixels
.padding(8, .sp) // 8 scale-independent pixels
.padding(h: 8, v: 16, .in) // 8 inches, 16 inches

The supported units are in DimensionUnit enum:

  • dp - density-independent pixels. It is a virtual unit of measurement that adjusts based on the screen density, ensuring consistent sizing across different devices. Best choice.
  • px - represents pixels, which are the smallest unit of measurement on a screen. It is an absolute unit and does not scale with screen density, making it less suitable for responsive designs.
  • sp - scale-independent pixels. Similar to dp, but also scales based on the user's font size preferences. It is primarily used for text sizes to ensure accessibility and readability.
  • pt - points. A physical unit of measurement equal to 1/72 of an inch. It is commonly used in typography and can vary in appearance depending on the screen density.
  • in - inches. Represents a physical measurement of length. It is an absolute unit and is rarely used in UI design due to its lack of adaptability to different screen sizes and densities.
  • mm - millimeters. Another physical unit of measurement. Like in, it is absolute and not commonly used in responsive design.

This enum also provides you with conversion methods to and from pixels:

let pixels: Int32 = DimensionUnit.dp.toPixels(16) // convert 16dp to pixels
let dp: Float = DimensionUnit.dp.fromPixels(48) // convert 48 pixels to dp

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
The Droid framework provides all the native Android views you need.

The full list of available views is in the left sidebar, categorized into sections like Classic, Android X, and Material Design.

The application documentation is under active development. If you encounter any 404 pages or typos, please be patient – new content is being added every day.

For quick reference, here are some of the most commonly used views: → LinearLayout → RelativeLayout → TextView → Button → ImageView → EditText → RecyclerView → ScrollView

Use the search bar to quickly find the view you need

Views can be placed inside activities, fragments, or other views.

docs.title: Building UI
docs.text: You either build UI declaratively like in SwiftUI, or imperatively by creating view instances and configuring them.

docs.title: Imperatively
docs.text:
It looks similar to how you would do it in Java, but using Swift syntax.

let linearLayout = LinearLayout()
linearLayout.orientation(.vertical)
let textView = TextView()
textView.text("Hello, World!")
textView.textSize(24)
textView.textColor(.black)
textView.padding(16)
textView.backgroundColor(.lightGray)
linearLayout.addSubview(textView)
contentView(linearLayout)

You may notice that property setters are without set prefix, this is intentional to make it more Swiftly. Getters are also without get prefix.

docs.title: Declaratively
docs.text:
Most natural way to build UI in Swift is using declarative syntax similar to SwiftUI.

LinearLayout {
    TextView("Hello, World!")
        .textSize(24)
        .textColor(.black)
        .padding(16)
        .backgroundColor(.lightGray)
}
.orientation(.vertical)

Allright, but how do we put this into an activity or fragment? There are → body and → buildUI methods:

override func buildUI() {
    super.buildUI()
    body {
        TextView("Hello, World!")
            .width(.matchParent)
            .height(.matchParent)
            .gravity(.center)
    }
}

docs.title: Context
docs.text: You may notice that View initializers do not require a Context parameter. This is because Droid framework automatically provides the correct context behind the scenes. You can prepare the view anywhere, and it will work correctly when added to the view hierarchy.

docs.title: Custom Views
docs.text:
Any view inherits from the base View class, which provides common properties and methods for all views. Inheritance is exactly the same as in Android SDK.

When you create a custom view, you need a few steps:

  1. inherit from the appropriate base class
  2. set the className property to specify the full Java class name
  3. set the layoutParamsClass property to specify the default layout params class
  4. set required gradle dependencies in gradleDependencies property
  5. add initializers
  6. add methods

Let's investigate each step.

docs.title: Inheritance and Dependencies
docs.text:
Your view may inherit from View, ViewGroup, or any other view class. This is how you declare a custom view that inherits from ViewGroup:

final class CustomView: ViewGroup {
    // ...
}

Then if your view is not just reimplementation of an existing one, you set the Java className:

override class var className: JClassName {
    "com/mycompany/customviews/CustomView"
}

Next, each view should provide its own LayoutParams class, otherwise it will use the default ViewGroup.LayoutParams, which may not be suitable and will cause runtime crash.

override class var layoutParamsClass: LayoutParams.Class {
    "com/mycompany/customviews/CustomView$LayoutParams"
}

Finally, if your view depends on any external Java libraries, you need to specify them in gradleDependencies property, so Swift Stream IDE knows which dependencies to include in the generated Gradle project.

override class var gradleDependencies: [AppGradleDependency] {[
    #"implementation "com.mycompany:customviews:1.0.0""#
]}

I also suggest creating a convenient static property for your custom dependency to avoid version mismatches if you use it in multiple places:

extension AppGradleDependency {
    static let customViews: Self = #"implementation "com.mycompany:customviews:1.0.0""#
}

and then use it in your view like this:

override class var gradleDependencies: [AppGradleDependency] {[
    .customViews
]}

Allright, this way, Droid framework knows which Java class to instantiate, which layout params to use, and which Gradle dependencies to include in your project. Easy and convenient.

docs.title: Initializer
docs.text:
Next, we add the required initializer:

@discardableResult
override init (id: Int32? = nil) {
    super.init(id: id)
}

And if your view inherits from ViewGroup you have to add another initializer with @BodyBuilder:

@discardableResult
override init (
    id: Int32? = nil,
    @BodyBuilder content: BodyBuilder.SingleView
) {
    super.init(id: id, content: content)
}

This means that this view accepts child views like this:

CustomView {
    TextView("Child 1")
    TextView("Child 2")
}

docs.title: View Properties
docs.text:
All properties of the view set not immediately, but later once the view is attached to the view hierarchy.

That's why you can declare views anywhere, even outside activities or fragments.

But to achieve this, you need to wrap all property setters into special structs that conform to ViewPropertyToApply protocol.

Let's say your Java view has a property called baselineAligned, which is a boolean. First you create a struct for it:

struct BaselineAlignedViewProperty: ViewPropertyToApply {
    let key: ViewPropertyKey = "setBaselineAligned"
    let value: Bool
    func applyToInstance(_ env: JEnv?, _ instance: View.ViewInstance) {
        // if it is Java field
        instance.booleanField(env, name: key.rawValue, value: value)
        // if it is Java method
        instance.callVoidMethod(env, name: key.rawValue, args: value)
    }
}

Then you create a convenient method in the view extension:

extension CustomView {
    @discardableResult
    public func baselineAligned(_ value: Bool = true) -> Self {
        BaselineAlignedViewProperty(value: value).applyOrAppend(nil, self)
    }
}

This method creates the property struct and applies it to the view instance immediately if it is already attached or appends it to be applied later. The rest is handled by the framework.

So now it can be used like this:

CustomView().baselineAligned()

Learn more about JNI usage in → JNIKit Fields and → JNIKit Methods

docs.title: ID
docs.text:
Views have unique integer IDs assigned automatically.

Access the ID simply via id property:

let view = CustomView()
let viewId = view.id

You can also set your own ID via initializer:

CustomView(id: 12345)

docs.title: View Methods
docs.text:
If your view has some methods that you want to expose, you can add them directly in the view extension.

extension CustomView {
    public func doSomething(param: Int) {
        instance?.callVoidMethod(name: "doSomething", args: param)
    }
}

This method will be called immediately on the view instance if it is already attached. Otherwise, you need to use → View Properties technique to queue the method call for later.

docs.title: Layout Params Properties
docs.text:
Layout Params are set similarly to view properties, but they conform to LayoutParamToApply protocol.

Let's say your Java view has a layout param called weight, which is a float. First you create a struct for it:

struct WeightLayoutParam: LayoutParamToApply {
    let key: LayoutParamKey = "weight"
    let value: Float
    func apply(_ env: JEnv?, _ context: View.ViewInstance, _ lp: LayoutParams) {
        // if it is Java field
        lp.setField(env, name: key.rawValue, arg: value)
        // if it is Java method
        lp.callVoidMethod(env, name: key.rawValue, args: value)
    }
}

Then you create a convenient method in the view extension:

extension CustomView {
    @discardableResult
    public func weight(_ value: Float) -> Self {
        WeightLayoutParam(value: value).applyOrAppend(self)
    }
}

This method creates the layout param struct and applies it to the view's layout params immediately if the view is already attached or appends it to be applied later.

docs.title: Layout Params Methods
docs.text:
If your layout params has some methods that you want to expose, you can add them directly in the view extension.

extension CustomView {
    public func changeSomething() {
        instance?.layoutParams()?.callVoidMethod(name: "changeSomething")
    }
}

docs.title: addSubview
docs.text:
You can add one subview:

let subView = TextView("Child 1")
addSubview(subView)

or multiple child views:

let subView1 = TextView("Child 1")
let subView2 = TextView("Child 2")
addSubviews(subView1, subView2) // or with array

docs.title: removeSubview
docs.text:
You can remove a specific child view like this:

removeSubview(subView)

docs.title: removeFromParent
docs.text:
You can remove the view from its parent view like this:

subView.removeFromParent()

docs.title: onAddToParent
docs.text:
You can listen for when the view is added to a parent view to perform additional setup.

.onAddToParent {
    Log.i("CustomView added to parent")
}

docs.title: onRemovedFromParent
docs.text:
You can listen for when the view is removed from its parent to perform cleanup actions.

.onRemovedFromParent {
    Log.i("CustomView removed from parent")
}

docs.title: willAddSubview
docs.text:
You can override this method to intercept when a subview is about to be added.

final class CustomView: ViewGroup {
    override func willAddSubview(_ subview: View) {
        super.willAddSubview(subview)
        Log.i("Subview \(subview) will be added")
    }
}

docs.title: didAddSubview
docs.text:
You can override this method to intercept when a subview has been added.

final class CustomView: ViewGroup {
    override func didAddSubview(_ subview: View) {
        super.didAddSubview(subview)
        Log.i("Subview \(subview) was added")
    }
}

docs.title: willRemoveSubview
docs.text:
You can override this method to intercept when a subview is about to be removed.

final class CustomView: ViewGroup {
    override func willRemoveSubview(_ subview: View) {
        super.willRemoveSubview(subview)
        Log.i("Subview \(subview) will be removed")
    }
}

docs.title: didRemoveSubview
docs.text:
You can override this method to intercept when a subview has been removed.

final class CustomView: ViewGroup {
    override func didRemoveSubview(_ subview: View) {
        super.didRemoveSubview(subview)
        Log.i("Subview \(subview) was removed")
    }
}

docs.title: willMoveToParent
docs.text:
You can override this method to intercept when the view is about to be moved to a parent view.

final class CustomView: View {
    override func willMoveToParent() {
        super.willMoveToParent()
        Log.i("CustomView will move to parent")
    }
}

Parent is still nil at this point.

docs.title: didMoveToParent
docs.text:
You can override this method to intercept when the view has been moved to a parent view.

final class CustomView: View {
    override func didMoveToParent() {
        super.didMoveToParent()
        Log.i("CustomView did move to parent")
    }
}

If the view is added as a child view, then you can access parent from the parent property.

If the view is a content view of an activity/fragment, then parent will stay nil.

docs.title: willMoveFromParent
docs.text:
You can override this method to intercept when the view is about to be removed from its parent view.

final class CustomView: View {
    override func willMoveFromParent() {
        super.willMoveFromParent()
        Log.i("CustomView will be removed its from parent")
    }
}

docs.title: didMoveFromParent
docs.text:
You can override this method to intercept when the view has been removed from its parent view.

final class CustomView: View {
    override func didMoveFromParent() {
        super.didMoveFromParent()
        Log.i("CustomView has been removed from its parent")
    }
}

docs.title: accessibilityDataSensitive

Sets whether this view contains sensitive information for accessibility services.

.accessibilityDataSensitive(.auto)

docs.title: accessibilityHeading
docs.text:

.accessibilityHeading(true)

docs.title: accessibilityLiveRegion
docs.text:
Sets the live region mode for this view

.accessibilityLiveRegion(.assertive)

docs.title: accessibilityPaneTitle
docs.text:

.accessibilityPaneTitle("Main Content")

docs.title: accessibilityTraversalAfter

.accessibilityTraversalAfter(anotherViewId)

docs.title: accessibilityTraversalBefore
docs.text:
Sets the id of a view that screen readers are requested to visit after this view.

.accessibilityTraversalBefore(anotherViewId)

docs.title: activated
docs.text:
Sets the activated state of this view.

.activated() // sets to true
.activated(false) // sets to false

docs.title: allowClickWhenDisabled
docs.text:
Sets whether this view should allow click events when it is disabled.

.allowClickWhenDisabled() // sets to true
.allowClickWhenDisabled(false) // sets to false

docs.title: allowedHandwritingDelegatePackage
docs.text:
Specifies that this view may act as a handwriting initiation delegator for a delegate editor view from the specified package.

.allowedHandwritingDelegatePackage("com.example.handwriting")

docs.title: alpha
docs.text:
Sets the alpha transparency of this view.

.alpha(0.5) // sets to 50% transparency

docs.title: autoHandwritingEnabled
docs.text:
Set whether this view enables automatic handwriting initiation.

.autoHandwritingEnabled() // sets to true
.autoHandwritingEnabled(false) // sets to false

docs.title: backgroundColor
docs.text:
Sets the background color of this view.

.backgroundColor(.lightGray)

Refer to → colors section for more details on colors.

docs.title: backgroundResource
docs.text:
Sets the background to a given resource ID.

.backgroundResource(R.drawable.my_background)

Refer to → R section for more details on resource IDs.

docs.title: bottom
docs.text:
Sets the bottom position of this view relative to its parent.

.bottom(100) // in dp units
.bottom(100, .px) // in pixels

Refer to → units section for more details on dimension units.

docs.title: cameraDistance
docs.text:
Sets the distance along the Z axis (orthogonal to the X/Y plane on which views are drawn) from the camera to this view.

.cameraDistance(1000) // in dp units
.cameraDistance(1000, .px) // in pixels

Refer to → units section for more details on dimension units.

docs.title: clickable
docs.text:
Enables or disables click events for this view.

.clickable() // sets to true
.clickable(false) // sets to false

docs.title: clipToOutline
docs.text:
Sets whether the View's Outline should be used to clip the contents of the View.

.clipToOutline() // sets to true
.clipToOutline(false) // sets to false

docs.title: contentDescription
docs.text:
Sets the content description of this view for accessibility purposes.

.contentDescription("This is a button")

docs.title: contentSensitivity
docs.text:
Sets content sensitivity mode to determine whether this view displays sensitive content (e.g. username, password etc.).

.contentSensitivity(.sensitive)
.contentSensitivity(.notSensitive)
.contentSensitivity(.auto) // uses heuristics

docs.title: contextClickable
docs.text:
Enables or disables context clicking for this view.

.contextClickable() // sets to true
.contextClickable(false) // sets to false

docs.title: defaultFocusHighlightEnabled
docs.text:
Sets whether this View should use a default focus highlight when it gets focused but doesn't have R.attr.state_focused defined in its background.

.defaultFocusHighlightEnabled() // sets to true
.defaultFocusHighlightEnabled(false) // sets to false

docs.title: drawingCacheBackgroundColor
docs.text:
Sets the drawing cache background color for this view.

.drawingCacheBackgroundColor(.white)

Refer to → colors section for more details on colors.

docs.title: drawingCacheEnabled
docs.text:
Enables or disables the drawing cache for this view.

.drawingCacheEnabled() // sets to true
.drawingCacheEnabled(false) // sets to false

This method was deprecated in API level 28.

docs.title: drawingCacheQuality
docs.text:
Sets the drawing cache quality for this view.

.drawingCacheQuality(.low)
.drawingCacheQuality(.high)
.drawingCacheQuality(.auto)

This method was deprecated in API level 28.

docs.title: duplicateParentStateEnabled
docs.text:
Enables or disables the duplication of the parent's state into this view.

.duplicateParentStateEnabled() // sets to true
.duplicateParentStateEnabled(false) // sets to false

docs.title: elevation
docs.text:
Sets the base elevation of this view relative to its parent.

.elevation(8) // in dp units
.elevation(8, .px) // in pixels

Refer to → units section for more details on dimension units.

docs.title: enabled
docs.text:
Set the enabled state of this view.

.enabled() // sets to true
.enabled(false) // sets to false

docs.title: fadingEdgeLength
docs.text:
Set the size of the faded edge used to indicate that more content in this view is available.

.fadingEdgeLength(16) // in dp units
.fadingEdgeLength(16, .px) // in pixels

Refer to → units section for more details on dimension units.

docs.title: filterTouchesWhenObscured
docs.text:
Sets whether the framework should discard touches when the view's window is obscured by another visible window at the touched location.

.filterTouchesWhenObscured() // sets to true
.filterTouchesWhenObscured(false) // sets to false

docs.title: fitsSystemWindows
docs.text:
Sets whether or not this view should account for system screen decorations such as the status bar and inset its content; that is, controlling whether the default implementation of fitSystemWindows(Rect) will be executed.

.fitsSystemWindows() // sets to true
.fitsSystemWindows(false) // sets to false

docs.title: focusable
docs.text:
Sets whether this view can receive focus.

.focusable() // sets to true
.focusable(false) // sets to false

docs.title: focusableInTouchMode
docs.text:
Sets whether this view can receive focus while in touch mode.

.focusableInTouchMode() // sets to true
.focusableInTouchMode(false) // sets to false

docs.title: focusedByDefault
docs.text:
Sets whether this View should receive focus when the focus is restored for the view hierarchy containing this view.

.focusedByDefault() // sets to true
.focusedByDefault(false) // sets to false

docs.title: forceDarkAllowed
docs.text:
Sets whether this view allows the system to automatically apply a dark theme to it when the system is in dark mode.

.forceDarkAllowed() // sets to true
.forceDarkAllowed(false) // sets to false

docs.title: foregroundGravity
docs.text:
Sets the gravity used to position the foreground drawable within this view.

.foregroundGravity(.center)
.foregroundGravity(.top | .start)

docs.title: frameContentVelocity
docs.text:
Sets the velocity at which content is moved within this view.

.frameContentVelocity(1.0) // normal speed
.frameContentVelocity(0.5) // half speed
.frameContentVelocity(2.0) // double speed

docs.title: handwritingBoundsOffsets
docs.text:
Set the amount of offset applied to this view's stylus handwriting bounds.

.handwritingBoundsOffsets(left: 10, top: 10, right: 5, bottom: 5) // in dp units
.handwritingBoundsOffsets(left: 10, top: 10, right: 5, bottom: 5, unit: .px) // in pixels

docs.title: handwritingDelegateFlags
docs.text:
Sets flags configuring the handwriting delegation behavior for this delegate editor view.

.handwritingDelegateFlags(.default)
.handwritingDelegateFlags(.homeDelegatorAllowed)

docs.title: hapticFeedbackEnabled
docs.text:
Set whether this view should have haptic feedback for events such as long presses.

.hapticFeedbackEnabled() // sets to true
.hapticFeedbackEnabled(false) // sets to false

docs.title: hasTransientState
docs.text:
Set whether this view is currently tracking transient state that the framework should attempt to preserve when possible.

.hasTransientState() // sets to true
.hasTransientState(false) // sets to false

docs.title: horizontalFadingEdgeEnabled
docs.text:
Define whether the horizontal edges should be faded when this view is scrolled horizontally.

.horizontalFadingEdgeEnabled() // sets to true
.horizontalFadingEdgeEnabled(false) // sets to false

docs.title: horizontalScrollBarEnabled
docs.text:
Define whether the horizontal scrollbar should be drawn or not.

.horizontalScrollBarEnabled() // sets to true
.horizontalScrollBarEnabled(false) // sets to false

docs.title: hovered
docs.text:
Sets the hovered state of this view.

.hovered() // sets to true
.hovered(false) // sets to false

docs.title: importantForAccessibility
docs.text:
Sets how to determine whether this view is important for accessibility which is if it fires accessibility events and if it is reported to accessibility services that query the screen.

.importantForAccessibility(.yes)
.importantForAccessibility(.no)
.importantForAccessibility(.noHideDescendants)
.importantForAccessibility(.auto)

docs.title: importantForAutofill
docs.text:
Sets how this view is important for autofill.

.importantForAutofill(.auto)
.importantForAutofill(.captureNo)
.importantForAutofill(.captureNoExcludeDescendants)
.importantForAutofill(.captureYes)
.importantForAutofill(.captureYesExcludeDescendants)

docs.title: importantForContentCapture
docs.text:
Sets the mode for determining whether this view is considered important for content capture.

.importantForContentCapture(.auto)
.importantForContentCapture(.captureNo)
.importantForContentCapture(.captureNoExcludeDescendants)
.importantForContentCapture(.captureYes)
.importantForContentCapture(.captureYesExcludeDescendants)

docs.title: isCredential
docs.text:
Sets whether this view is a credential for Credential Manager purposes.

.isCredential() // sets to true
.isCredential(false) // sets to false

docs.title: isHandwritingDelegate
docs.text:
Sets whether this view is a handwriting delegate editor view.

.isHandwritingDelegate() // sets to true
.isHandwritingDelegate(false) // sets to false

docs.title: keepScreenOn
docs.text:
Sets whether to keep the screen on while this view is visible to the user.

.keepScreenOn() // sets to true
.keepScreenOn(false) // sets to false

docs.title: keyboardNavigationCluster
docs.text:
Set whether this view is a root of a keyboard navigation cluster.

.keyboardNavigationCluster() // sets to true
.keyboardNavigationCluster(false) // sets to false

docs.title: labelFor
docs.text:
Sets the id of a view for which this view serves as a label for accessibility purposes.

.labelFor(anotherViewId)

docs.title: layoutDirection
docs.text:
Sets the layout direction for this view.

.layoutDirection(.ltr)
.layoutDirection(.rtl)
.layoutDirection(.locale)

docs.title: left
docs.text:
Sets the left position of this view relative to its parent.

.left(50) // in dp units
.left(50, .px) // in pixels

docs.title: leftTopRightBottom
docs.text:

docs.title: AbsSeekBar
docs.text:
AbsSeekBar is the shared Android base behind interactive progress controls such as SeekBar and RatingBar.

Android treats AbsSeekBar as an abstract base. Prefer the concrete control for real UI. In the current Droid source pin this type only adds the inheritance chain above ProgressBar; thumb, tick, and range APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use this page to understand what the concrete seek-style controls currently inherit. For a draggable slider, start with SeekBar. For stars, use RatingBar.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
AbsSeekBar participates in the view hierarchy like other controls through its ProgressBar parent.

The current type does not expose thumb(_:), thumbTintList(_:), tickMark(_:), splitTrack(_:), keyProgressIncrement(_:), or related seek APIs at this pin.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Prefer the concrete controls:

SeekBar(id: 1501)
RatingBar(id: 1502)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
AbsSeekBar()
AbsSeekBar(id: 1501)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Thumb, tick, and range configuration live on Android’s AbsSeekBar API. None of that is part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: AbsoluteLayout
docs.text:
AbsoluteLayout positions children using explicit X and Y coordinates.

Android deprecates this layout because fixed coordinates do not adapt well to different screen sizes, font sizes, or layout directions. Prefer flexible layouts such as FrameLayout for overlays, or a constraint-based layout for relationships between views.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use AbsoluteLayout only for legacy UI or tightly controlled fixed-coordinate layouts where adapting to different device configurations is not a requirement.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Each child receives its position through the x(_:_:) and y(_:_:) layout params. Both use .dp by default, so the values are converted using the current display density.

The coordinates remain fixed relative to the parent. If content size or available space changes, AbsoluteLayout does not automatically reflow the children.

docs.title: Place a label at a fixed position
docs.text:
AbsoluteLayout {
    TextView("Tap here")
        .x(16)
        .y(24)
}
.width(.matchParent)
.height(160)
.backgroundColor(.lightGray)

The label starts 16 dp from the left and 24 dp from the top of the layout.

docs.title: Position two children independently
docs.text:
AbsoluteLayout {
    TextView("A")
        .x(16)
        .y(16)

    TextView("B")
        .x(120)
        .y(60)
}
.height(120)

Each child keeps the coordinates assigned to it rather than participating in a row, column, or relative positioning rule.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Create an empty layout, assign an id when you need one, or provide its children directly:

AbsoluteLayout()
AbsoluteLayout(id: 1001)

AbsoluteLayout {
    TextView("Child")
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
Use x(_:_:) and y(_:_:) on children. Pass a different DimensionUnit only when the coordinate should not use the default .dp.

TextView("Hello")
    .x(24)
    .y(24)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Avoid AbsoluteLayout for responsive screens. Fixed coordinates are difficult to maintain when available space, text size, or layout direction changes.

docs.title: ActionMenuView
docs.text:
ActionMenuView is Android’s action-bar menu container.

In the current Droid source pin it inherits LinearLayout and has a single-child content initializer plus its own layout-param class. Menu presentation APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ActionMenuView when the screen needs the classic Android action-menu container name and menu APIs can land later.

For ordinary vertical/horizontal stacks, use LinearLayout directly.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ActionMenuView can take declarative content and keeps the current LinearLayout surface, including orientation(_:) and shared view configuration such as padding and onClick(_:).

The current type does not expose setPresenter(_:), overflow helpers, or menu-model binding at this pin.

docs.title: Place an action menu row
docs.text:
ActionMenuView(id: 4101) {
    TextView("Action")
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ActionMenuView()
ActionMenuView(id: 4101)

ActionMenuView(id: 4101) {
    // single child content via BodyBuilder
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text: ActionMenuView declares its own LayoutParams class at this pin. Use the shared layout-param surface when configuring children.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s ActionMenuView binds an action menu model and presenter. That surface is not part of the current Droid API.

docs.title: ActionProvider
docs.text:
ActionProvider wraps an Android action provider associated with a MenuItem.

Droid lets you inspect provider visibility and submenu state, refresh item visibility, and use the supported configuration on ShareActionProvider and MediaRouteActionProvider.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use ActionProvider when a menu item already has an Android action provider and your Swift code needs to inspect or configure that provider.

docs.title: Inspect a menu item's provider
docs.text:
MenuItem.actionProvider() returns the provider currently attached to the item:

if let provider = item.actionProvider() {
    print(provider.hasSubMenu())
    print(provider.isVisible())

    if provider.overridesItemVisibility() {
        provider.refreshVisibility()
    }
}

MenuItem.actionProvider(_:) can also attach an ActionProvider instance to a menu item.

docs.title: Configure sharing
docs.text:
When you already have a ShareActionProvider, configure its history file and share intent directly:

func configureShare(
    _ provider: ShareActionProvider,
    intent: Intent
) {
    provider.shareHistoryFileName("share_history.xml")
    provider.shareIntent(intent)
}

defaultShareHistoryFileName exposes Android's default share-history filename.

MediaRouteActionProvider.routeTypes(_:) sets the route type mask used by the Android media-route chooser.

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text: onPrepareSubMenu(_:), MediaRouteActionProvider.onCreateActionView(_:), and MediaRouteActionProvider.onPerformDefaultAction() currently do not perform Android work. Do not rely on those hooks.

docs.title: AdapterView
docs.text:
AdapterView is the base type behind classic Android widgets whose visible items come from an adapter.

You normally encounter it through concrete controls such as ListView, GridView, or Spinner rather than creating an AdapterView directly.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use AdapterView as a type boundary when code needs to work with a classic adapter-backed view without depending on one concrete widget.

For new list and grid interfaces, prefer RecyclerView when its more flexible recycling model fits the screen.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Droid currently provides the generic AdapterView<T: Adapter> base and its inherited view-group behavior. Adapter population, selection, and callback APIs are not exposed on this type yet.

That makes the type useful mainly as a base class and generic constraint in current code.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A helper can accept any concrete AdapterView whose adapter type satisfies Adapter:

func fillAvailableWidth<A: Adapter>(_ view: AdapterView<A>) {
    view.width(.matchParent)
}

The helper works with the common view surface without assuming list-, grid-, or spinner-specific behavior.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Do not instantiate the generic base just to display content. Choose the concrete adapter-backed widget that matches the UI you are building.

docs.title: AutoCompleteTextView
docs.text:
AutoCompleteTextView is Android’s text field with completion suggestions.

In the current Droid source pin it inherits EditText. Text editing from that family works. Completion adapters, thresholds, and suggestion APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use AutoCompleteTextView when the field should grow completion behavior and the adapter surface can land later.

For plain text input, use EditText.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
AutoCompleteTextView keeps the current EditText / TextView text surface, including text(_:), plus shared view configuration such as onClick(_:), padding, enabled(_:), and visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose adapter(_:), setThreshold(_:), showDropDown(), dismissDropDown(), or item-click listeners at this pin.

docs.title: Place a completion field
docs.text:
AutoCompleteTextView(id: 3901)
    .hint("City")
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Start from a known value
docs.text: AutoCompleteTextView(id: 3902, "Berlin")

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
AutoCompleteTextView()
AutoCompleteTextView(id: 3901)
AutoCompleteTextView(id: 3901, someStringState)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s AutoCompleteTextView is defined by its adapter and threshold. That surface is not part of the current Droid API.

docs.title: Button
docs.text:
Button presents a text action that the user can tap. Use it for explicit choices such as Save, Continue, Retry, or Delete when the action should be visible as a control rather than attached to another piece of content.

A button uses the same text surface as TextView, so text size and other verified text configuration can be applied directly. Click handling comes from the shared view interaction API through onClick(_:).

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a Button when the user should deliberately trigger an action and the action deserves its own visible control. Short labels that describe the result, such as "Save" or "Try again", make the intent clear.

For text that only communicates information and is not interactive, use TextView instead.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The button participates in layout like other views and displays its label through the inherited text behavior. Register onClick(_:) to run work when the user activates it.

The click handler is attached as part of view configuration, so it can be declared alongside the button in the body builder. Text styling remains available through the inherited TextView behavior.

docs.title: Run an action when tapped
docs.text:
@State var message = "Nothing saved yet"

body {
    VStack {
        TextView($message)

        Button("Save")
            .onClick {
                message = "Saved"
            }
    }
    .padding(16)
}

Tapping Save changes the state, and the status label updates to show the result.

docs.title: Style the label while keeping button behavior
docs.text:
body {
    Button("Continue")
        .textSize(18)
        .width(.matchParent)
        .onClick {
            Log.i("Continue tapped")
        }
}

Text configuration is inherited from TextView; the button still handles the click through onClick(_:).

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
A button can be created with a text value and may also use an explicit view id:

Button("Save")
Button(id: 1001, "Continue")

docs.title: Click handling
docs.text:
onClick(_:) registers the action that runs when the button is clicked.

Button("Retry")
    .onClick {
        Log.i("Retry requested")
    }

The shared view API also has an event form when the click event itself is needed.

docs.title: Text configuration
docs.text:
Because Button inherits the text behavior documented on TextView, you can configure its label with methods such as text(_:), textSize(_:_:), maxLines(_:), and gravity(_:) when those choices are useful for the control.

Button("Open details")
    .textSize(16)
    .maxLines(1)

docs.title: CalendarView
docs.text:
CalendarView shows a month-style calendar for choosing or inspecting a date when surrounding days matter to the decision.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control with a single-child content initializer. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; selection, min/max bounds, week display, and date-change listeners are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use CalendarView when the user should see a full month grid in the screen instead of opening a separate picker, such as booking or scheduling layouts.

Because it takes substantial vertical space, prefer a compact picker for short forms.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
CalendarView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type inherits FrameLayout at this pin and accepts declarative child content. It does not expose minDate(_:), maxDate(_:), date(), shownWeekCount(_), firstDayOfWeek(_), or date-change listeners.

docs.title: Place a calendar
docs.text:
CalendarView(id: 1101)
    .padding(h: 8, v: 8)

docs.title: Add a caption under the calendar
docs.text:
CalendarView(id: 1101) {
    TextView("Selected date")
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
CalendarView()
CalendarView(id: 1101)

CalendarView(id: 1101) {
    // single child content via BodyBuilder
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s CalendarView owns selection and range behavior. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: CheckBox
docs.text:
CheckBox is the classic Android control for an independent yes/no option.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; checked-state helpers and button drawable/tint configuration are not wrapped on this type.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a checkbox for independent selections such as remembering a device, accepting terms, or enabling an optional feature.

For mutually exclusive choices, use RadioGroup. For a settings switch look, see Switch.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
CheckBox participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

At this pin CheckBox inherits View only. It does not inherit CompoundButton and does not conform to Checkable. Methods such as checked(_:), isChecked(), toggle(), buttonTintList(_:), and buttonDrawable(_:) are not available on CheckBox.

docs.title: Place an options checkbox
docs.text:
CheckBox(id: 9001)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: React to a tap
docs.text:
let accept = CheckBox(id: 9002)

accept.onClick {
    // Handle activation. Checked-state reads/writes are not wrapped yet.
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
CheckBox()
CheckBox(id: 9001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s CheckBox is a CompoundButton. The current Droid type is not. Use CompoundButton when you need the verified Checkable methods (checked(_:), isChecked(), toggle()).

docs.title: CheckedTextView
docs.text:
CheckedTextView is Android’s text row that can show a checked state.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; checked state, check-mark drawables, and Checkable methods are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use CheckedTextView when the screen needs the classic Android checked text row and those APIs can land later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
CheckedTextView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit TextView, does not conform to Checkable, and does not expose checked(_:), isChecked(), toggle(), checkMarkDrawable(_:), or checkMarkTintList(_:) at this pin.

docs.title: Place a checked text row
docs.text:
CheckedTextView(id: 3401)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
CheckedTextView()
CheckedTextView(id: 3401)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s CheckedTextView combines text with a check mark. That surface is not part of the current Droid API. Use CompoundButton when you need verified Checkable methods.

docs.title: Chronometer
docs.text:
Chronometer is Android’s elapsed-time text widget.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; base time, format, started state, and tick listeners are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use Chronometer when the screen should show a classic running timer and the timer APIs can land later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Chronometer participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit TextView at this pin and does not expose setBase(_:), start(), stop(), setFormat(_:), or tick listeners.

docs.title: Place a timer slot
docs.text:
Chronometer(id: 2701)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 8)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Chronometer()
Chronometer(id: 2701)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s Chronometer counts from a base SystemClock value. Start/stop and format APIs are not part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: CompoundButton
docs.text:
CompoundButton is the shared Android base for controls with a checked/unchecked state. In the current Droid source pin it is the type that actually exposes the Checkable methods.

Use the concrete control that best matches the interaction when one exists. Reach for CompoundButton itself when you need the verified checked-state API on a live instance.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use this surface when you need to read, set, or toggle checked state on a live checkable control.

Button drawable/tint configuration and checked-change listeners are not wrapped yet, so this page documents the checked-state methods only.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
CompoundButton inherits Button and conforms to Checkable. Text configuration from the TextView family and shared view interaction from View remain available through those parents.

checked(_:), isChecked(), and toggle() operate on the live Android instance. checked(_:) is a live operation and does not return the control for chaining.

docs.title: Change live checked state
docs.text:
func enable(_ control: CompoundButton) {
    control.checked(true)
}

docs.title: Read the current state
docs.text:
if !control.isChecked() {
    control.checked(true)
}

docs.title: Flip a setting
docs.text: control.toggle()

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
CompoundButton()
CompoundButton(id: 1001)

docs.title: Checked state
docs.text:
isChecked() reads the live state. checked(_:) sets it, and toggle() flips it.

let on = control.isChecked()
control.checked(!on)

These three methods come from the Checkable protocol and are the verified checked-state surface at this pin.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: At this pin CheckBox does not inherit CompoundButton and does not receive these methods. buttonDrawable(_:), buttonTintList(_:), onCheckedChangeListener(_:), and performClick() are not part of the current Droid CompoundButton API.

docs.title: DatePicker
docs.text:
DatePicker is Android’s calendar-date selection control.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; selected-date reads, min/max bounds, updateDate, calendar/spinner presentation, and date-change listeners are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a date picker when the user should choose a valid calendar date instead of typing and parsing date text.

For a compact list of dates or a custom calendar UI, build the selection surface yourself and keep the validated date in app state.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
DatePicker participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit FrameLayout and does not expose updateDate(...), minDate(_:), maxDate(_:), calendarViewShown(_:), spinnersShown(_:), year() / month() / dayOfMonth(), or listener bridges at this pin.

docs.title: Place a date control
docs.text:
DatePicker(id: 6001)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Hide it until the user opts in
docs.text:
let picker = DatePicker(id: 6002)
    .visibility(.gone)

// later
picker.visibility(.visible)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
DatePicker()
DatePicker(id: 6001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s DatePicker owns the selected date, bounds, and spinner/calendar chrome. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: EditText
docs.text:
EditText is a text field for values the user can enter and modify. It is a good fit for form fields, search queries, settings, and other places where text should move between the UI and application state.

Passing a string state gives the field two-way synchronization: the current state becomes the field text, later state changes update the field, and user edits are written back to that state.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use EditText when typing is part of the interaction. It is appropriate for names, email addresses, search terms, notes, and other editable strings.

If the value is only being displayed, use TextView instead.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
EditText inherits the text configuration available on TextView, including useful setters such as hint(_:). With EditText($value), Droid installs text-change handling in addition to the normal state-backed text update, which is what makes the binding two-way.

Selection methods such as selectAll() and setSelection(index:) are imperative: they call the existing Android view instance. Invoke them after the field has been created, for example from a button or another user event, rather than chaining them onto a newly constructed field before it is on screen.

docs.title: Bind a field to state
docs.text:
@State var email = ""

body {
    VStack {
        TextView("Email")

        EditText($email)
            .hint("name@example.com")

        TextView($email)
    }
    .padding(16)
}

Typing in the field changes email, and the second label reflects the same state. Changing email elsewhere also updates the field.

docs.title: Select the current value from an action
docs.text:
@State var query = "Swift"
let searchField = EditText()

body {
    VStack {
        searchField
            .text($query)
            .hint("Search")

        Button("Select all")
            .onClick {
                searchField.selectAll()
            }
    }
    .padding(16)
}

The selection call runs after the field exists, so it can act on the underlying Android instance.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Create an empty field or bind it directly to a string state:

EditText()
EditText($email)
EditText(id: 1001)

docs.title: Select all text
docs.text:
selectAll() selects the field's current text. Because it operates on the existing view instance, call it after the field has been built.

Button("Select all")
    .onClick {
        searchField.selectAll()
    }

docs.title: Move or extend the selection
docs.text:
setSelection(index:) moves the caret to an offset. The range overload selects between two offsets, while extendSelection(index:) extends the current selection.

Button("Move cursor")
    .onClick {
        searchField.setSelection(index: 0)
    }

For a range:

Button("Select first word")
    .onClick {
        searchField.setSelection(start: 0, end: 5)
    }

docs.title: Style shortcuts
docs.text:
setStyleShortcutsEnabled(_:) enables or disables supported keyboard style shortcuts on the existing field instance.

Button("Enable style shortcuts")
    .onClick {
        searchField.setStyleShortcutsEnabled()
    }

Use it after the field has been created for the same reason as the selection methods.

docs.title: Observe text changes
docs.text:
The inherited textChangedListener(beforeTextChanged:onTextChanged:afterTextChanged:) API is useful when you need a callback in addition to state binding.

EditText()
    .textChangedListener(
        beforeTextChanged: nil,
        onTextChanged: { event in
            Log.i("Current input: \(event.p0 ?? "")")
        },
        afterTextChanged: nil
    )

docs.title: ExpandableListView
docs.text:
ExpandableListView is Android’s two-level list: groups that expand to show their children.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; expandable adapters, group/child APIs, and expansion listeners are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ExpandableListView when the screen needs classic expandable group/child list behavior and you can wait for the adapter surface to land.

For a flat list name only, see ListView. For highly customized lists, prefer RecyclerView.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ExpandableListView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose adapter assignment, expand/collapse helpers, or group/child selection APIs at this pin.

docs.title: Place an expandable list
docs.text:
ExpandableListView(id: 2101)
    .padding(h: 0, v: 0)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ExpandableListView()
ExpandableListView(id: 2101)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s ExpandableListView is defined by ExpandableListAdapter and group/child callbacks. None of that is part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: FrameLayout
docs.text:
FrameLayout stacks children in the same area, making it useful when one piece of content needs overlays such as a loading indicator, badge, or centered action.

Later children are drawn above earlier children. Child layout params such as gravityInParent(_:) and margins control where an overlay sits inside the frame.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use FrameLayout when the screen has a primary layer with a small number of views placed over it.

When many views need relationships to one another rather than simple overlay placement, use a layout designed for those relationships instead.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Children share the frame's bounds. Their order determines their visual stacking order: the first child forms the lower layer and later children appear above it.

Use gravityInParent(_:) on a child to place it within the frame. Margins can offset that placement from the selected edge or corner.

docs.title: Show a loading indicator over content
docs.text:
FrameLayout {
    ScrollView {
        TextView("Content goes here…")
            .padding(16)
    }

    ProgressBar()
        .gravityInParent(.center)
}
.width(.matchParent)
.height(.matchParent)

The scrollable content remains the lower layer while the progress indicator is centered above it.

docs.title: Put a badge in the top-right corner
docs.text:
FrameLayout {
    TextView("Inbox")
        .padding(16)

    TextView("3")
        .padding(h: 8, v: 4)
        .textColor(.black)
        .backgroundColor(.lightGray)
        .gravityInParent([.top, .end])
        .marginTop(12)
        .marginEnd(12)
}

The badge is drawn above the Inbox label and offset from the top-end corner.

docs.title: Center an action above a background layer
docs.text:
FrameLayout {
    View()
        .backgroundColor(.lightGray)

    Button("Get started")
        .gravityInParent(.center)
}
.height(220)

The background fills the lower layer and the button is positioned at the center of the frame.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Create an empty frame or provide its children directly:

FrameLayout()

FrameLayout {
    TextView("Child")
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
Apply gravityInParent(_:) to a child when it needs a specific position within the frame.

FrameLayout {
    ProgressBar()
        .gravityInParent(.center)
}

docs.title: Gallery
docs.text:
Gallery is a legacy Android widget for horizontally browsing items.

Android deprecated the widget long ago. Keep it for maintenance of existing Gallery-based screens; for new UI, prefer a modern list or scrolling layout.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use Gallery only when an existing Android screen already depends on it and replacing the widget is outside the current change.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Droid currently supports constructing the Gallery and applying inherited view configuration such as size.

Keep usage to that stable surface. Lower-level gesture, spacing, and layout-management controls are intentionally outside this page.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Create the legacy container and size it like any other view:

Gallery()
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(220)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Create a Gallery with an optional stable id:

Gallery()
Gallery(id: 1001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Treat Gallery as compatibility UI. New browsing interfaces are usually better served by RecyclerView or another modern layout that is designed for current Android patterns.

docs.title: GridLayout
docs.text:
GridLayout places children in a fixed grid of rows and columns. It fits small, known structures: keypads, settings groups, two-column fact rows, and dashboards where the cell count is decided at layout time.

Each child gets a rowSpec and columnSpec that say where it starts, how wide/tall it is, and how it aligns inside the cell. The parent can also set overall row/column counts and whether missing cells keep Android’s default margins.

For large or dynamic collections, prefer a recycled list instead. GridLayout is for compact, intentional matrices.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use GridLayout when the screen shows a small, fixed matrix of controls or labels and you want each cell positioned explicitly.

Do not use it for infinite grids, adapter-driven feeds, or masonry layouts. Those need a recycled or custom layout strategy.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Children occupy cells described by rowSpec(...) / columnSpec(...). Overloads accept start, optional size, optional weight, and optional alignment.

The grid itself exposes live configuration: rowCount, columnCount, orientation, alignmentMode, useDefaultMargins, and row/column order preservation. Matching set* methods are immediate void calls on the native grid.

GridLayout.Alignment controls how a child sits inside its cell. The exposed cases are leading, trailing, top, bottom, start, end, left, right, center, baseline, and fill.

docs.title: Build a 2×2 action grid
docs.text:
GridLayout {
    Button("A")
        .rowSpec(start: 0)
        .columnSpec(start: 0)
    Button("B")
        .rowSpec(start: 0)
        .columnSpec(start: 1)
    Button("C")
        .rowSpec(start: 1)
        .columnSpec(start: 0)
    Button("D")
        .rowSpec(start: 1)
        .columnSpec(start: 1)
}
.padding(16)

Four equal buttons appear in a 2×2 matrix.

docs.title: Lay out a two-column info block
docs.text:
GridLayout {
    TextView("Name")
        .rowSpec(start: 0)
        .columnSpec(start: 0)
    TextView("Mihael")
        .rowSpec(start: 0, alignment: .leading)
        .columnSpec(start: 1)

    TextView("Version")
        .rowSpec(start: 1)
        .columnSpec(start: 0)
    TextView("1.0")
        .rowSpec(start: 1, alignment: .leading)
        .columnSpec(start: 1)
}
.padding(16)

Labels and values line up in two columns.

docs.title: Size a grid and span a cell
docs.text:
let grid = GridLayout {
    TextView("Header")
        .rowSpec(start: 0, size: 1)
        .columnSpec(start: 0, size: 2)
    Button("Left")
        .rowSpec(start: 1)
        .columnSpec(start: 0)
    Button("Right")
        .rowSpec(start: 1)
        .columnSpec(start: 1)
}

grid.setRowCount(2)
grid.setColumnCount(2)
grid.setUseDefaultMargins(true)

The header spans both columns. setRowCount / setColumnCount / setUseDefaultMargins are void calls that configure the live grid.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
GridLayout()

GridLayout(id: 1001)

GridLayout(id: 1001) {
    // children
}

Pass an id when other code must find the grid later. The content block is the ordinary Droid view builder.

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
Place children with rowSpec and columnSpec. Overloads combine start, size, weight, and alignment:

TextView("A")
    .rowSpec(start: 0, size: 1, alignment: .fill, weight: 1)
    .columnSpec(start: 0, size: 1, alignment: .center, weight: 1)

TextView("B")
    .rowSpec(start: 1, weight: 2)
    .columnSpec(start: 1, alignment: .end)

start is zero-based. size is the span. weight distributes extra space. alignment is a GridLayout.Alignment case.

docs.title: Grid counts and orientation
docs.text:
rowCount() / setRowCount(_:) and columnCount() / setColumnCount(_:) read or set the grid size. orientation() / setOrientation(_:) read or set layout orientation.

grid.setRowCount(3)
grid.setColumnCount(2)
grid.setOrientation(orientation)

The setters are immediate void calls.

docs.title: Alignment mode and default margins
docs.text:
alignmentMode() / setAlignmentMode(_:) control cell alignment rules. useDefaultMargins() / setUseDefaultMargins(_:) toggle Android’s default cell margins.

grid.setAlignmentMode(mode)
grid.setUseDefaultMargins(true)

docs.title: Order preservation
docs.text:
isRowOrderPreserved() / setRowOrderPreserved(_:) and isColumnOrderPreserved() / setColumnOrderPreserved(_:) decide whether undefined cells keep declared order.

grid.setRowOrderPreserved(true)
grid.setColumnOrderPreserved(true)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: rowSpec / columnSpec are layout params on the child, not methods on the grid. Configure the grid with its set* methods before measurement when counts or margins must be exact.

docs.title: GridView
docs.text:
GridView is Android’s two-dimensional adapter-backed grid.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; column count, spacing, stretch mode, and adapter APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use GridView when the screen needs the classic Android grid widget and will grow into adapter-backed cells later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
GridView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose numColumns(_:), horizontalSpacing(_:), verticalSpacing(_:), stretchMode(_:), adapter(_:), or selection helpers at this pin.

docs.title: Place a grid container
docs.text:
GridView(id: 2201)
    .padding(h: 8, v: 8)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
GridView()
GridView(id: 2201)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s GridView is defined by columns, spacing, and its adapter. None of that is part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: HSpace
docs.text:
HSpace creates an empty horizontal gap with an explicit width. HSpace(16), for example, means a 16 dp gap because the unit defaults to .dp.

Its default weight is 0, so it behaves as a fixed-width spacer unless you deliberately give it weight. Use Space when the gap should be flexible by default rather than start from a chosen width.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use HSpace in a row when the horizontal distance between neighboring views is part of the design: between an icon and a label, between buttons, or between compact groups that should keep a predictable separation.

Choose Space() instead when the important behavior is "consume the room that is left" rather than "leave this much room here."

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The width is required. You can provide it as an integer dimension or as a layout-size value, and the unit defaults to .dp.

Weight defaults to 0. If you pass a nonzero weight:, the spacer also participates in the parent's compatible horizontal weight distribution; the final allocation then depends on that layout rather than on the width alone.

docs.title: Keep a 16 dp gap
docs.text:
No unit is needed for the common dp case:

body {
    HStack {
        TextView("Filter")
        HSpace(16)
        Button("Apply")
    }
}

The label and button remain separated by the explicit horizontal spacer instead of relying on either view's padding.

docs.title: Let the gap participate in weight distribution
docs.text:
A weighted HSpace is useful when you still want to declare a horizontal dimension while allowing a compatible parent to distribute extra room by weight.

body {
    HStack {
        TextView("Details")
        HSpace(8, weight: 1)
        Button("Open")
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
}

For a spacer whose normal job is to absorb remaining room, Space communicates that intent more directly.

docs.title: HStack
docs.text:
Horizontal container view used to arrange child views in a left-to-right order.

It is a thin, convenience wrapper around Android’s LinearLayout with its orientation fixed to .horizontal. Its purpose is to make horizontal layouts concise, readable, and familiar to Swift developers.

body {
    HStack {
        TextView("Some Text")
            .width(.wrapContent)
            .height(.wrapContent)
        Button("Tap Me")
            .width(.wrapContent)
            .height(48, .dp)
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(.wrapContent)
    .gravityForSubviews(.center)
    .padding(16, .dp)
}

All child views are laid out horizontally in the order they are declared.

docs.title: HorizontalScrollView
docs.text:
HorizontalScrollView is Android’s classic horizontal scrolling container.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; child content, scroll commands, and scroll-state callbacks are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use HorizontalScrollView when a row of content should scroll sideways and you need the classic Android control name in the hierarchy.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
HorizontalScrollView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

Unlike ScrollView at this pin, it does not offer a content initializer and is not a ViewGroup subclass in the current Droid type. Horizontal scroll commands and smooth scrolling are not wrapped.

docs.title: Place a horizontal scroller
docs.text:
HorizontalScrollView(id: 2401)
    .padding(h: 0, v: 8)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
HorizontalScrollView()
HorizontalScrollView(id: 2401)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s HorizontalScrollView owns horizontal scrolling of its child. That child-content and scroll API is not part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: ImageButton
docs.text:
ImageButton is the image-only button control.

In the current Droid source pin it inherits ImageView and adds no extra wrapped methods. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; image sources and button chrome are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ImageButton when an image is the visual surface of an action, such as a toolbar icon button.

For display-only image content, use ImageView.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ImageButton behaves like the current ImageView shell: placeable in the hierarchy, with onClick(_:), padding, enabled(_:), and visibility(_:).

Image assignment and tinting are not part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: Place an icon action
docs.text:
ImageButton(id: 1901)
    .onClick {
        // handle the action
    }

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ImageButton()
ImageButton(id: 1901)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: There is no image-source API on this type at the current pin. Wire content when the image wrappers grow, then document the real methods here.

docs.title: ImageSwitcher
docs.text:
ImageSwitcher is Android’s two-view control for switching between images.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; image setters, factory bridges, and switcher animations are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ImageSwitcher when the screen needs a dedicated control that will later switch images with Android’s built-in two-view behavior.

For a single image slot, use ImageView.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ImageSwitcher participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit ViewSwitcher / ViewAnimator APIs. It does not expose imageDrawable(_:), imageResource(_:), imageURI(_:), factory(_:), or animation helpers at this pin.

docs.title: Place an image switcher
docs.text:
ImageSwitcher(id: 2001)

ImageSwitcher()
ImageSwitcher(id: 2001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s ImageSwitcher depends on factory callbacks and image sources. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: ImageView
docs.text:
ImageView displays image content in the view hierarchy.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work. A ScaleType enum is declared, but drawable/resource/URI assignment, tinting, and bounds helpers are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use ImageView for avatars, icons, thumbnails, and illustrations that belong inside a layout.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ImageView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose imageDrawable(_:), imageResource(_:), imageURI(_:), imageIcon(_:), imageTintList(_:), adjustViewBounds(_:), scaleType(_:), maxWidth(_:), or maxHeight(_:) at this pin.

docs.title: Place an image slot
docs.text:
ImageView(id: 1801)
    .padding(h: 8, v: 8)

docs.title: Hide a missing avatar slot
docs.text:
let avatar = ImageView(id: 1802)
    .visibility(.gone)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ImageView()
ImageView(id: 1801)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The nested ImageView.ScaleType cases exist in the Swift surface at this pin, but no Droid method currently applies a scale type to a live view. Image-source APIs are not available yet.

docs.title: LinearLayout
docs.text:
LinearLayout arranges children along one axis: vertically as a column or horizontally as a row.

It is a practical choice for forms, settings sections, button rows, and other layouts whose structure is naturally one-dimensional.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use LinearLayout when the content can be described as a row or a column and children do not need to overlap.

For overlay content, use FrameLayout. For more complex relationships between views, use a layout that supports explicit constraints or relative rules.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
orientation(_:) selects vertical or horizontal flow. In a vertical layout children are placed from top to bottom; in a horizontal layout they are placed from start to end.

Child weight(_:) values distribute remaining space between weighted children. Container methods such as gravityForSubviews(_:) and showDividers(_:) configure how the layout presents its children.

docs.title: Build a vertical account section
docs.text:
LinearLayout {
    TextView("Account")
        .textSize(18)

    TextView("Signed in as mihael@example.com")
        .textSize(12)
        .textColor(.lightGray)
}
.orientation(.vertical)
.padding(16)

The labels appear one below the other in declaration order.

docs.title: Give one item the remaining width
docs.text:
LinearLayout {
    TextView("Storage")
        .weight(1)

    TextView("2.1 GB")
}
.orientation(.horizontal)
.padding(16)

The Storage label receives the remaining horizontal space, leaving the value at the end of the row.

docs.title: Create two equal-width actions
docs.text:
LinearLayout {
    Button("Cancel")
        .width(0)
        .weight(1)

    Button("Save")
        .width(0)
        .weight(1)
}
.orientation(.horizontal)
.padding(16)

Both buttons request the same weight, so they share the available row width evenly.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Create an empty layout, provide children directly, or assign an id when a stable reference is useful:

LinearLayout()

LinearLayout {
    TextView("Child")
}

LinearLayout(id: 1001)

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
Layout params such as weight(_:) and gravityInParent(_:) are applied to children inside the LinearLayout.

LinearLayout {
    TextView("Left")
        .weight(1)

    TextView("Right")
}
.orientation(.horizontal)

docs.title: Choose the orientation
docs.text:
orientation(_:) switches between vertical and horizontal child flow.

LinearLayout {
    TextView("First")
    TextView("Second")
}
.orientation(.vertical)

docs.title: Align the children
docs.text:
gravityForSubviews(_:) controls how children are aligned within unused space in the layout.

LinearLayout {
    TextView("Centered")
}
.orientation(.vertical)
.gravityForSubviews(.centerHorizontal)

docs.title: Control divider positions
docs.text:
showDividers(_:) selects where the layout shows its configured child dividers.

LinearLayout {
    TextView("Profile")
    TextView("Notifications")
    TextView("About")
}
.orientation(.vertical)
.showDividers(.middle)

docs.title: ListPopupWindow
docs.text:
ListPopupWindow is a dropdown list anchored to a view. Android uses it for spinner-style choices, autocomplete panels, and any compact list that should appear next to the control that triggered it.

In Droid, ListPopupWindow is a live object wrapper. It is not a view you place in a layout builder. You receive an existing android.widget.ListPopupWindow from Android, then configure its anchor, size, adapter, and selection from Swift.

Every setter and action runs immediately on the wrapped Android object. There is no queued layout-property pipeline because this type is not a Droid View subclass.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ListPopupWindow when another Android API hands you a real popup list and you need to show, dismiss, or reconfigure that dropdown from Swift.

Do not use it as a general list screen. For large or persistent collections, use a list destination or a recycled list component.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The popup attaches to an anchor view. Width, height, and pixel offsets control how the dropdown fits under that anchor. Gravity and overlap settings decide alignment when space is tight.

Items come from an Android ListAdapter. Selection APIs read or move the highlighted row, and listView() returns the internal list once Android has created one.

Show and dismiss are live operations. show() opens immediately; postShow() posts the show work to the Android UI thread. dismiss() uses the usual dismiss path; dismissImmediate() closes the popup immediately without that usual path. isShowing() reports current visibility.

Item-click, item-selected, and dismiss listeners accept Android/JNI-compatible listener objects. Droid does not wrap those events in Swift closures.

docs.title: Open a dropdown under a text field
docs.text:
func showChoices(_ popup: ListPopupWindow, anchor: View) {
    popup
        .anchorView(anchor)
        .modal(true)
        .width(320)
        .horizontalOffset(8)

    popup.show()
}

The list appears under the field and closes when the user taps outside.

docs.title: Move selection from application state
docs.text:
func selectSecondRow(_ popup: ListPopupWindow) {
    popup.selection(1)
}

func readSelection(_ popup: ListPopupWindow) -> Int {
    popup.selectedItemPosition()
}

selection(_:) highlights a row. selectedItemPosition() reports the current index.

docs.title: Close after a commit
docs.text:
func onRowChosen(_ popup: ListPopupWindow) {
    popup.dismiss()
}

Dismiss the dropdown as soon as the user commits so the anchor control is usable again.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ListPopupWindow(androidObject)

The initializer accepts an existing JNI object for android.widget.ListPopupWindow. Droid does not construct this popup from an activity context or a view-builder block.

docs.title: Popup lifecycle
docs.text:
show() opens the dropdown. postShow() schedules showing on the Android message queue. dismiss() closes it. dismissImmediate() closes without the usual animation path. isShowing() reports visibility.

popup.show()
popup.postShow()
popup.dismiss()
popup.dismissImmediate()

docs.title: Anchor and geometry
docs.text:
anchorView() reads the anchor. anchorView(_:) sets it. Width, height, and offsets are available as width, height, horizontalOffset, and verticalOffset getters/setters. contentWidth(_:) sets content width. dropDownGravity(_:) and overlapAnchor(_:) tune alignment.

popup
    .anchorView(button)
    .width(320)
    .height(240)
    .horizontalOffset(8)
    .verticalOffset(0)

docs.title: Adapter, selection, and internal list
docs.text:
adapter(_:) accepts a JNI-compatible Android ListAdapter. selection(_:) selects a row. clearListSelection() clears the highlight. selectedItem(), selectedItemId(), selectedItemPosition(), and selectedView() read selection state. listView() returns the live internal View? wrapping Android’s list when available.

popup.adapter(listAdapter)
popup.selection(0)

let index = popup.selectedItemPosition()
let list = popup.listView()

docs.title: Styling and input behavior
docs.text:
backgroundDrawable(_:) sets the popup background. animationStyle(_:) sets the enter/exit animation. inputMethodMode(_:) and softInputMode(_:) control IME behavior. listSelector(_:) sets the row selector drawable. promptPosition(_:) / promptView(_:) configure the optional prompt. epicenterBounds(_:) and windowLayoutType(_:) tune window placement. modal(_:), dropDownAlwaysVisible(_:), and forceIgnoreOutsideTouch(_:) adjust outside-touch behavior.

popup
    .modal(true)
    .animationStyle(style)
    .listSelector(selector)

docs.title: Listeners
docs.text:
onDismissListener(_:), onItemClickListener(_:), and onItemSelectedListener(_:) attach Android-compatible listener objects.

popup.onDismissListener(dismissListener)
popup.onItemClickListener(clickListener)
popup.onItemSelectedListener(selectedListener)

docs.title: Keyboard and drag-to-open helpers
docs.text:
onKeyDown(_:_:), onKeyUp(_:_:), and onKeyPreIme(_:_:) forward key events to the live popup. performItemClick(_:) invokes a popup item by position. createDragToOpenListener(_:) returns Android’s drag-to-open touch-listener object when available.

let handled = popup.performItemClick(0)
let dragListener = popup.createDragToOpenListener(anchor)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Configure anchor and adapter before the first show(). Use isShowing() before relying on listView() or selection reads so Android has created the internal list.

docs.title: ListView
docs.text:
ListView is Android’s classic vertical adapter-backed list.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; adapter assignment, headers/footers, dividers, selection, and scroll helpers are not wrapped yet.

For new highly customized lists, RecyclerView is usually more flexible. ListView remains the name for classic Android list behavior.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use ListView when you need the classic Android list widget name in the hierarchy and will fill it later as the wrapper grows.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ListView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose adapter(_:), header/footer APIs, divider configuration, selection(_:), smooth scrolling, or list listeners at this pin.

docs.title: Place a list container
docs.text:
ListView(id: 1301)
    .padding(h: 0, v: 0)

docs.title: Show an empty list area while data loads
docs.text:
ListView(id: 1302)
    .enabled(false)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ListView()
ListView(id: 1301)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s ListView is defined by its adapter and row behavior. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: Magnifier
docs.text:
Magnifier shows a floating loupe over the screen so the user can see a zoomed copy of content under their finger. It is the same interaction Android uses when text becomes hard to read while selecting or dragging.

In Droid, Magnifier is a live object wrapper. It is not a view you drop into a layout builder. You receive an existing android.widget.Magnifier from Android, then show, move, zoom, and dismiss that loupe from Swift.

Because the loupe is a temporary overlay, treat it as interaction chrome rather than permanent UI. It appears near the finger, magnifies a source region, and disappears when the gesture ends.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use Magnifier when custom drag, selection, or precision controls need a platform-style zoom bubble over the touched content.

Skip it for ordinary zoom buttons or full-screen magnification. Those are better handled with layout scale, a dedicated zoom surface, or accessibility magnification.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
show places the loupe over a source point and optionally moves the magnified image to a center point. While it is visible, update() refreshes the captured content and position as the finger moves. dismiss() removes it.
