zoom controls magnification. Geometry getters report the current source rectangle, loupe size, position, elevation, and default offsets Android uses when you do not override the center.

content() returns the magnified bitmap when Android has one. originalContent() returns the unzoomed capture. overlay() returns the drawable used as the loupe chrome.

isClippingEnabled() reports whether the source is clipped to the window bounds. setOnOperationCompleteCallback attaches an Android callback object for show/update/dismiss completion events.

docs.title: Show a loupe during a drag
docs.text:
func onDragMove(_ magnifier: Magnifier, x: Float, y: Float) {
    magnifier.show(x, y)
    magnifier.update()
}

The loupe follows the finger and keeps the magnified region in sync.

docs.title: Pin the magnified image while the source moves
docs.text:
func onPrecisionDrag(_ magnifier: Magnifier, x: Float, y: Float) {
    magnifier.show(x, y, 240, 120)
}

Android samples the source near (x, y) and draws the zoomed image near the requested center.

docs.title: Finish the gesture cleanly
docs.text:
func onDragEnd(_ magnifier: Magnifier) {
    magnifier.dismiss()
}

func tuneZoom(_ magnifier: Magnifier) {
    magnifier.setZoom(2.5)
}

dismiss() ends the overlay. setZoom(_:) changes magnification before the next show.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Magnifier(androidObject)

The initializer accepts an existing JNI object for android.widget.Magnifier. Droid does not construct a magnifier from a view-builder block.

docs.title: Show and dismiss
docs.text:
show(_:_:) opens the loupe at source coordinates. show(_:_:_:_:) also places the magnified image at a requested center. update() refreshes content and position. dismiss() closes the loupe.

magnifier.show(x, y)
magnifier.update()
magnifier.dismiss()

Call update() during a continuous gesture so the preview does not freeze.

docs.title: Zoom
docs.text:
zoom() reads the current magnification. setZoom(_:) changes it and returns the same magnifier for chaining.

let current = magnifier.zoom()
magnifier.setZoom(3.0)

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
sourceWidth(), sourceHeight(), and sourcePosition() describe the sampled region. width(), height(), and position() describe the loupe itself. cornerRadius() and elevation() report the chrome styling Android applies.

let source = magnifier.sourcePosition()
let loupeSize = magnifier.width()

defaultHorizontalSourceToMagnifierOffset() and defaultVerticalSourceToMagnifierOffset() return the offsets Android uses when the loupe center is not overridden.

docs.title: Content and overlay
docs.text:
content() returns the magnified bitmap when available. originalContent() returns the pre-zoom capture. overlay() returns the drawable used as loupe background.

if let bitmap = magnifier.content() {
    // inspect the magnified frame
}

magnifierDefaultSize() returns Android’s default loupe size. Both instance and class forms are available.

docs.title: Clipping and callbacks
docs.text:
isClippingEnabled() reports whether source sampling is clipped. setOnOperationCompleteCallback(_:) attaches a JNI-compatible callback object for operation completion.

magnifier.setOnOperationCompleteCallback(callback)

The callback must already be an Android-compatible listener object.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The loupe is gesture chrome. Create or obtain the native Magnifier through the Android API that owns the interaction, then drive it with these methods for the lifetime of the gesture.

docs.title: MediaController
docs.text:
MediaController is Android’s classic media playback control panel.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control with an additional existing-object initializer. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; player attachment, show/hide, and transport controls are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use MediaController when the screen needs the classic Android media controller name and player APIs can land later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
MediaController participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose setMediaPlayer(_:), setAnchorView(_:), show(), hide(), or transport button wiring at this pin.

docs.title: Place a media controller
docs.text:
MediaController(id: 3501)
    .padding(h: 0, v: 0)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
MediaController()
MediaController(id: 3501)
MediaController(id: 3501, existingObject) { activityContext }

The third form wraps an already-created Android MediaController object and a context link.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s MediaController drives a MediaPlayer / VideoView. That binding surface is not part of the current Droid API.

docs.title: Menu
docs.text:
Menu contains the actions shown by an Activity options menu, including toolbar actions and overflow items.

Build the menu from the Activity lifecycle, update state-dependent items before display, and handle selections separately.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a menu for a small set of screen-level actions such as Refresh, Search, Share, or Settings.

Keep primary workflow actions in the screen itself when hiding them in overflow would make the interface harder to discover.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
onCreateOptionsMenu(menu:) is the normal place to create items. Android can call onPrepareOptionsMenu(menu:) again before display, which makes it suitable for state-dependent changes.

Selections arrive through onOptionsItemSelected(item:).

docs.title: Add toolbar and overflow actions
docs.text:
override func onCreateOptionsMenu(menu: Menu) -> Bool {
    menu.add("Search").showAsAction(.always)
    menu.add("Settings").showAsAction(.never)
    return true
}

docs.title: Rebuild state-dependent items
docs.text:
override func onPrepareOptionsMenu(menu: Menu) -> Bool {
    menu.clear()
    menu.add(isConnected ? "Disconnect" : "Connect")
    return true
}

docs.title: Add a submenu
docs.text:
override func onCreateOptionsMenu(menu: Menu) -> Bool {
    let more = menu.addSubMenu("More")
    more?.add("Help")
    more?.add("About")
    return true
}

docs.title: Add an item
docs.text:
Use add(_:) for a title-only item, or the identified form when later code needs a stable id.

menu.add("Refresh")
menu.add(groupId: 0, itemId: 100, order: 0, title: "Settings")

docs.title: Add a submenu
docs.text:
let more = menu.addSubMenu("More")
more?.add("Help")

docs.title: Clear or find items
docs.text:
menu.clear()

let settings = menu.findItem(100)

docs.title: MultiAutoCompleteTextView
docs.text:
MultiAutoCompleteTextView is Android’s multi-token completion field.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; tokenizers, adapters, and completion APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use MultiAutoCompleteTextView when the field should complete multiple tokens and those APIs can land later.

For a single completion field, see AutoCompleteTextView.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
MultiAutoCompleteTextView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit EditText at this pin and does not expose adapter(_:), tokenizer(_:), setThreshold(_:), or dropdown helpers.

docs.title: Place a multi-token field
docs.text:
MultiAutoCompleteTextView(id: 4001)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
MultiAutoCompleteTextView()
MultiAutoCompleteTextView(id: 4001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s MultiAutoCompleteTextView completes each token after a tokenizer boundary. That surface is not part of the current Droid API.

docs.title: NumberPicker
docs.text:
NumberPicker is Android’s wheel control for choosing a value from a bounded range or a short label list.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; min/max/value, wrapping, displayed labels, and listeners are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a number picker when the user should choose one value from a small, obvious range and a wheel feels faster than typing.

For free numeric input, use EditText. For one-of-few named options, a radio group or spinner-shaped control is usually clearer.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
NumberPicker participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose minValue(_:), maxValue(_:), value(_:), wrapSelectorWheel(_:), displayedValues(_:), formatters, or value-change listeners at this pin.

docs.title: Place a quantity control
docs.text:
NumberPicker(id: 4001)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Disable it until a range is known
docs.text:
NumberPicker(id: 4002)
    .enabled(false)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
NumberPicker()
NumberPicker(id: 4001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s NumberPicker owns range, wrapping, and displayed labels. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: OverScroller
docs.text:
OverScroller is Android’s fling and scroll-physics helper. It is not a widget you place on screen; it computes animated coordinates that custom scrolling code then applies.

Droid does not expose an OverScroller wrapper in the current source pin. The type and its methods are not part of the public Swift surface yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Do not plan screen work against Droid OverScroller until a wrapper lands in a source release and this page documents a verified method set.

For ordinary scrolling containers, use ScrollView or a layout that already scrolls.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
There is no Droid OverScroller type to construct, no startScroll / fling / computeScrollOffset API to call, and no existing-object initializer for this helper at the current pin.

Android upstream documents a rich scroller API. That upstream surface must not be treated as available from Droid.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Earlier drafts of this page described wrapper methods that were never part of the pinned Droid source. Those claims were removed on purpose. This entry will grow only after OverScroller appears in a commit pin with real methods.

docs.title: PopupMenu
docs.text:
PopupMenu shows a small anchored list of menu items above or below a view. Android uses this pattern for overflow actions, row menus, and compact “more” controls that should not take over the whole screen.

In Droid, PopupMenu is a live object wrapper. It is not a layout node. You receive an existing android.widget.PopupMenu from Android, configure gravity, inflate or build items, then show() and dismiss() that popup from Swift.

Keep it for short action lists tied to a specific anchor. For full-screen navigation or long scrolling choices, use a dialog, sheet, or list screen instead.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use PopupMenu when a button or row needs a compact list of actions that appear next to the control the user just tapped.

Do not use it as a general menu system. If every screen needs the same top-level destinations, prefer an app bar menu or navigation drawer.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The popup anchors to the view Android associates with it. gravity(_:) controls how the list aligns relative to that anchor. show() displays the popup; dismiss() closes it.

Items come from a Menu?. You can inflate a menu resource with inflate(_:), or obtain menu() and work with the live menu object when it exists. forceShowIcon keeps item icons visible even when Android would normally hide them.

menuListView() returns a View? wrapping the internal list once Android has created it. dragToOpenListener() returns Android’s drag-to-open touch listener so a long drag on the anchor can open the same popup.

Dismiss and item-click listeners accept Android/JNI-compatible listener objects. Droid does not wrap those events in Swift closures.

docs.title: Show actions from a row button
docs.text:
func showRowActions(_ popup: PopupMenu) {
    popup.show()
}

Tapping the row’s “more” control displays the menu anchored to that button.

docs.title: Align and force icons
docs.text:
func configureOverflow(_ popup: PopupMenu) {
    popup
        .gravity(0)
        .forceShowIcon(true)

    popup.show()
}

The list stays icon-visible for scanable action rows.

docs.title: Dismiss after a command
docs.text:
func onCommandChosen(_ popup: PopupMenu) {
    popup.dismiss()
}

Close the popup as soon as the user commits to an action so the anchor control does not stay covered.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
PopupMenu(androidObject)

The initializer accepts an existing JNI object for android.widget.PopupMenu. Droid does not build a popup menu from a view-builder block.

docs.title: Show and dismiss
docs.text:
show() opens the menu. dismiss() closes it.

popup.show()
popup.dismiss()

docs.title: Gravity
docs.text:
gravity() reads the current alignment. gravity(_:) sets alignment relative to the anchor and returns the same popup for chaining.

popup.gravity(0)

docs.title: Menu content
docs.text:
menu() returns the live Menu?. inflate(_:) fills the popup from a menu resource id. forceShowIcon(_:) keeps icons visible. menuInflater() returns Android’s inflater for this popup.

popup.inflate(menuResId)
popup.forceShowIcon(true)

if let menu = popup.menu() {
    menu.add("Rename")
}

docs.title: Internal list and drag-to-open
docs.text:
menuListView() returns the popup’s ListView when available. dragToOpenListener() returns the touch listener that opens the popup on drag.

let list = popup.menuListView()
let dragListener = popup.dragToOpenListener()

docs.title: Listeners
docs.text:
onDismissListener(_:) attaches a JNI-compatible dismiss listener. onMenuItemClickListener(_:) attaches a JNI-compatible item-click listener.

popup.onDismissListener(dismissListener)
popup.onMenuItemClickListener(clickListener)

Both methods accept Android-compatible listener objects, not Swift closures.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Icons stay optional unless you call forceShowIcon(true). Close the popup after a committed action so the user can continue interacting with the underlying screen.

docs.title: PopupWindow
docs.text:
PopupWindow is a floating panel that sits above the current window. Android uses it for tooltips, custom dropdowns, lightweight editors, and any UI that must appear near a control without replacing the screen.

In Droid, PopupWindow is a live object wrapper. It is not a layout node. You receive an existing android.widget.PopupWindow from Android, set its content and window flags, then show it at a location or drop it under an anchor.

Prefer this when the panel is temporary and tightly coupled to a control on screen. For full workflows, use a dialog fragment or a separate destination.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use PopupWindow when a custom floating panel must appear over the current UI: anchored dropdowns, suggestion cards, or compact editors.

Do not use it when the user needs a full form or long scrolling content. Those belong in dialogs or dedicated screens.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The popup hosts one content view. contentView(_:) assigns that view; width and height size the window. showAsDropDown places it under an anchor, while showAtLocation places it at a gravity-relative point.

Window flags decide focus and touch behavior. A focusable popup can take keyboard input; outsideTouchable and touchModal control whether touches outside dismiss or pass through. clippingEnabled keeps the popup on screen.

isShowing() reports visibility. dismiss() closes the popup. onDismissListener and touchInterceptor accept Android/JNI-compatible listener objects rather than Swift closures.

docs.title: Drop a panel under a button
docs.text:
func showTooltip(_ popup: PopupWindow, _ anchor: View) {
    popup
        .contentView(tooltipView)
        .width(280)
        .height(120)
        .focusable(true)
        .outsideTouchable(true)

    popup.showAsDropDown(anchor)
}

The panel appears under the button and closes when the user taps outside.

docs.title: Place a popup at a parent origin
docs.text:
func showNearParentOrigin(_ popup: PopupWindow, _ parent: View) {
    popup
        .contentView(card)
        .width(320)
        .height(200)

    popup.showAtLocation(parent, 0, 0, 0)
}

Android positions the popup relative to parent using the supplied gravity and offsets.

docs.title: Dismiss after a choice
docs.text:
func onOptionPicked(_ popup: PopupWindow) {
    popup.dismiss()
}

Close the popup once the user commits so the underlying screen stays interactive.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
PopupWindow(androidObject)

The initializer accepts an existing JNI object for android.widget.PopupWindow. Droid does not build a popup window from a view-builder block.

docs.title: Show and dismiss
docs.text:
showAsDropDown(_:) anchors the popup under a view. showAsDropDown(_:_:_:) adds pixel offsets. showAsDropDown(_:_:_:_:) also applies gravity. showAtLocation(_:_:_:_:) places the popup at a gravity-relative point. dismiss() closes it.

popup.showAsDropDown(anchor)
popup.showAsDropDown(anchor, 0, 8)
popup.dismiss()

isShowing() reports whether the popup is currently visible.

docs.title: Content and size
docs.text:
contentView() reads the hosted view. contentView(_:) assigns it. width() / width(_:) and height() / height(_:) get or set window size. windowLayoutMode(widthSpec:heightSpec:) applies Android measure specs. background() reads the background drawable; backgroundDrawable(_:) sets it. elevation() / elevation(_:) get or set shadow elevation.

popup
    .contentView(panel)
    .width(300)
    .height(200)
    .elevation(8)

popup.backgroundDrawable(bg)
popup.windowLayoutMode(widthSpec: widthSpec, heightSpec: heightSpec)
let currentBg = popup.background()

docs.title: Focus, touch, and screen flags
docs.text:
focusable(_:) decides whether the popup takes keyboard focus. touchable, touchModal, and outsideTouchable shape hit testing. clippingEnabled, clipToScreenEnabled, isClippedToScreen, layoutInScreenEnabled, layoutInsetDecor, attachedInDecor, splitTouchEnabled, overlapAnchor, and dropDown tune window embedding.

popup
    .focusable(true)
    .outsideTouchable(true)
    .touchModal(false)

popup.clippingEnabled(true)
popup.overlapAnchor(true)
popup.dropDown(true)

Matching is* getters report the current flag values (isFocusable, isOutsideTouchable, isShowing, and the other flag reads exposed on this surface). isClippedToScreen is also a setter on this surface.

docs.title: Input and window type
docs.text:
inputMethodMode / softInputMode control IME behavior. windowLayoutType selects the Android window type used when the popup attaches.

popup
    .inputMethodMode(mode)
    .softInputMode(softMode)
    .windowLayoutType(layoutType)

docs.title: Geometry helpers
docs.text:
maxAvailableHeight(anchor:) and its offset variants report how much space remains below an anchor. updateAboveAnchor(_:) updates above-anchor state. createPopupLayoutParams and findDropDownPosition expose Android’s placement parameter helpers for advanced cases.

let available = popup.maxAvailableHeight(anchor: button, yOffset: 8)
popup.updateAboveAnchor(true)

let params = popup.createPopupLayoutParams(token)

docs.title: Transitions and listeners
docs.text:
enterTransition / exitTransition get or set Android transition objects. epicenterBounds / transitionEpicenter tune transition origin. onDismissListener(_:) attaches a JNI-compatible dismiss listener. touchInterceptor(_:) attaches a JNI-compatible touch interceptor.

popup.enterTransition(enter)
popup.exitTransition(exit)
popup.epicenterBounds(bounds)

popup.onDismissListener(dismissListener)
popup.touchInterceptor(interceptor)

Listeners are Android-compatible objects, not Swift closures.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Set contentView before the first show. A focusable popup should also consider outsideTouchable so the user can leave the panel without a dedicated close control.

docs.title: ProgressBar
docs.text:
ProgressBar shows work that is measurable or still open-ended.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; progress values, min/max bounds, and indeterminate mode are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use a progress bar when a screen should show that work is happening. A determinate bar is the usual choice once the operation can report a fraction; an indeterminate bar fits open-ended waits.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ProgressBar participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose setProgress(_:), max(_:), min(_:), secondaryProgress(_:), indeterminate(_:), or incremental update helpers at this pin.

docs.title: Place a progress indicator
docs.text:
ProgressBar(id: 1401)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Hide it when the operation finishes
docs.text:
let bar = ProgressBar(id: 1402)

// while working
bar.visibility(.visible)

// when done
bar.visibility(.gone)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ProgressBar()
ProgressBar(id: 1401)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s ProgressBar owns determinate/indeterminate state and numeric bounds. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: QuickContactBadge
docs.text:
QuickContactBadge is Android’s contact-affordance badge.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; contact assignment, mode filtering, and badge image APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use QuickContactBadge when the screen needs the classic Android contact badge and the contact APIs can land later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
QuickContactBadge participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose contact URI assignment, setExcludeMimes(_:), onClick(_:) contact dispatch helpers, or badge drawable APIs at this pin.

docs.title: Place a contact badge
docs.text:
QuickContactBadge(id: 2601)
    .padding(h: 8, v: 8)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
QuickContactBadge()
QuickContactBadge(id: 2601)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s QuickContactBadge launches QuickContact for a Contacts URI. That behavior is not part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: RadioButton
docs.text:
RadioButton is one option in a mutually exclusive choice.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; checked state, button tint, and group coordination are not wrapped on this type.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a radio button when the choice is one-of-many and the user should see the classic Android radio affordance.

For independent on/off options, see CheckBox. For group selection APIs, see RadioGroup.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
RadioButton participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

At this pin RadioButton inherits View only. It does not inherit CompoundButton and does not conform to Checkable. Methods such as checked(_:), isChecked(), toggle(), buttonTintList(_:), and buttonDrawable(_:) are not available on RadioButton.

docs.title: Place one option
docs.text:
RadioButton(id: 5001)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: React to a tap
docs.text:
let option = RadioButton(id: 5002)

option.onClick {
    // Handle activation. Checked-state reads/writes are not wrapped yet.
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
RadioButton()
RadioButton(id: 5001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s RadioButton is a CompoundButton. The current Droid type is not. Use CompoundButton when you need the verified Checkable methods (checked(_:), isChecked(), toggle()), and RadioGroup for group-level check(_:) / clearCheck() / checkedRadioButtonId().

docs.title: RadioGroup
docs.text:
RadioGroup keeps a small set of radio buttons mutually exclusive: selecting one option clears the previous selection.

It is useful for choices such as billing period, delivery speed, or a small list of modes where exactly one option should be active at a time.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use RadioGroup when the user needs to choose one item from a short, visible set of alternatives.

For independent on/off choices, use separate checkable controls instead. For a long or dynamic list, a recycled list with explicit selection state is usually a better fit.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Place RadioButton children inside the group and give each button a stable id when application code needs to select or identify it.

check(_:), clearCheck(), and checkedRadioButtonId() are live operations. Call them after the Android view has been realized.

The checked-change listener surface accepts an Android/JNI-compatible listener object. There is no Swift closure convenience for group selection changes in the current API.

docs.title: Build a billing-period choice
docs.text:
RadioGroup(id: 2000) {
    RadioButton(id: 2001)
        .text("Monthly")

    RadioButton(id: 2002)
        .text("Annual")

    RadioButton(id: 2003)
        .text("Lifetime")
}
.orientation(.vertical)

The group coordinates the three buttons so only one can remain selected.

docs.title: Select an option from application state
docs.text:
After the group is on screen, select a button by its id:

func chooseAnnualPlan(_ group: RadioGroup) {
    group.check(2002)
}

The button with id 2002 becomes the selected radio button.

docs.title: Read or clear the live selection
docs.text:
let selectedID = group.checkedRadioButtonId()

group.clearCheck()

checkedRadioButtonId() returns the current selected button id. clearCheck() removes the group's current selection.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Create an empty group, provide its radio buttons directly, or assign an id for later access:

RadioGroup()

RadioGroup {
    RadioButton(id: 2001)
        .text("Standard")
    RadioButton(id: 2002)
        .text("Express")
}

RadioGroup(id: 2000)

Use the inherited LinearLayout configuration when the options should be vertical or horizontal.

docs.title: Select a radio button
docs.text:
check(_:) selects the child radio button whose id matches the supplied value.

group.check(2002)

This is a live call, so use it after the native group exists.

docs.title: Clear the selection
docs.text:
clearCheck() removes the current checked radio button.

group.clearCheck()

Use it when the UI is allowed to return to a no-selection state.

docs.title: Read the selected id
docs.text:
checkedRadioButtonId() reads the id of the currently checked child from the live group.

let selectedID = group.checkedRadioButtonId()

The Android API uses -1 when no radio button is selected.

docs.title: Attach Android listener objects
docs.text:
onCheckedChangeListener(_:) configures an Android-compatible RadioGroup.OnCheckedChangeListener object.

group.onCheckedChangeListener(listener)

The listener can be configured before realization, but listener must already be a JNI-compatible listener object; this method does not accept a Swift closure.

onHierarchyChangeListener(_:) follows the same pattern for Android hierarchy-change listener objects.

docs.title: RatingBar
docs.text:
RatingBar is the classic star-rating control.

In the current Droid source pin it inherits AbsSeekBar and ProgressBar. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; rating, star count, step size, and indicator mode are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use RatingBar when the value is genuinely a rating and stars communicate the scale better than a plain number.

For an arbitrary numeric range, use SeekBar.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
RatingBar participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose rating(_:), numStars(_:), stepSize(_:), isIndicator(_:), or rating-change listeners at this pin.

docs.title: Place a rating control
docs.text:
RatingBar(id: 1701)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Show a read-only rating slot
docs.text:
RatingBar(id: 1702)
    .enabled(false)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
RatingBar()
RatingBar(id: 1701)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s RatingBar owns star count, step size, and indicator mode. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: RelativeLayout
docs.text:
RelativeLayout positions children using rules relative to the parent or to other sibling views, such as placing one view below another or aligning a child with a parent edge.

Sibling-relative rules use view ids as anchors, which makes this layout useful when a small number of relationships can be expressed directly.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use RelativeLayout when the layout has a small number of views and their relationships are easy to describe with parent and sibling rules.

For larger screens with many interdependent relationships, a constraint-based layout is usually easier to maintain.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Give an anchor view an explicit id, then refer to that id from sibling layout params such as below(_:), toEndOf(_:), or alignBaseline(_:).

Parent-relative helpers such as alignParentStart(), alignParentBottom(), centerHorizontal(), and centerVertical() do not need an anchor id.

docs.title: Place a subtitle below a title
docs.text:
RelativeLayout {
    TextView(id: 1, "Title")
        .alignParentTop()
        .alignParentStart()

    TextView("Subtitle")
        .below(1)
        .alignStart(1)
}
.padding(16)

The subtitle is positioned below the title and aligned to the title's start edge.

docs.title: Pin an action to the bottom center
docs.text:
RelativeLayout {
    Button("Continue")
        .alignParentBottom()
        .centerHorizontal()
        .marginBottom(16)
}
.width(.matchParent)
.height(220)

The button stays aligned with the parent's bottom edge and horizontal center.

docs.title: Align an action with a labeled row
docs.text:
RelativeLayout {
    TextView(id: 1, "Username")
        .alignParentStart()
        .centerVertical()

    Button("Edit")
        .toEndOf(1)
        .alignBaseline(1)
        .marginStart(12)
}
.padding(16)

The Edit button is placed after the Username label and shares its text baseline.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Create an empty layout or provide its children directly:

RelativeLayout()

RelativeLayout {
    TextView("Child")
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
Use parent-relative helpers when placement depends only on the container:

Button("Continue")
    .alignParentBottom()
    .centerHorizontal()

Use an explicit id when another child is the anchor:

TextView(id: 1, "Title")

TextView("Subtitle")
    .below(1)
    .alignStart(1)

docs.title: ScrollView
docs.text:
ScrollView is the classic Android scrolling container for one scrolling child.

In the current Droid source pin it is a ViewGroup with a single-child content initializer. You can build a scrolling stack through the hierarchy APIs. Scroll-state callbacks, smooth scrolling, and fillViewport-style controls are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ScrollView when a short screenful of content may grow taller than the device and should scroll as one block.

Do not put a vertically scrolling list widget inside it; use one scrolling strategy per axis.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ScrollView accepts declarative single-child content and participates in the view hierarchy. Shared view configuration such as onClick(_:), padding, enabled(_:), and visibility(_:) remains available.

The current type does not expose smoothScrollTo(_:_:), fullScroll(_:), arrowScroll(_:), isFillViewport(), or scroll-change listeners at this pin.

docs.title: Scroll a settings column
docs.text:
ScrollView(id: 2301) {
    LinearLayout(id: 2302) {
        TextView("Account")
        TextView("Privacy")
        TextView("About")
    }
}

The column becomes scrollable when it is taller than the viewport.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ScrollView()
ScrollView(id: 2301)

ScrollView(id: 2301) {
    // single child content via BodyBuilder
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text: Children use the shared view layout-param surface. The scroll view itself uses frame-style layout params at this pin.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Smooth-scroll and fill-viewport helpers from Android’s ScrollView are not part of the current Droid API. Place one primary scrolling child and size it through normal layout.

docs.title: SearchView
docs.text:
SearchView is Android’s dedicated search control: an expandable field for typing a query and submitting it.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; query, hint, iconify, suggestion, and searchable-info APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use SearchView when search is a first-class action on the screen and you want the familiar expand/collapse search chrome.

Do not use it as a generic text field. For free-form input, use EditText.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
SearchView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit LinearLayout. It does not expose query(_:), queryHint(_:), iconified(_:), submitButtonEnabled(_:), suggestion adapters, or listener bridges at this pin.

docs.title: Place a search entry point
docs.text:
SearchView(id: 3001)
    .padding(h: 12, v: 8)

The control is created and can sit in an app bar or search row.

docs.title: Keep it hidden until the user opens search
docs.text:
let search = SearchView(id: 3002)
    .visibility(.gone)

// later
search.visibility(.visible)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
SearchView()
SearchView(id: 3001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s SearchView can own query text, submit behavior, and suggestions. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: SeekBar
docs.text:
SeekBar is a draggable slider for choosing a value in a range, such as volume, brightness, or filter strength.

In the current Droid source pin it inherits AbsSeekBar and ProgressBar. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work. The declared progress(...) overloads and onSeekBarChangeListener(_:) exist as method names but are not wired to Android at this pin — do not rely on them.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use SeekBar when dragging is faster than typing an exact value and a slider communicates the range clearly.

For stars, use RatingBar. For a non-interactive meter, use ProgressBar.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
SeekBar participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

Range, thumb, tick, and live progress APIs from the Android seek family are not wrapped yet. In particular, min(_:) / max(_:) / setProgress(_:) are not available on this Droid type.

docs.title: Place a slider
docs.text:
SeekBar(id: 1601)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Disable scrubbing until media is ready
docs.text:
SeekBar(id: 1602)
    .enabled(false)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
SeekBar()
SeekBar(id: 1601)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
onSeekBarChangeListener(_:), progress(_:), and progress(_:animated:) are present in the Swift surface at this pin but their Android calls are not implemented. Treat them as unavailable until a later pin wires them.

Do not document or use SeekBarOnSeekBarChangeListener as a working callback bridge yet.

docs.title: ShareActionProvider
docs.text:
ShareActionProvider is the Android action provider that turns a menu item into the system share chooser.

Droid exposes the share-history file name and the share intent. Wrap the provider attached to a menu item, then set what should be shared. Visibility helpers come from ActionProvider.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ShareActionProvider when a menu item should open Android’s share sheet for text, a link, or other payload the user is currently viewing.

Do not use it for custom in-app share buttons that skip the system chooser.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The type wraps android.widget.ShareActionProvider and inherits ActionProvider behavior such as isVisible() and refreshVisibility().

shareIntent(_:) sets the payload Android offers to share targets. shareHistoryFileName(_:) names the file Android uses to remember target order; the default is ShareActionProvider.defaultShareHistoryFileName.

Configure these on a live provider after the menu item exists. The history file name can be set at any time, but only action views created afterward are backed by the new file.

docs.title: Share text from a menu item
docs.text:
func attachShare(to item: MenuItem, text: String) {
    guard let base = item.actionProvider() else { return }
    let provider = ShareActionProvider(base.object)

    if let intent = Intent(.send) {
        intent.putExtra("android.intent.extra.TEXT", text)
        intent.type("text/plain")
        provider.shareIntent(intent)
    }
}

Android opens the share sheet when the user activates that menu item.

docs.title: Persist share-target order
docs.text:
provider.shareHistoryFileName("article_share_history.xml")
provider.shareIntent(intent)

Targets the user picked before move toward the top of the chooser. Use the default name when a screen has one share payload:

provider.shareHistoryFileName(ShareActionProvider.defaultShareHistoryFileName)

docs.title: shareIntent(_:)
docs.text:
Sets the Android Intent that describes what to share.

provider.shareIntent(intent)

docs.title: shareHistoryFileName(_:)
docs.text:
Sets the file used to persist share-target history.

provider.shareHistoryFileName("share_history.xml")

docs.title: defaultShareHistoryFileName
docs.text:
Android’s default history file name (share_history.xml).

let name = ShareActionProvider.defaultShareHistoryFileName

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: setOnShareTargetSelectedListener is not wrapped yet. Build the share Intent with the regular Intent helpers (IntentActionType.send, putExtra(_:_), type(_:)).

docs.title: SlidingDrawer
docs.text:
SlidingDrawer is a legacy Android panel that stays collapsed behind a handle until the user opens it. Opening slides the content into view; closing slides it away again.

Droid exposes the drawer as a View you can build with a content block and then drive with live open / close / toggle calls. The native widget also tracks whether it is opened or currently moving, so application code can keep controls in sync with the panel.

Treat this component as a compatibility surface. Android deprecated SlidingDrawer because the interaction feels dated next to modern navigation drawers and bottom sheets. Prefer those patterns for new screens; keep SlidingDrawer only when a legacy design must keep its old open/close behavior.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use SlidingDrawer on a legacy screen that already depends on a handle-plus-panel metaphor and must keep that exact interaction after migrating to Droid.

Do not choose it for new navigation. For app-level navigation, use a modern drawer (for example Material NavigationView inside a drawer container). For temporary detail content, a bottom sheet or dialog is usually a better fit.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The drawer has two roles: a handle the user drags or taps, and content that appears when the drawer opens. After the native view is realized, handle() and content() return those child views when Android has assigned them.

open(), close(), and toggle() change state immediately. The animate* variants play the native open/close animation instead of jumping. lock() freezes interaction so the handle cannot change state; unlock() restores it.

isOpened() reports the current open state. isMoving() is true only while an open/close animation or drag is in flight. Use both when enabling buttons that would otherwise fight the animation.

Drawer listeners (onDrawerOpenListener, onDrawerCloseListener, onDrawerScrollListener) accept Android/JNI-compatible listener objects. They are live bridges: Droid does not wrap them in Swift closures.

docs.title: Open and close a settings panel
docs.text:
let drawer = SlidingDrawer(id: 1001) {
    // handle
    LinearLayout {
        ImageView()
            .width(48)
            .height(48)
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(48)

    // content
    LinearLayout {
        TextView("Quick settings")
        Switch(id: 1101)
            .text("Airplane mode")
    }
    .orientation(.vertical)
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(.matchParent)
    .padding(16)
}
.width(.matchParent)
.height(240)

drawer.open()

The panel slides out from behind the handle and shows the settings row. drawer.close() slides it away again.

docs.title: Toggle from a button and lock during load
docs.text:
func onHandleTap(_ drawer: SlidingDrawer) {
    guard !drawer.isMoving() else { return }
    drawer.animateToggle()
}

func refreshPanel(_ drawer: SlidingDrawer) {
    drawer.lock()
    // reload panel data here
    drawer.unlock()
}

animateToggle() keeps the native transition. isMoving() avoids stacking animations, and lock() prevents the user from opening the drawer while the panel reloads.

docs.title: Track open state after the drawer is realized
docs.text:
func syncChrome(_ drawer: SlidingDrawer, _ title: TextView) {
    if drawer.isOpened() {
        title.text("Details")
    } else {
        title.text("Tap the handle")
    }

    let handle = drawer.handle()
    let body = drawer.content()
}

Call these after Android has created the live drawer instance. handle() and content() return the live child views when they are available.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
SlidingDrawer()

SlidingDrawer(id: 1001)

SlidingDrawer(id: 1001) {
    // handle and content views
}

Pass a stable id when other code needs to find the drawer later. The content block is the ordinary Droid view builder used to place the drawer’s child views.

docs.title: Open, close, and toggle
docs.text:
open(), close(), and toggle() switch state immediately.

drawer.open()
drawer.toggle()
drawer.close()

Use the immediate forms when the UI must snap without animation.

docs.title: Animated open, close, and toggle
docs.text:
animateOpen(), animateClose(), and animateToggle() run the native drawer animation.

drawer.animateOpen()
drawer.animateToggle()

Prefer these for user-driven handle taps so the movement matches platform expectations.

docs.title: Lock and unlock
docs.text:
lock() disables drawer interaction. unlock() enables it again.

drawer.lock()
drawer.unlock()

Lock the drawer during short critical sections such as loading panel content.

docs.title: Read state and child views
docs.text:
isOpened() reports whether the drawer is open. isMoving() reports whether it is currently animating or being dragged. handle() and content() return the live handle and content views when Android has assigned them.

if drawer.isOpened() && !drawer.isMoving() {
    let panel = drawer.content()
}

docs.title: Drawer listeners
docs.text:
onDrawerOpenListener(_:), onDrawerCloseListener(_:), and onDrawerScrollListener(_:) attach Android-compatible listener objects for open, close, and scroll events.

drawer.onDrawerOpenListener(openListener)
drawer.onDrawerCloseListener(closeListener)
drawer.onDrawerScrollListener(scrollListener)

Each method accepts a JNI-compatible listener object. This surface does not take Swift closures.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Android deprecated SlidingDrawer. Keep it only for legacy parity; new screens should use modern drawer or sheet patterns instead.

The current Droid surface reads handle() and content() after native assignment. It does not expose separate handle/content setters.

docs.title: Space
docs.text:
Space() creates flexible empty room inside a layout. Use it when two pieces of content should move apart and the container, rather than a hard-coded gap, should decide how much room belongs between them.

A new Space() starts with weight 1. In a compatible weight-aware linear layout such as HStack or VStack, that makes the spacer eligible to take remaining space. When the gap has a deliberate horizontal or vertical size instead, use HSpace or VSpace.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use Space() between views that should stay anchored to opposite sides of the available room: a title and an action, a leading value and a trailing control, or two groups that should separate as the screen grows.

If the design calls for a specific gap such as 8 or 16 dp, prefer HSpace or VSpace. They make the direction and fixed dimension explicit; Space is the flexible choice.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Space contributes layout space without visible content. Its public initializer applies weight 1, so one spacer can absorb the remaining room in a compatible weighted parent.

When a layout contains more than one Space(), each starts with the same weight 1. They therefore participate in the parent's flexible-space distribution with equal weight.

docs.title: Push an action to the other side
docs.text:
Here the spacer expands between the title and button. As the row gets wider or narrower, the middle gap changes while the content stays at opposite sides.

body {
    HStack {
        TextView("Inbox")
        Space()
        Button("Compose")
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(.wrapContent)
}

docs.title: Split flexible space evenly
docs.text:
Both spacers start with weight 1, so they participate equally in distribution of the row's remaining flexible space.

body {
    HStack {
        TextView("Start")
        Space()
        TextView("Middle")
        Space()
        TextView("End")
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(.wrapContent)
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
When declaring a new spacer inline, keep Space() at its default weight. Chaining .weight(...) onto a newly constructed Space() does not replace that initializer-applied weight in the current API.

If a directional spacer needs an explicit construction-time weight, HSpace and VSpace expose weight: in their public initializers.

docs.title: Spinner
docs.text:
Spinner is Android’s compact single-choice control that shows the current option and opens a popup or dialog for the rest.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; adapter, prompt, dropdown geometry, and item-click APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a spinner when the user picks one value from a short set and keeping every option permanently visible would take too much space.

For always-visible exclusive choices, use RadioGroup.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Spinner participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose adapter(_:), prompt(_:), dropdown width/offsets, popup background, or item-click listeners. There is no Droid SpinnerAdapter type at this pin.

docs.title: Place a country or option picker
docs.text:
Spinner(id: 5001)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Disable the control while options load
docs.text:
Spinner(id: 5002)
    .enabled(false)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Spinner()
Spinner(id: 5001)

There is also a single-child content initializer:

Spinner(id: 5001) {
    // declarative child content via BodyBuilder
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s Spinner is defined by its adapter and dropdown. None of that adapter surface is part of the current Droid API. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: StackView
docs.text:
StackView is Android’s stacked-card browser for one item at a time.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view with a single-child content initializer. Shared view APIs work; adapter-backed stacking, advance/defer helpers, and stack animations are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use StackView when the screen should show a deck-like control and the adapter surface can come later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
StackView can take declarative single-child content and participates in the view hierarchy. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose adapter(_:), showNext(), showPrevious(), or stack-mode APIs at this pin.

docs.title: Place a stack control
docs.text:
StackView(id: 2501) {
    TextView("Card")
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
StackView()
StackView(id: 2501)

StackView(id: 2501) {
    // single child content via BodyBuilder
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s StackView is defined by its adapter and stack navigation. None of that is part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: SurfaceView
docs.text: SurfaceView provides a dedicated Android drawing surface. It is useful for content such as camera previews, video output, or custom rendering that benefits from a separate surface.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use SurfaceView when the rendered content should live on a dedicated surface and does not need to behave exactly like ordinary composited UI.

If transforms and view-hierarchy composition matter more than the dedicated-surface model, consider TextureView.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
A SurfaceView is backed by a separate surface layer. Normal inherited view APIs still control the wrapper's size and placement, while the rendered surface has its own lifecycle and rendering concerns.

Surface-holder callbacks are not exposed on this type yet.

docs.title: Reserve a preview area
docs.text:
SurfaceView()
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(220)

docs.title: Place controls over a surface
docs.text:
FrameLayout {
    SurfaceView()
        .width(.matchParent)
        .height(220)

    Button("Capture")
        .gravityInParent([.bottom, .end])
        .margin(16)
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
SurfaceView uses the inherited view initializer:

SurfaceView()
SurfaceView(id: 1001)

docs.title: Switch
docs.text:
Switch is the classic Android two-state control for settings that should look immediately on or off.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work as on any other control; switch-specific checked-state and track/thumb styling are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a switch for a persistent setting or mode where the on/off meaning should be obvious at a glance, such as enabling notifications or dark theme.

Do not use it when the user is choosing among several exclusive options — that is radio-group territory — or when a compact checkbox fits the form better.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Switch participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and toggle enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit CompoundButton and does not conform to Checkable. Methods such as checked(_:), isChecked(), toggle(), switchMinWidth(_:), trackTintList(_:), and similar Android switch APIs are not available on this Droid type at the current pin.

docs.title: Place a settings switch
docs.text:
Switch(id: 2001)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

The control is created and can sit in a settings row like any other view.

docs.title: React to a tap
docs.text:
let syncSwitch = Switch(id: 2001)

syncSwitch.onClick {
    // Handle the user activating the control.
    // Checked-state reads/writes are not wrapped yet.
}

docs.title: Disable the control until setup finishes
docs.text:
Switch(id: 2002)
    .enabled(false)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Switch()
Switch(id: 2001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s full Switch widget has checked state, thumb/track drawables, and text appearance. None of that is part of the current Droid Switch surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: TableLayout
docs.text:
TableLayout arranges children in rows (usually → TableRow)—it’s the old-school way to build “tables” in classic Android UIs.

For modern, flexible layouts, you’ll often reach for → LinearLayout or → RecyclerView instead, but TableLayout can still be handy for small, fixed sets of key/value info.

Android reference: android.widget.TableLayout

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use it when your UI is truly tabular: rows of values, simple summaries, or compact settings where columns line up.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
TableLayout lays out each TableRow and tries to keep columns aligned. It’s not meant for large datasets—think “a dozen rows”, not “a scrollable feed”.

Ownership of layout params is split:

  • a TableRow child of TableLayout uses TableLayout layout params;
  • each cell inside that row uses TableRow layout params (column(_:), span(_:)).

docs.title: Example 1: Key/value summary
docs.text:
TableLayout {
    TableRow {
        TextView("Name")
        TextView("Mihael")
    }
    TableRow {
        TextView("Plan")
        TextView("Pro")
    }
}
.padding(16)

Two aligned columns of label/value pairs.

docs.title: Example 2: A cell that spans both columns
docs.text:
TableLayout {
    TableRow {
        TextView("Billing")
            .span(2)
            .textSize(18)
    }
    TableRow {
        TextView("Next charge")
        TextView("$9.99")
    }
}
.padding(16)

The first row has a single cell spanning two columns; the second row has two ordinary cells.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
TableLayout()
TableLayout(id: 1001)
TableLayout {
    TableRow {
        TextView("Name")
    }
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
TableLayout owns row-level params for its TableRow children.

Cell-level placement (column(_:)) and multi-column occupancy (span(_:)) belong to cells inside each row — see → TableRow.

docs.title: TableRow
docs.text:
TableRow is the row container used inside → TableLayout.

Think of it as a horizontal strip of cells. Each row usually contains the same number of children so columns line up.

Android reference: android.widget.TableRow

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when you’re building a small table-like layout with aligned columns.

If you need complex row content, you’ll typically get better results with → LinearLayout (and accept that columns won’t align automatically).

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Children are laid out left-to-right. Each child is a cell and carries TableRow layout params:

  • column(_:) places the cell at a zero-based column index.
  • span(_:) makes the cell occupy several adjacent columns.

Those two modifiers belong to cells inside a TableRow. The TableRow itself, when placed in a TableLayout, uses TableLayout layout params instead.

docs.title: Example 1: A simple two-column row
docs.text:
TableRow {
    TextView("Subtotal")
    TextView("$12.34")
}

The two cells occupy the first two columns of the row.

docs.title: Example 2: A cell that spans both columns
docs.text:
TableRow {
    TextView("Shipping")
        .span(2)
        .textSize(18)
}

One cell occupies two columns instead of two separate cells.

docs.title: Example 3: Pin a cell to a column
docs.text:
TableRow {
    TextView("Total")
        .column(0)
    TextView("$24.68")
        .column(1)
        .textSize(18)
}

The first cell sits in column 0 and the second in column 1.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
TableRow()
TableRow(id: 1001)
TableRow {
    TextView("Left")
    TextView("Right")
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
Apply these to a cell inside a TableRow:

Modifier Meaning column(_:) zero-based column index for this cell span(_:) number of adjacent columns this cell occupies

A spanning header row is separate from numbered cells in later rows:

TableLayout {
    TableRow {
        TextView("Billing")
            .span(2)
            .textSize(18)
    }
    TableRow {
        TextView("Next charge")
            .column(0)
        TextView("$9.99")
            .column(1)
    }
}

column and span are TableRow cell fields. Do not use them as row-level params on the TableRow itself; a TableRow child of TableLayout uses TableLayout layout params.

docs.title: TextClock
docs.text:
TextClock is Android’s live clock text widget.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; format, time-zone, and 12/24-hour APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use TextClock when the screen needs the classic Android clock control and format APIs can land later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
TextClock participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose format12Hour(_:), format24Hour(_:), timeZone(_:), or is24HourMode() at this pin.

docs.title: Place a clock
docs.text:
TextClock(id: 2801)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 8)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
TextClock()
TextClock(id: 2801)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s TextClock follows the system time and locale. Format controls are not part of the current Droid surface.

docs.title: TextSwitcher
docs.text:
TextSwitcher is Android’s two-view control for switching between text values.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; factory bridges, text setters, and switcher animations are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use TextSwitcher when the screen needs the classic Android text-switching control and those APIs can land later.

For a single text slot, use TextView.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
TextSwitcher participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit ViewSwitcher / ViewAnimator APIs and does not expose setText(_:), factory(_:), or animation helpers at this pin.

docs.title: Place a text switcher
docs.text:
TextSwitcher(id: 2901)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 8)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
TextSwitcher()
TextSwitcher(id: 2901)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s TextSwitcher alternates two text views with transitions. That surface is not part of the current Droid API.

docs.title: TextView
docs.text:
TextView displays text that the user reads but does not edit. It works well for titles, labels, status messages, helper copy, and values that change while a screen is open.

Pass a plain String for fixed text or a string state when the label should stay synchronized with application state. A state-backed TextView applies the current value when the view is created and updates the Android view when that state changes.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use TextView whenever text is output rather than input: headings, descriptions, counters, validation messages, connection status, or values derived from state.

When the user needs to type or edit the value, use EditText instead.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Text configuration is applied to the underlying text view when the view is built. Methods such as textSize(_:_:), maxLines(_:), and gravity(_:) let the text participate naturally in the surrounding layout without turning the page into a list of Android properties.

When text comes from state, Droid keeps listening to that state after the view is created. Changing the state updates the displayed text without requiring you to replace the TextView yourself.

docs.title: Show a title and supporting text
docs.text:
body {
    VStack {
        TextView("Account")
            .textSize(24)

        TextView("Manage the details used to sign in.")
            .textSize(14)
            .maxLines(2)
    }
    .padding(16)
}

The title is visually distinct while the supporting copy is allowed to wrap to at most two lines.

docs.title: Keep a status label in sync with state
docs.text:
@State var status = "Not connected"

body {
    VStack {
        TextView($status)

        Button("Connect")
            .onClick {
                status = "Connected"
            }
    }
    .padding(16)
}

The label receives the current state value when it is built. Tapping the button changes the state, and the displayed text follows that change.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Create an empty view, pass fixed text directly, or bind a string state:

TextView()
TextView("Hello")
TextView($status)
TextView(id: 1001, "Title")

docs.title: Text and state
docs.text:
text(_:) changes the displayed text and accepts either a plain string value or a compatible string state.

TextView()
    .text("Ready")

A state can be attached the same way when the value should keep updating:

TextView()
    .text($status)

docs.title: Text size
docs.text:
textSize(_:_:) sets the text size. The default unit is .sp.

TextView("Headline")
    .textSize(22)

docs.title: Line limits
docs.text:
maxLines(_:) limits the maximum number of displayed lines and is useful when surrounding layout height should stay predictable.

TextView("A longer message that may wrap when space is narrow.")
    .maxLines(2)

docs.title: Gravity
docs.text:
gravity(_:) controls the alignment of text inside the view when its bounds have extra room.

TextView("Centered")
    .width(.matchParent)
    .gravity(.center)

docs.title: Text changes
docs.text:
textChangedListener(beforeTextChanged:onTextChanged:afterTextChanged:) registers callbacks for text changes. It is especially useful with editable subclasses such as EditText.

EditText()
    .textChangedListener(
        beforeTextChanged: nil,
        onTextChanged: { event in
            Log.i("Text changed to: \(event.p0 ?? "")")
        },
        afterTextChanged: nil
    )

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Some TextView operations are imperative rather than deferred. For example, append(_:) talks to the existing Android instance, so use it only after the view has been created. For ordinary declarative text changes, prefer text(_:) or state-backed text.

docs.title: TextureView
docs.text:
TextureView displays content through an Android texture while still participating in the normal view hierarchy.

That makes it useful when rendered content needs ordinary view transforms or composition. When a dedicated surface is the priority, consider SurfaceView.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use TextureView for rendered content that needs to move, scale, fade, rotate, or otherwise behave like a normal view in your layout.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The texture is composited as part of the view hierarchy, so inherited view APIs control size and placement normally.

The current API exposes the base view surface only; texture-listener and lower-level rendering callbacks are not exposed on this type yet.

docs.title: Create a preview tile
docs.text:
TextureView()
    .width(160)
    .height(90)

docs.title: Put an overlay above the texture
docs.text:
FrameLayout {
    TextureView()
        .width(.matchParent)
        .height(220)

    TextView("LIVE")
        .padding(h: 8, v: 4)
        .gravityInParent([.top, .start])
        .margin(16)
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
TextureView uses the inherited view initializer:

TextureView()
TextureView(id: 1001)

docs.title: TimePicker
docs.text:
TimePicker is Android’s time-of-day selection control.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; hour/minute configuration, 12/24-hour presentation, and mode inspection are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a time picker when the user should choose a valid time of day instead of typing free-form time text.

For duration input or a custom clock face, build that surface yourself and keep the validated time in app state.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
TimePicker participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose hour(_:), minute(_:), currentHour(_:) / currentMinute(_:), is24HourView(_:), or mode() at this pin.

docs.title: Place a time control
docs.text:
TimePicker(id: 8001)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Disable it until a schedule exists
docs.text:
TimePicker(id: 8002)
    .enabled(false)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
TimePicker()
TimePicker(id: 8001)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s TimePicker owns hour/minute and AM/PM or 24-hour presentation. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: Toast
docs.text:
Toast shows a short-lived message that does not require a response.

Use it for lightweight feedback such as "Saved" or "Copied". When the user may need an action such as Undo, use an interactive surface such as Snackbar instead.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a toast for brief, low-risk information that can disappear automatically.

Do not use it for critical errors or decisions the user must acknowledge.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Toast.makeText(_:context:duration:) creates the message. show() displays it, and cancel() can hide it early.

The duration defaults to .short; use .long when the message needs a little more reading time.

docs.title: Show a short confirmation
docs.text: Toast.makeText("Saved", context: self)?.show()

docs.title: Use the longer duration
docs.text:
Toast.makeText(
    "Upload finished",
    context: self,
    duration: .long
)?.show()

docs.title: Update a toast before showing it
docs.text:
Toast.makeText("Working…", context: self)?
    .text("Done")
    .duration(.long)
    .show()

docs.title: makeText(_:context:duration:)
docs.text: Creates a text toast and returns it when Android can create the underlying object.

docs.title: show()
docs.text: Displays the toast and returns the same Toast instance for chaining.

docs.title: duration(_:)
docs.text: Changes the duration between .short and .long.

docs.title: text(_:)
docs.text: Updates the toast text.

docs.title: cancel()
docs.text: Hides a toast that is currently showing.

docs.title: ToggleButton
docs.text:
ToggleButton is Android’s two-state button that shows on/off labels.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; checked state and text-on/text-off labels are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ToggleButton when the control should look like a labeled button that stays pressed in one of two states.

For a settings switch look, see Switch. For an independent checkbox, see CheckBox.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ToggleButton participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not conform to Checkable and does not expose checked(_:), isChecked(), toggle(), textOn(_:), or textOff(_:) at this pin.

docs.title: Place a toggle button
docs.text:
ToggleButton(id: 3301)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ToggleButton()
ToggleButton(id: 3301)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s ToggleButton is a CompoundButton with on/off text. That checked-state and label surface is not part of the current Droid API. Use CompoundButton when you need verified Checkable methods.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
The platform Android toolbar is currently exposed by Droid as Toolbar1.

At the current source pin Toolbar1 is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; title/subtitle, navigation and overflow icons, menu inflation, content insets, and toolbar listeners are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use Toolbar1 when you intentionally want Android’s platform android.widget.Toolbar and only need to place it in the hierarchy for now.

Apps built around AppCompat or Material components will usually prefer their corresponding toolbar wrappers once those surfaces match your screen.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Toolbar1 participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type is not a ViewGroup. It does not expose title(_:), subtitle(_:), navigationIcon(_:), logo(_:), inflateMenu(_:), overflow helpers, content-inset setters, or menu-click listeners at this pin.

docs.title: Place a platform toolbar
docs.text:
Toolbar1(id: 7001)
    .padding(h: 0, v: 0)

docs.title: Keep it visible only on detail screens
docs.text:
let bar = Toolbar1(id: 7002)
    .visibility(.gone)

// when showing detail
bar.visibility(.visible)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Toolbar1()
Toolbar1(id: 7001)

There is no content initializer at this pin.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The Swift type name is Toolbar1 while the JNI class name remains android.widget.Toolbar. Earlier drafts described a full ViewGroup toolbar API that is not in the pinned source. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: TwoLineListItem
docs.text:
TwoLineListItem is Android’s classic two-line list row.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; primary/secondary text accessors and row-mode APIs are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use TwoLineListItem when the screen needs the classic Android two-line row name and those APIs can land later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
TwoLineListItem participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit RelativeLayout and does not expose getText1() / getText2() or mode setters at this pin.

docs.title: Place a two-line row
docs.text:
TwoLineListItem(id: 3801)
    .padding(h: 16, v: 12)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
TwoLineListItem()
TwoLineListItem(id: 3801)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s TwoLineListItem binds two TextView children for list rows. That surface is not part of the current Droid API.

docs.title: VSpace
docs.text:
VSpace inserts an empty vertical gap with a chosen height. Calling VSpace(16) creates a 16 dp spacer by default, which makes repeated vertical rhythm easy to express directly in a VStack.

Unlike Space, VSpace starts with weight 0. Its normal role is therefore a fixed vertical separation, not a flexible spacer that immediately consumes leftover room.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use VSpace between stacked sections whose separation should stay deliberate as the screen changes: a heading and its content, two form groups, or a control and the content that follows it.

Use Space() when the empty area should stretch to fill what remains, such as keeping a button near the bottom of a taller column.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The height is required and may be supplied as an integer dimension or a layout-size value. The unit defaults to .dp, so the common fixed-gap form stays compact.

The default weight is 0. Supplying a nonzero weight: lets the spacer participate in compatible vertical weight distribution, allowing the parent layout to give it a share of additional available height.

docs.title: Keep sections evenly separated
docs.text:
The same fixed spacer can be repeated to give a column a consistent vertical rhythm:

body {
    VStack {
        TextView("Account")
        VSpace(16)
        TextView("Signed in")
        VSpace(16)
        Button("Continue")
    }
}

docs.title: Allow a vertical gap to grow
docs.text:
Here the spacer has an explicit height and also participates in the column's weight distribution:

body {
    VStack {
        TextView("Header")
        VSpace(8, weight: 1)
        Button("Continue")
    }
    .height(.matchParent)
}

If the intended behavior is simply to consume the remaining height, Space is usually the clearer choice because it starts with weight 1.

docs.title: VStack
docs.text:
Vertical container view used to arrange child views in a top-to-bottom order.

It is a thin, convenience wrapper around Android’s LinearLayout with its orientation fixed to .vertical. Its purpose is to make vertical layouts concise, readable, and familiar to Swift developers.

body {
    VStack {
        TextView("Some Text")
            .width(.matchParent)
            .height(.wrapContent)
        Button("Tap Me")
            .width(.matchParent)
            .height(48, .dp)
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(.wrapContent)
    .gravityForSubviews(.center)
    .padding(16, .dp)
}

All child views are laid out vertically in the order they are declared.

docs.title: VideoView
docs.text:
VideoView is Android’s classic built-in video playback widget.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; source assignment, playback control, seeking, and media-controller hooks are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use VideoView when Android’s classic playback widget is enough and you do not need a custom player surface yet.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
VideoView participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not expose setVideoPath(_:), start(), pause(), seekTo(_:), isPlaying(), setMediaController(_:), or player listener bridges at this pin.

docs.title: Place a video surface
docs.text:
VideoView(id: 1201)
    .padding(h: 0, v: 0)

docs.title: Keep playback UI hidden until the source is ready
docs.text:
let video = VideoView(id: 1202)
    .visibility(.gone)

// later
video.visibility(.visible)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
VideoView()
VideoView(id: 1201)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Android’s VideoView owns path/URI assignment and playback commands. None of that is part of the current Droid surface. Treat this page as placement plus shared view behavior only.

docs.title: ViewAnimator
docs.text:
ViewAnimator is Android’s base container for switching among child views.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; child factories, displayed-child control, and in/out animations are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use ViewAnimator when you need the classic Android animator container name and the switching APIs can land later.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ViewAnimator participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit FrameLayout and does not expose setFactory(_:), showNext(), showPrevious(), setInAnimation(_:), or setOutAnimation(_:) at this pin.

docs.title: Place an animator container
docs.text:
ViewAnimator(id: 3001)
    .padding(h: 0, v: 0)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ViewAnimator()

docs.title: ViewFlipper
docs.text:
ViewFlipper is Android’s auto-flipping child container.

In the current Droid source pin it is a placeable view control. Shared view interaction and layout APIs work; flip intervals, auto-start, and child switching are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Use it when…

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ViewFlipper participates in the view hierarchy like other controls. You can assign an id, attach onClick(_:), set padding, and control enabled(_:) / visibility(_:).

The current type does not inherit ViewAnimator APIs and does not expose setFlipInterval(_:), startFlipping(), stopFlipping(), or child-switch helpers at this pin.
