docs.title: ViewStub
docs.text:
ViewStub is a zero-size placeholder that inflates a real layout only when you ask for it. Until then it costs almost nothing on screen, so heavy panels, error states, and rare UI branches can stay out of the first layout pass.

Droid exposes the stub as a View you can place in a hierarchy, point at a layout resource, and later replace with the inflated content. After inflate(), the stub is gone from the tree and you get the live inflated view back.

Use it when a subtree is optional or expensive. Skip it when the UI is always visible — a normal child is simpler.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use ViewStub when a panel, error block, or advanced controls should not be built until the user actually needs them.

Do not use it for content that appears immediately on every screen. For always-visible UI, add the views directly.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The stub occupies no meaningful space until inflation. layoutResource(_:) names the layout to build. inflatedId(_:) names the id Android assigns to the inflated root so later lookups still work.

inflate() builds that layout, replaces the stub in its parent, and returns the new View?. After a successful inflate the stub is gone, so a second inflate() has nothing left to replace — do not rely on it as a retry path.

Read layoutResource() / inflatedId() back when you need to confirm configuration before inflating.

docs.title: Defer a heavy settings panel
docs.text:
let stub = ViewStub(id: 3001)
    .layoutResource(R.layout.settings_panel)
    .inflatedId(3002)

// later, when the user opens settings
if let panel = stub.inflate() {
    // settings_panel is now in the hierarchy
}

The screen stays light until inflate() runs.

docs.title: Keep a stable id after inflation
docs.text:
let stub = ViewStub(id: 3001)
    .layoutResource(R.layout.error_banner)
    .inflatedId(4100)

let banner = stub.inflate()

Android gives the inflated root id 4100, so other code can still find it after the stub is gone.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ViewStub()

ViewStub(id: 3001)

ViewStub(id: 3001) {
    // single child content via BodyBuilder
}

Most apps only need the id form plus layoutResource / inflatedId.

docs.title: Point at a layout
docs.text:
layoutResource(_:) sets the resource id to inflate. layoutResource() reads the current value.

stub.layoutResource(R.layout.settings_panel)
let res = stub.layoutResource()

Set the resource before the first inflate().

docs.title: Assign the inflated id
docs.text:
inflatedId(_:) sets the id of the view that replaces the stub. inflatedId() reads it.

stub.inflatedId(4100)
let id = stub.inflatedId()

Use this when later code looks up the inflated root by id.

docs.title: Inflate the stub
docs.text:
inflate() builds the layout, replaces the stub, and returns the inflated View?.

if let panel = stub.inflate() {
    // use the live view
}

Inflation is a one-shot replacement. Do not expect the stub to remain in the hierarchy afterward.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Point layoutResource at a real layout id before calling inflate(). The wrapper returns View? from inflate(); treat nil as “no inflated view” and inspect the resource before trying again.

docs.title: AppBarLayout
docs.text:
AppBarLayout is the “top strip” of a Material screen that can collapse, snap, and react to scrolling content. It usually hosts a toolbar, a large title, tabs, or a search field — anything that should feel connected to the scroll.

In Droid, AppBarLayout shines when it lives inside a CoordinatorLayout. That pairing is what turns it from “a vertical stack” into “a collapsing app bar”.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when the top of the screen should move with the content: collapse away as you scroll down, then return quickly when you scroll up.

Use it when you want the scroll view below to drive the app bar’s motion instead of you manually hiding/showing views.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
AppBarLayout lays out its children vertically. Each child can opt into scrolling behavior via layout params like scrollFlags(...) and scrollEffect(...).

For the scroll choreography to work, AppBarLayout should be a direct child of CoordinatorLayout, and your scrolling content should use AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior() as its behavior(...). If you skip that, AppBarLayout still renders — it just won’t respond to scroll.

docs.title: Pinned top bar
docs.text:
body {
    AppBarLayout {
        MaterialToolbar()
            .title("Settings")
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(.wrapContent)
}

docs.title: Collapsing app bar with scrolling content
docs.text:
import Droid

final class FeedActivity: AppCompatActivity {
    override func buildUI() {
        super.buildUI()
        body {
            CoordinatorLayout {
                AppBarLayout {
                    MaterialToolbar()
                        .title("Inbox")
                        .scrollFlags(.scroll, .enterAlways)

                    TextView("Today")
                        .textSize(20)
                        .padding(16)
                        .scrollFlags(.scroll, .exitUntilCollapsed)
                        .scrollEffect(.compress)
                }
                .width(.matchParent)
                .height(.wrapContent)

                NestedScrollView {
                    LinearLayout {
                        ForEach(0..<40) { i in
                            TextView("Message #\(i)")
                                .padding(16)
                        }
                    }
                    .orientation(.vertical)
                }
                .width(.matchParent)
                .height(.matchParent)
                .behavior(AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior())
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Snapping on scroll end
docs.text:
body {
    CoordinatorLayout {
        AppBarLayout {
            MaterialToolbar()
                .title("Library")
                .scrollFlags(.scroll, .snap)
        }

        NestedScrollView {
            LinearLayout {
                ForEach(0..<20) { i in
                    TextView("Book \(i)")
                        .padding(16)
                }
            }
            .orientation(.vertical)
        }
        .behavior(AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior())
    }
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
These params apply to views inside an AppBarLayout:

  • scrollFlags(...) chooses how a child enters/exits (scroll, snap, quick return). Cases: .scroll, .enterAlways, .enterAlwaysCollapsed, .exitUntilCollapsed, .snap, .snapMargins, .noScroll.
  • scrollEffect(...) adds .none or .compress for large titles.
  • scrollInterpolator(...) controls the collapse animation feel.
AppBarLayout {
    MaterialToolbar()
        .title("Inbox")
        .scrollFlags(.scroll, .enterAlways)

    TextView("Big header")
        .textSize(20)
        .padding(16)
        .scrollFlags(.scroll, .exitUntilCollapsed)
        .scrollEffect(.compress)
}

AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior is the coordinator behavior for the scrolling content:

NestedScrollView {
    // …
}
.behavior(AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior())

That behavior also exposes overlayTop(_:), leftAndRightOffset(_:), topAndBottomOffset(_:), verticalOffsetEnabled(_:), and horizontalOffsetEnabled(_:).

AppBarLayout itself accepts init(id:) and a single-child content initializer, plus scrollEffect(_:) / scrollFlags(_:) / scrollInterpolator(_:) on the bar when that is clearer than child layout params.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
AppBarLayout is happiest as a direct child of CoordinatorLayout. If you nest it inside other containers, the scroll behavior usually stops working.

AppBarLayout.LayoutParams field getters (scrollEffect, scrollFlags, scrollInterpolator as layout-param fields) are not wrapped at this pin — use the View helpers above. Nested ChildScrollEffect / CompressChildScrollEffect / LiftOnScrollProgressListener types exist for advanced integrations; do not assume full listener wiring.

docs.title: BadgeDrawable
docs.text:
A badge is the tiny dot or number that sits on top of an icon: “3”, “99+”, “new”.

In Droid it is a drawable you create, configure, and attach to an existing view with BadgeUtils. Navigation bars can also own badges through getOrCreateBadge(at:).

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when a piece of UI needs a subtle “there’s something here” signal: unread count, pending requests, a new-feature dot.

Use it when the user should keep context on the current screen while still noticing that something changed elsewhere.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
A badge lives relative to an anchor view. When attached, it draws in the anchor’s overlay (or a custom parent’s foreground), so it visually sits on top of the anchor.

Badges can show either a number (number(_:)) or a short text label (text(_:)). If the content is longer than maxCharacterCount(_:), Android truncates it to keep the badge readable. clearNumber() / clearText() remove the content again.

Gravity, offsets, padding, text color, and visibility are live drawable configuration. Attach only after the anchor has an Android instance.

docs.title: Badge on a notification icon
docs.text:
final class InboxActivity: AppCompatActivity {
    private let bell = TextView("Notifications").textSize(18)
    private var badge: BadgeDrawable?

    override func buildUI() {
        super.buildUI()
        body {
            FrameLayout {
                bell.padding(16)
            }
        }
    }

    override func onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        guard let context else { return }

        if badge == nil {
            badge = BadgeDrawable.create(context)?
                .number(3)
                .visible(true)
        }

        guard let badge else { return }
        BadgeUtils.attachBadgeDrawable(badge, to: bell)
    }
}

docs.title: Badge on a navigation item
docs.text:
if let badge = bottomNav.getOrCreateBadge(at: 3) {
    badge.number(12).visible(true)
}

bottomNav.removeBadge(at: 2)

docs.title: Short text badge
docs.text:
badge.text("NEW")
    .maxCharacterCount(3)
    .badgeGravity([.top, .end])

docs.title: Creating and attaching
docs.text:
BadgeDrawable.create(_:) needs an ActivityContext and returns BadgeDrawable?.

let badge = BadgeDrawable.create(context)

Attach and detach through BadgeUtils:

BadgeUtils.attachBadgeDrawable(badge, to: anchorView)
BadgeUtils.detachBadgeDrawable(badge, from: anchorView)

Toolbar menu items have parallel helpers: attachBadgeDrawable(_:toMenuItem:in:in:) and detachBadgeDrawable(_:fromMenuItem:in:).

docs.title: Content
docs.text:
badge.number(7)
badge.clearNumber()

badge.text("NEW")
badge.clearText()

number() / text() read the live values. hasNumber() / hasText() report whether content is present.

docs.title: Visibility and placement
docs.text:
badge.visible(true)
badge.badgeGravity([.top, .end])
badge.maxCharacterCount(2)
badge.horizontalOffset(4)
badge.verticalOffset(2)

badgeFixedEdge(_:) pins the badge to .start or .end of the anchor. Offsets come in plain, WithText, and WithoutText variants so the badge can shift depending on content.

docs.title: Colors and appearance
docs.text: badgeTextColor(_:) and backgroundColor() cover text and fill. textAppearance(_:) points at a style resource. Shape-appearance resource setters exist for with-text and without-text badges.

docs.title: Navigation-bar integration
docs.text:
NavigationBarView.badge(at:), getOrCreateBadge(at:), and removeBadge(at:) create or remove item badges without manual BadgeUtils calls.

BadgeUtils.setBadgeDrawableBounds(_:for:in:) and updateBadgeBounds(_:_:_:_:_:_:) (Rect, centerX, centerY, halfWidth, halfHeight, optional unit) are lower-level bounds helpers when you host the badge yourself.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Attach in onStart() or later — before the anchor has an instance there is nothing to draw on.

BadgeDrawable.createFromResource and saved-state helpers are not wrapped at this pin. badgeGravity() getter is present but marked for verification in source; prefer the setter for configuration.

docs.title: BottomNavigationView
docs.text:
BottomNavigationView is the Material bottom navigation bar: a persistent row of top-level destinations.

It works best for 3–5 sections users jump between all the time (Home / Search / Inbox / Profile). In Droid it inherits NavigationBarView, so menu, selection, label, and badge APIs come from that base.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when the app has a small number of stable top-level destinations and navigation should stay visible.

Use it when a drawer would be overkill and switching sections should be one tap away.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Items come from a Menu. Inflate a menu resource with inflateMenu(_:) or build items programmatically.

selectedItemId(_:) selects a destination and selectedItemId() reads the current one. Item selection listeners are not wrapped yet — drive selection from your own navigation state.

Label visibility, icon/text appearance, active-indicator chrome, and item tint are configurable on the inherited NavigationBarView surface. BottomNavigationView adds itemHorizontalTranslationEnabled(_:).

Badges attach per menu item id through getOrCreateBadge(at:) / removeBadge(at:). See BadgeDrawable.

docs.title: Three destinations with an inbox badge
docs.text:
final class MainActivity: AppCompatActivity {
    private let bottomNav = BottomNavigationView()

    override func buildUI() {
        super.buildUI()
        body {
            LinearLayout {
                FrameLayout()
                    .height(0)
                    .weight(1)

                bottomNav
                    .width(.matchParent)
                    .height(.wrapContent)
                    .itemHorizontalTranslationEnabled(false)
                    .labelVisibilityMode(.labeled)
            }
            .orientation(.vertical)
        }
    }

    override func onStart() {
        super.onStart()

        guard let menu = bottomNav.menu() else { return }
        menu.clear()
        menu.add(itemId: 1, title: "Home")
        menu.add(itemId: 2, title: "Search")
        menu.add(itemId: 3, title: "Inbox")

        bottomNav.selectedItemId(1)

        bottomNav.getOrCreateBadge(at: 3)?
            .number(4)
            .visible(true)
    }
}

docs.title: Jump to a destination from code
docs.text:
MaterialButton("Go to Inbox")
    .onClick { bottomNav.selectedItemId(3) }

docs.title: Selection and menu
docs.text:
bottomNav.selectedItemId(2)
let current = bottomNav.selectedItemId()

bottomNav.inflateMenu(R.menu.main)
if let menu = bottomNav.menu() {
    // inspect or mutate items
}

selectedItemId(), menu(), menuViewGroup(), maxItemCount(), and isSubMenuSupported() read live state.

docs.title: Badges

bottomNav.getOrCreateBadge(at: 3)?.number(12).visible(true)
bottomNav.badge(at: 3)
bottomNav.removeBadge(at: 3)

bottomNav.labelVisibilityMode(.labeled)
bottomNav.labelMaxLines(1)
bottomNav.itemIconSize(24)
bottomNav.itemIconTintList(tint)
bottomNav.itemTextColor(tint)

bottomNav.itemActiveIndicatorEnabled(true)
bottomNav.itemActiveIndicatorHeight(32)
bottomNav.itemActiveIndicatorWidth(.wrapContent) // or .matchParent

bottomNav.itemRippleColor(ripple)

docs.title: Notes

BadgeUtils attach/detach helpers remain available if you host badges outside getOrCreateBadge.

docs.title: NavigationView
docs.text:
NavigationView is the menu surface you put inside a drawer or side sheet: the place where “Home”, “Settings”, “Help”, and similar destinations live.

In Droid it owns a Menu, renders checked state, and exposes Material spacing, inset, and header configuration. Keep a reference so you can populate the menu after the view is attached.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when the app has many destinations, or when switching sections is not something users do every few seconds.

Use it when you want a consistent place for secondary screens: Settings, About, Feedback, legal links.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
NavigationView renders a vertical list of menu items. One item can be checked (checkedItem(_:) / checkedItem()), which helps users see where they are.

It is usually hosted by a drawer container such as DrawerLayout, or used as a static side panel in a two-pane layout. Header views, divider insets, item padding, and scrim inset flags are configurable. Navigation item-selected listeners are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Static side navigation
docs.text:
final class TwoPaneActivity: AppCompatActivity {
    private let nav = NavigationView()

    override func buildUI() {
        super.buildUI()
        body {
            LinearLayout {
                nav
                    .width(280)
                    .height(.matchParent)
                    .itemHorizontalPadding(16)
                    .itemIconPadding(12)

                FrameLayout()
                    .width(0)
                    .height(.matchParent)
                    .weight(1)
            }
            .orientation(.horizontal)
        }
    }

    override func onStart() {
        super.onStart()

        guard let menu = nav.menu() else { return }
        menu.clear()
        let home = menu.add(itemId: 1, title: "Home")
        _ = menu.add(itemId: 2, title: "Downloads")
        _ = menu.add(itemId: 3, title: "Settings")

        if let home {
            nav.checkedItem(home)
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Header and inset tuning
docs.text:
let header = TextView("Account").padding(16)

NavigationView()
    .addHeaderView(header)
    .dividerInsetStart(16)
    .dividerInsetEnd(16)
    .itemVerticalPadding(8)
    .startInsetScrimEnabled(false)

docs.title: Menu and checked item
docs.text:
guard let menu = nav.menu() else { return }
menu.add(itemId: 1, title: "Home")

nav.checkedItem(item)
let current = nav.checkedItem()

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
nav.addHeaderView(headerView)
nav.removeHeaderView(headerView)
let count = nav.headerCount()
let first = nav.headerView(at: 0)

docs.title: Item appearance
docs.text:
nav.itemHorizontalPadding(16)
nav.itemIconPadding(12)
nav.itemVerticalPadding(8)
nav.itemMaxLines(1)
nav.itemTextAppearance(R.style.NavItem)
nav.itemTextAppearanceActiveBoldEnabled(true)
nav.itemIconTintList(tint)
nav.itemTextColor(tint)
nav.itemBackgroundResource(R.drawable.nav_item_bg)

Resource overloads exist for horizontal/icon/vertical padding.

docs.title: Insets and dividers
docs.text:
nav.dividerInsetStart(16)
nav.dividerInsetEnd(16)
nav.subheaderInsetStart(8)
nav.subheaderInsetEnd(8)

Scrim inset flags: bottomInsetScrimEnabled(_:), topInsetScrimEnabled(_:), startInsetScrimEnabled(_:). The end side has only the live getter isEndInsetScrimEnabled() — there is no endInsetScrimEnabled(_:) setter at this pin.

Foreground helpers: drawTopInsetForeground(_:), drawBottomInsetForeground(_:), drawLeftInsetForeground(_:), drawRightInsetForeground(_:), and scrimInsetForeground(_:).

Back-progress helpers cancelBackProgress() / handleBackInvoked() are present; the intermediate back-progress setters are not wrapped yet.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
setNavigationItemSelectedListener is not wrapped at this pin, so reacting to taps is limited. Drive checked state from your own navigation logic.

itemIconSize(_:) is available for icon sizing. Do not assume Android’s full NavigationView listener surface.

docs.title: Navigation rail
docs.text:
Material navigation rail is the side navigation strip for large-screen layouts (3–7 destinations).

Droid does not wrap NavigationRailView at the current source pin. The JNI name exists in the package namespace, but the Swift wrapper type is not live.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Do not plan navigation-rail UI against Droid yet. BottomNavigationView is the pin-backed Material destination bar available today.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
There is no NavigationRailView() constructor to place, no menu/badge API, and no rail listener bridge at this pin.

Android’s Material navigation-rail API (header, item badges, label visibility) must not be treated as available from Droid.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: This page will grow only after a live NavigationRailView wrapper lands in a commit pin with real methods.

docs.title: Notes

docs.text:

docs.title: Snackbar
docs.text:
A Snackbar is a short message that appears at the bottom of the screen, optionally with one action (“Undo”, “Retry”). It’s great for confirming an operation without interrupting the user.

In Droid, you create one with Snackbar.make(...), optionally add an action, then call show().

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when the user should notice something, but you don’t want a modal dialog: “Saved”, “Moved to trash”, “Offline”.

Use it when there’s a quick recovery action: Undo delete, Retry network request, Reconnect.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Snackbars sit above your content and dismiss themselves after a duration unless you choose .indefinite. Only one snackbar is shown at a time; a new one replaces the old.

If your layout uses CoordinatorLayout, Android can automatically move other UI (like a FAB) so the snackbar doesn’t cover it.

docs.title: Undo after delete
docs.text:
Snackbar.make(contentView!, "Item removed", .long)?
    .action("Undo") { restoreLastItem() }
    .show()

docs.title: Retry after a failed upload
docs.text:
Snackbar.make(contentView!, "Upload failed", .long)?
    .action("Retry") { uploadAgain() }
    .show()

docs.title: Quiet confirmation
docs.text: Snackbar.make(contentView!, "Copied", .short)?.show()

docs.title: Create
docs.text: let api = Snackbar.make(contentView!, "Saved", .short)

docs.title: Action
docs.text:
Snackbar.make(contentView!, "Draft deleted", .long)?
    .action("Undo") { restoreDraft() }
    .actionTextColor(.white)
    .show()

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
Snackbar.make(contentView!, "Offline", .long)?
    .backgroundTint(.black)
    .textColor(.white)
    .textMaxLines(2)
    .animationMode(.fade)
    .show()

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
contentView is the easiest anchor view in an Activity. If it’s nil, pass any view that’s already in your hierarchy.

text(_:), text(resId:), and maxInlineActionWidth(_:) exist on the type but currently call the wrong Android method (setBackgroundTint) at this pin. Prefer setting message text through Snackbar.make(...) and avoid those three until a later pin fixes them.

duration() and isShown() read live state. dismiss() hides a visible snackbar.

docs.title: MaterialToolbar
docs.text:
MaterialToolbar is a top app bar that matches Material theming (elevation overlays, centered titles, etc.). In Droid it behaves like a toolbar you configure — title, optional subtitle, and room for actions — rather than a generic “layout container”.

You’ll most often place it inside AppBarLayout (for scroll/collapse) or just at the top of a vertical layout for a simple screen.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when your screen needs a recognizable top bar: a title, optional subtitle, and space for actions.

Use it when you want Material styling without hand-tweaking elevation, overlays, and typography on every screen.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The toolbar draws a background and lays out its title/subtitle and action area. In Droid, title(...) and subtitle(...) accept String or State<String> — if you pass state, the toolbar updates live.

If you put the toolbar inside an AppBarLayout, you can give it scrollFlags(...) so it collapses and snaps with scrolling content.

docs.title: Simple toolbar at the top of a screen
docs.text:
body {
    LinearLayout {
        MaterialToolbar()
            .title("Profile")
            .subtitle("Signed in")
            .width(.matchParent)
            .height(.wrapContent)

        TextView("Content goes here")
            .padding(16)
    }
    .orientation(.vertical)
}

docs.title: Toolbar inside an AppBarLayout (scrolling)
docs.text:
body {
    CoordinatorLayout {
        AppBarLayout {
            MaterialToolbar()
                .title("Inbox")
                .scrollFlags(.scroll, .enterAlways)
        }

        NestedScrollView {
            LinearLayout {
                ForEach(0..<30) { i in
                    TextView("Message \(i)")
                        .padding(16)
                }
            }
            .orientation(.vertical)
        }
        .behavior(AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior())
    }
}

docs.title: Title driven by state
docs.text:
@State var query = ""

body {
    MaterialToolbar()
        .title($query.map { $0.isEmpty ? "Search" : $0 })
}

docs.title: Titles
docs.text:
title(_:) and subtitle(_:) accept String and State<String> (_SetTitleable / _SetSubtitleable):

MaterialToolbar()
    .title("Settings")
    .subtitle("Account")

docs.title: Menu refresh and overflow
docs.text:
Call invalidateMenu() when menu content changes and the toolbar should re-render.

toolbar.invalidateMenu()

let showing = toolbar.isOverflowMenuShowing()
let hid = toolbar.hideOverflowMenu()
let expanded = toolbar.hasExpandedActionView()

isBackInvokedCallbackEnabled() reports whether the predictive-back callback is enabled.

docs.title: Low-level event hooks
docs.text:
toolbar.onTouchEvent(event)
toolbar.onHoverEvent(event)
toolbar.onRtlPropertiesChanged(.ltr)

These forward to the live Android view for custom touch/hover/RTL handling.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
removeMenuProvider is not wrapped at this pin. Menu provider population across the framework is still growing — you can place a toolbar before a full Swift-first menu story exists.

MaterialToolbar is a ViewGroup with init(id:) and a single-child content initializer. Combined with AppBarLayout scrollFlags / scrollEffect helpers it can collapse with scrolling content.

docs.title: Tooltips
docs.text:
Material tooltips show short helper text over a control.

Droid does not wrap Material tooltip APIs at the current source pin. There is no live Material tooltip Swift type.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Do not plan Material tooltip UI against Droid yet. Use a visible TextView helper label under the control.

docs.title: MaterialButton
docs.text:
MaterialButton is the Material-styled button: it matches your Material theme out of the box.

In Droid it inherits the text and click surface from Button / TextView. Its own methods at this pin are mostly getters for corner radius, icon placement, and insets — configure look through the theme.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when the action should look like part of a Material design system: primary/secondary actions, dialogs, forms, and call-to-action rows.

Use it when shape, ripple, and typography should come from the theme instead of per-screen tweaks.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
A MaterialButton draws and owns its Material background. Label text comes from the inherited TextView / SetTextable surface (text(_:), or a string/state initializer).

onClick(_:) handles taps like any other view. Icon, corner, and inset setters are not wrapped at this pin — only the matching getters exist for inspection after layout.

docs.title: Form submit
docs.text:
MaterialButton("Sign in")
    .width(.matchParent)
    .onClick { status = "Signed in" }
    .padding(left: 16, top: 0, right: 16, bottom: 8)

docs.title: Two actions side by side
docs.text:
body {
    LinearLayout {
        MaterialButton("Cancel")
            .width(0)
            .weight(1)
            .marginEnd(8)

        MaterialButton("Save")
            .width(0)
            .weight(1)
    }
    .orientation(.horizontal)
    .padding(16)
}

docs.title: Inspect theme-derived geometry
docs.text:
let radius = button.cornerRadius()
let iconMode = button.iconGravity()
let topInset = button.insetTop()

docs.title: Material getters
docs.text:
button.cornerRadius()
button.icon()
button.iconGravity()
button.iconPadding()
button.iconSize()
button.insetTop()
button.insetBottom()
button.clearOnCheckedChangeListeners()

IconGravity cases: .start, .end, .textStart, .textEnd, .top, .textTop.

clearOnCheckedChangeListeners() removes previously registered checked-change listeners (listener registration is not wrapped yet).

docs.title: Inherited text and click
docs.text:
MaterialButton("Save")
    .textSize(16)
    .maxLines(1)
    .onClick { /* handle */ }

Text, padding, visibility, and click behavior come from TextView and the shared view API.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
There are no fluent setters for icon(_:), cornerRadius(_:), iconPadding(_:), iconSize(_:), insetTop(_:), insetBottom(_:), or iconGravity(_:) at this pin. XML app:icon / app:cornerRadius attributes are not Swift API.

Also not wrapped yet: addOnCheckedChangeListener, getBackgroundTintList, getBackgroundTintMode. Style those from the Material theme.

AppCompatButton inheritance is thin at this pin (emoji-compat helpers only) plus classic Button → TextView.

docs.title: Extended FABs
docs.text:
Extended FABs are wider Material floating actions with a label next to the icon.

Droid does not wrap ExtendedFloatingActionButton at the current source pin. The JNI name exists in the package namespace, but the Swift wrapper type is not live.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Do not plan extended-FAB UI against Droid yet. FloatingActionButton is the pin-backed FAB today.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
There is no ExtendedFloatingActionButton() constructor, expand/collapse API, or extended-FAB listener at this pin.

Do not use FloatingActionButton.expanded(_:) as if it were a full extended-FAB API — that flag exists on the regular FAB only.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: This page will grow only after a live ExtendedFloatingActionButton wrapper lands in a commit pin with real methods.

docs.title: FAB menu
docs.text:
FAB menu is the Material pattern of a primary FAB that opens a small menu of secondary actions.

Droid does not wrap Material FAB-menu APIs at the current source pin. There is no live FAB-menu Swift type.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Do not plan FAB-menu UI against Droid yet. Place one FloatingActionButton and drive secondary actions from ordinary buttons.

docs.title: How it behaves

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: This page will grow only after a live FAB-menu wrapper lands in a commit pin with real methods.

docs.title: FloatingActionButton
docs.text:
FloatingActionButton (FAB) is the circular, promoted action that floats above your content. It’s at its best when there’s one obvious “primary” action: compose, add, scan, create.

In Droid it’s a normal view you place in your layout — most commonly inside a CoordinatorLayout so it can cooperate with scrolling and snackbars.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when the screen has a single high-priority action that should stay reachable while the user scrolls.

Use it when you want an icon-only action button that feels native to Material.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
A FAB draws a circular background and an icon, and it can animate when shown/hidden. You can pick a standard size (.normal, .mini) or set a custom size.

On some devices/platform versions, the FAB can add internal padding (useCompatPadding) so it keeps consistent shadows and touch area.

docs.title: A “compose” FAB above a scrolling list
docs.text:
import Droid

final class MessagesActivity: AppCompatActivity {
    override func buildUI() {
        super.buildUI()
        body {
            CoordinatorLayout {
                NestedScrollView {
                    LinearLayout {
                        ForEach(0..<30) { i in
                            TextView("Message \(i)")
                                .padding(16)
                        }
                    }
                    .orientation(.vertical)
                }
                .width(.matchParent)
                .height(.matchParent)

                FloatingActionButton()
                    .imageResource(R().drawable.ic_add)
                    .size(.normal)
                    .useCompatPadding()
                    .gravityInParent([.bottom, .end])
                    .margin(16)
                    .onClick {
                        Snackbar.make(contentView!, "Compose tapped", .short)?.show()
                    }
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: A mini FAB as a secondary action
docs.text:
body {
    FrameLayout {
        TextView("Map goes here")
            .width(.matchParent)
            .height(.matchParent)
            .gravity(.center)

        FloatingActionButton()
            .imageResource(R().drawable.ic_my_location)
            .size(.mini)
            .gravityInParent([.bottom, .start])
            .margin(16)
    }
}

docs.title: Icon
docs.text:
FloatingActionButton()
    .imageResource(R().drawable.ic_add)

// or a Drawable instance
fab.imageDrawable(drawable)

maxImageSize(_:) caps the icon size.

docs.title: Size and touch target
docs.text:
FloatingActionButton()
    .size(.mini) // or .normal
    .customSize(56)
    .ensureMinTouchTargetSize(true)
    .useCompatPadding(true)
    .clearCustomSize()

docs.title: Elevation and motion
docs.text:
fab.compatElevation(6)
fab.compatHoveredFocusedTranslationZ(8)
fab.compatPressedTranslationZ(12)
fab.showMotionSpecResource(R.animator.fab_show)
fab.hideMotionSpecResource(R.animator.fab_hide)

Resource overloads exist for the elevation family.

docs.title: Show and hide
docs.text:
show() and hide() are imperative (they run an animation if the view is laid out), so call them in response to events.

fab.hide()
fab.show()

isExpanded(), isOrWillBeShown(), and isOrWillBeHidden() read live visibility state. expanded(_:) / expandedComponentIdHint(_:) relate to extended-FAB expansion.

docs.title: Appearance extras
docs.text:
fab.rippleColor(color)
fab.gravity([.bottom, .end])

shapeAppearanceModel(_:) accepts a ShapeAppearanceModel (corner sizing via withCornerSize(_:)). That helper type is support-only — no separate page.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
If you want the FAB to move out of the way of a Snackbar, put both in a CoordinatorLayout.

Extended FAB APIs are not wrapped on this type at the current pin. internalSetVisibility / onTouchEvent / jumpDrawablesToCurrentState exist for low-level integrations.

docs.title: ComponentActivity
docs.text:
ComponentActivity provides lower-level building blocks for composing higher-level activity components. It keeps that foundation small so components can work together without a deep activity hierarchy or strong coupling.

Its exposed helpers let you add an existing view, initialize view-tree owners, refresh a menu after a state change, and enable edge-to-edge display.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use ComponentActivity when you are composing activity components and need these content, menu, or display helpers.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
ComponentActivity is an open, main-actor-isolated subclass of Activity. The inherited Activity.onCreate calls body() and then buildUI() when it builds the content.

All four helpers log and return when the activity context is missing. addContentView also returns immediately if the supplied view has no underlying instance. enableEdgeToEdge returns with a debug log if the AndroidX edge-to-edge class cannot be loaded.

docs.title: Display a ready message
docs.text:
import Droid

final class ReadyActivity: ComponentActivity {
    override var body: BodyBuilder.Result {
        TextView("Ready")
    }
}

docs.title: Install existing content
docs.text:
This function accepts a view and layout params that already exist. Initialize the view-tree owners before adding the content so inflation and attach listeners see the owners already present.

@MainActor
func installContent(
    in activity: ComponentActivity,
    view: View,
    layoutParams: LayoutParams
) {
    activity.initializeViewTreeOwners()
    activity.addContentView(view, layoutParams)
}

docs.title: addContentView
docs.text:
Adds an existing view with the supplied layout params through the underlying activity call. The view must have an underlying instance; otherwise the call returns without adding it.

@MainActor
func addContent(to activity: ComponentActivity, view: View, layoutParams: LayoutParams) {
    activity.addContentView(view, layoutParams)
}

docs.title: initializeViewTreeOwners()
docs.text:
Sets view-tree owners before content is set. Call it before installing content, as in the example above.

@MainActor
func prepareContent(in activity: ComponentActivity) {
    activity.initializeViewTreeOwners()
}

docs.title: invalidateMenu()
docs.text:
Invalidates the menu so its displayed state matches its current internal state. Call it after a menu state change, such as removing or disabling an item in response to a user event.

@MainActor
func menuStateDidChange(in activity: ComponentActivity) {
    activity.invalidateMenu()
}

docs.title: enableEdgeToEdge()
docs.text:
Enables edge-to-edge display for the activity. If androidx/activity/EdgeToEdge cannot be loaded, the call logs a debug message and returns.

@MainActor
func enableEdgeToEdgeDisplay(in activity: ComponentActivity) {
    activity.enableEdgeToEdge()
}

docs.title: ConstraintLayout
docs.text:
Use ConstraintLayout to describe where a child view belongs by relating its edges to the parent or to another view. This keeps those relationships on the views they position.

In Droid, the constraint methods are layout parameters on each child View. Use them to align edges or place one child beside another by its ID.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use it when a screen is easier to describe with explicit parent-edge and sibling relationships than with nested layout groups.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Each constraint is configured on the child view whose position it describes. ConstraintLayout accepts its supported constraint parameters along with the inherited size and margin parameters.

Directional anchors such as startToParent() follow the layout direction: start is left in LTR and right in RTL. An ID-based anchor such as topToBottom(id) relates the child's top edge to the referenced view's bottom edge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
This aligns the start and top edges of Account status with the parent:

@MainActor
func accountPanel() -> FrameLayout {
    FrameLayout {
        ConstraintLayout {
            TextView("Account status")
                .startToParent()
                .topToParent()
        }
    }
}

This places Plan: Standard below the child with ID 1 and aligns its start edge with the parent:

@MainActor
func accountDetails() -> FrameLayout {
    FrameLayout {
        ConstraintLayout {
            TextView(id: 1, "Account")
                .startToParent()
                .topToParent()

            TextView("Plan: Standard")
                .startToParent()
                .topToBottom(1)
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
ConstraintLayout has an initializer with an optional id and a builder initializer that accepts child content and an optional id. View construction and body-builder closures use main-actor-isolated APIs, so keep these calls in a @MainActor context as shown above.

Use the ID-only form when the container needs an ID without a child-content builder. This constructs a ConstraintLayout whose view ID is 2:

@MainActor
func identifiedLayout() -> ConstraintLayout {
    ConstraintLayout(id: 2)
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text:
Set constraints on the child view:

  • Use parent anchors such as startToParent() and topToParent() to align a child with a parent edge.
  • Use ID-based anchors such as startToStart(id), startToEnd(id), topToBottom(id), and baselineToBaseline(id) to relate one child to another.
  • Constraint-specific parameters also cover bias, chains, circular positioning, aspect ratio, and margins for views whose visibility is gone.

The container applies its supported constraint parameters together with the standard size and margin parameters inherited from View.

docs.title: CoordinatorLayout
docs.text: CoordinatorLayout configures relationships between children, such as an app bar and its scrolling sibling or a child that references another view as its anchor.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when an AppBarLayout and scrolling content need the app-bar relationship provided by AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior. Both views belong directly inside the CoordinatorLayout, with the behavior attached to the scrolling sibling.

Use it when a child needs to reference another child's ID as an anchor and supply anchor gravity.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
CoordinatorLayout is a ViewGroup. Configure child relationships through View layout-param methods called on its direct children. For example, .behavior(...) assigns a behavior to that child, while .anchorId(...) supplies the ID of its anchor.

The container's body builder can contain multiple children. Each child's layout params describe that child's relationship within the container.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Place these expressions in a main-actor UI body.

docs.title: App bar and scrolling content
docs.text:
This configures the app-bar/scrolling-sibling relationship, with enough content to exercise scrolling inside the bounded container. The scroll flags belong to the TextView inside AppBarLayout; the scrolling sibling receives ScrollingViewBehavior.

CoordinatorLayout {
    AppBarLayout {
        TextView("Inbox")
            .width(.matchParent)
            .height(56)
            .scrollFlags(.scroll, .enterAlways)
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(.wrapContent)

    NestedScrollView {
        TextView(String(repeating: "Message\n", count: 100))
            .width(.matchParent)
            .height(.wrapContent)
    }
    .width(.matchParent)
    .height(.matchParent)
    .behavior(AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior())
}
.width(.matchParent)
.height(320)

docs.title: Reference an anchor
docs.text:
The second child references the first child's ID, 10, and supplies combined bottom/end anchor gravity.

CoordinatorLayout {
    TextView(id: 10, "Header")
        .width(160)
        .height(56)

    TextView("Related content")
        .width(.wrapContent)
        .height(.wrapContent)
        .anchorId(10)
        .anchorGravity([.bottom, .end])
}
.width(.matchParent)
.height(160)

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
init(id: Int32? = nil) creates a container without builder content. The optional ID defaults to nil.

CoordinatorLayout()
CoordinatorLayout(id: 20)

init(id: Int32? = nil, @BodyBuilder content: BodyBuilder.SingleView) accepts a content builder and the same optional ID. Despite the SingleView name, the builder can contain multiple children, as in the examples above.

CoordinatorLayout(id: 20) {
    TextView("First")
    TextView("Second")
}

docs.title: Layout params
docs.text: These six public View methods configure layout params on direct children of a CoordinatorLayout. Each takes an explicit value and returns the same view for chaining; the return value can also be discarded. The small snippets below show parameter calls to use on children inside the container.

docs.title: behavior(_:)
docs.text:
Assigns a Behavior to the child. For the app-bar relationship, attach the concrete AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior to the scrolling sibling shown above.

TextView("List").behavior(AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior())

docs.title: anchorId(_:)
docs.text:
Sets the child's anchor reference using an Int32 view ID. Give the referenced view a matching ID, as in the anchor example.

TextView("Related").anchorId(10)

docs.title: anchorGravity(_:)
docs.text:
Supplies the child's gravity relative to its anchor. Gravity is an OptionSet: [.bottom, .end] constructs one combined Gravity value passed to this method.

TextView("Related").anchorGravity([.bottom, .end])

docs.title: dodgeInsetEdges(_:)
docs.text:
Sets the child's dodgeInsetEdges parameter, which selects edges for inset dodging. Its current argument type is Gravity.

TextView("Inset").dodgeInsetEdges(.bottom)

docs.title: insetEdge(_:)
docs.text:
Sets the child's insetEdge parameter to the supplied edge value. Its current argument type is also Gravity.

TextView("Top inset").insetEdge(.top)

docs.title: keyline(_:)
docs.text:
Sets the child's keyline parameter using a raw Int32 value. This call supplies the parameter; it does not define keylines on the container.

TextView("Marker").keyline(0)

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Behavior is a global, non-generic Swift class with a public no-argument initializer, Behavior(). It maps to the Java inner class CoordinatorLayout.Behavior. The Swift API does not expose user-implementable scroll, drag, or swipe callbacks. Use an exposed concrete behavior such as AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior for the relationship it supports.

dodgeInsetEdges and insetEdge currently accept Gravity; a dedicated edge-flags type remains a source TODO. keyline accepts raw Int32, with a position type also left as a TODO. These parameter calls alone do not specify keyline units or guarantee a particular layout result.

docs.title: DialogFragment
docs.text:
DialogFragment displays a dialog window in front of its activity and lets a FragmentManager manage the fragment that owns it. Supply visible content through the inherited body builder, then show the fragment with a tag.

Control showing, hiding, and dismissing through the fragment APIs. Direct calls on its Dialog can bypass the fragment's control of the window; configure cancelability through DialogFragment too.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use it for a focused message or task that belongs in a dialog window while remaining managed as a fragment. For content embedded in the activity instead, follow the fragment content and transaction flow.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The manager-based show creates an add transaction with your tag and commits it without adding it to the back stack. Its commit is scheduled on the main thread. showNow adds immediately using commitNow, also without adding to the back stack. Dismissing either causes a new transaction to remove the fragment.

The transaction-based show adds the dialog fragment using your supplied transaction and commits that transaction. Do not commit it again yourself. Ordinary commits and synchronous commits must happen before the host activity saves its state.

Set showsDialog(_:) from onCreate; setting it later has no effect. Apply style(_:_:) before the dialog is created; changing it afterward has no effect.

DialogFragment-specific on… methods and the requireDialog / requireComponentDialog helpers are marked TODO and are not declared in Droid's DialogFragment source. Inherited NativeFragment hooks such as onCreate(_:) remain available. The example uses inherited fragment content rather than an onCreateDialog override.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Pass the host's FragmentManager into this function. It creates a dialog containing a visible sync-status message, disables cancellation, and shows it under the sync-status tag. Keep the returned fragment if you need to dismiss it when the operation finishes.

import Droid

@MainActor
func showSyncStatus(using manager: FragmentManager) -> DialogFragment? {
    guard let dialog = DialogFragment() else { return nil }
    dialog.body {
        TextView("Syncing your notes. Please wait.")
    }
    dialog.cancelable(false)
    dialog.show(manager, "sync-status")
    return dialog
}

The snippets below use dialog for this fragment and manager for the supplied manager. Each showing snippet is an alternative way to present it.

docs.title: Presenting the dialog
docs.text:
show(_:_:) with a FragmentManager adds the fragment with a tag and schedules its transaction without a back-stack entry.

dialog.show(manager, "sync-status")

show(_:_:) with a FragmentTransaction uses and commits that transaction, returning an Int32 result. Start the transaction through the manager:

if let transaction = manager.beginTransaction() {
    let result = dialog.show(transaction, "sync-status")
}

showNow(_:_:) adds the fragment synchronously using commitNow, without a back-stack entry. Use it when the addition must finish before the call returns, before the activity has saved its state.

dialog.showNow(manager, "sync-status")

docs.title: Configuring the window
docs.text:
cancelable(_:) controls whether the shown dialog can be canceled. Use this setter so the fragment can adjust its own behavior.

dialog.cancelable(false)

showsDialog(_:) controls whether the fragment displays its content in a dialog window. Set it inside the inherited onCreate(_:) hook:

class SyncStatusDialog: DialogFragment {
    override func onCreate(_ savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        showsDialog(true)
    }
}

style(_:_:) selects a basic appearance and an Int32 theme value before dialog creation. The styles are .normal, .noTitle, .noFrame (content draws the window), and .noInput (also disables input). This call requests no title area:

dialog.style(.noTitle, 0)

docs.title: Reading current state
docs.text:
dialog() returns the controlled Dialog as an optional. Inspect its presence without using it to show or dismiss the window.

let hasDialog = dialog.dialog() != nil

showsDialog() reads whether the fragment is configured to display a dialog.

let displaysDialog = dialog.showsDialog()

theme() returns the Int32 theme value used to create the dialog.

let dialogTheme = dialog.theme()

isCancelable() reads whether the dialog is cancelable.

let canCancel = dialog.isCancelable()

docs.title: Dismissing the dialog
docs.text:
dismiss() dismisses the fragment and its dialog. Call it when the sync operation finishes.

dialog.dismiss()

dismissAllowingStateLoss() uses commitAllowingStateLoss, permitting the commit after activity state has been saved. The commit can be lost when the activity is restored, so use it only when an unexpected UI-state change is acceptable.

dialog.dismissAllowingStateLoss()

dismissNow() uses synchronous commitNow. It must run before the activity saves its state; it does not allow state loss.

dialog.dismissNow()

docs.title: DrawerLayout
docs.text: DrawerLayout is available in Droid as an AndroidX container. The Swift API documented here supports construction, with or without child views.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use this page when you need to construct the available AndroidX DrawerLayout ViewGroup. At the verified source version, the Swift wrapper documents construction only.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text: You can create the container without body content or provide children through a BodyBuilder closure. The builder accepts multiple children, despite its closure type being named BodyBuilder.SingleView.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Construct a container with an explicit ID and no body content:

let drawerLayout = DrawerLayout(id: 100)

Provide multiple ordinary child views through the builder:

DrawerLayout {
    TextView("Main content")
    TextView("Additional content")
}

Both snippets demonstrate construction only. They do not assign a drawer role or side, open a drawer, or establish Android runtime behavior.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
init(id: Int32? = nil) constructs the container without body content. The optional ID defaults to nil.

init(id: Int32? = nil, @BodyBuilder content: BodyBuilder.SingleView) constructs the container with builder content. The ID has the same default; the content closure is required and can provide multiple children. The builder and its closure run in main-actor context.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: At the verified source version, the Swift wrapper does not expose supported drawer-role or placement configuration, open/close calls, lock-mode controls, state callbacks/listeners, or a verified drawer interaction API.

docs.title: FragmentActivity
docs.text:
FragmentActivity is a ComponentActivity-based activity that can host support fragments. Use it to give a screen a fragment-managed content area.

The activity owns the fragment manager; each Fragment supplies its own content. A FragmentContainerView provides a place for that content in the activity's layout.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use FragmentActivity when a screen needs to install or manage fragments and does not need AppCompat-specific activity features.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
supportFragmentManager() returns the manager associated with this activity as FragmentManager!, an implicitly unwrapped optional. It can return nil when the activity context is unavailable or the Java class or method lookup fails. Unwrap it before starting a transaction.

Create and commit transactions before the activity saves its state. commit() schedules the change on the main thread; the fragment does not appear synchronously when that call returns.

docs.title: Show a welcome fragment
docs.text:
This activity creates a full-size fragment container, then installs a fragment displaying “Welcome to your library”. The shared container ID connects the transaction to the view. If the manager already has a fragment for that ID, the example leaves it in place instead of adding another one.

import Droid

final class LibraryActivity: FragmentActivity {
    private let contentId: Int32 = 1001

    override func onCreate(
        _ context: ActivityContext,
        savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ) {
        super.onCreate(context, savedInstanceState: savedInstanceState)

        contentView(
            FragmentContainerView(id: contentId)
                .width(.matchParent)
                .height(.matchParent)
        )

        guard let manager = supportFragmentManager(),
              manager.findFragmentById(contentId) == nil,
              let fragment = Fragment(),
              let transaction = manager.beginTransaction()
        else { return }

        fragment.body {
            TextView().textKeepState("Welcome to your library")
        }

        guard let addition = transaction.add(
            containerViewId: contentId,
            fragment: fragment
        ) else { return }

        addition.commit()
    }
}

For fragment content and further transaction operations, continue with the fragment guide.

docs.title: Get the activity's fragment manager
docs.text:
Use supportFragmentManager() to obtain the manager for this host. For example, a fragment operation can first check whether the host has already saved its state:

if let manager = supportFragmentManager() {
    let stateSaved = manager.isStateSaved()
    print("Library fragment state saved: \(stateSaved)")
}

docs.title: Launch an activity on behalf of a fragment
docs.text:
startActivityFromFragment(_:_:requestCode:) forwards a fragment, an Intent, and an Int request code to the activity. The second overload adds options: Bundle. Options are optional in the sense that you can choose the overload without them; the options parameter itself does not accept nil.

The source describes these as the host-side implementation of fragment launches for a result. It does not expose Fragment.startActivityForResult(), so these methods alone are not a complete fragment result-handling flow. Both return without launching if the activity context is unavailable.

Given an existing fragment and an intent configured for the activity to open, call one of the two forms on the host:

@MainActor
func launchFromFragment(
    host: FragmentActivity,
    fragment: Fragment,
    intent: Intent,
    options: Bundle?
) {
    if let options {
        host.startActivityFromFragment(
            fragment, intent, requestCode: 42, options: options
        )
    } else {
        host.startActivityFromFragment(fragment, intent, requestCode: 42)
    }
}

docs.title: FragmentContainerView
docs.text:
FragmentContainerView is a fragment-specific container based on FrameLayout. A fragment transaction can address this view by its ID.

Pass an explicit ID when transaction code needs a known container ID. If id is omitted, the inherited View initializer generates one.

The component provides an initializer without a body closure and a builder-closure overload. Fragment manager and transaction APIs belong to FragmentActivity, FragmentManager, and FragmentTransaction.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use it when a layout needs a dedicated fragment host that a transaction can target by ID. An explicit ID lets the layout and the transaction refer to the same slot.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
FragmentContainerView extends FrameLayout, so its inherited width and height modifiers can request .matchParent sizing for a child of a FrameLayout. These modifiers express a sizing request; they do not establish final geometry or window attachment.

FragmentActivity provides access to a fragment manager. The manager creates transactions and reports whether its state has been saved; a transaction can request replacement for a container ID. These APIs are separate from the container view.

docs.title: Add a fragment slot to a host
docs.text:
This builds a FrameLayout with a FragmentContainerView child whose ID is 300. The child requests the host's available width and height.

@MainActor
func fragmentHost() -> FrameLayout {
    FrameLayout {
        FragmentContainerView(id: 300)
            .width(.matchParent)
            .height(.matchParent)
    }
}

docs.title: Request a fragment replacement
docs.text:
When the guard passes, this requests a replacement transaction for the container with ID 300. The helper skips transaction setup when the manager reports saved state and checks each optional API result.

@MainActor
func install(_ fragment: Fragment, in activity: FragmentActivity) {
    guard let manager = activity.supportFragmentManager(),
          !manager.isStateSaved(),
          let transaction = manager.beginTransaction(),
          let replacement = transaction.replace(
              containerViewId: 300,
              fragment: fragment
          ),
          replacement.commit() != nil else {
        return
    }
}

commit() schedules the request on the main thread; it does not execute immediately. The source warns that committing after the containing Activity has saved its state throws. The saved-state check is a guard, not a guarantee that the commit succeeds. A non-nil commit ID does not prove execution or display.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
• init(id: Int32? = nil) creates the container without a content closure.
  • init(id: Int32? = nil, @BodyBuilder content: BodyBuilder.SingleView) accepts a builder closure.

Both initializers accept an optional ID. With no explicit ID, the inherited View initializer generates one. Supply an explicit ID when another API needs to target this container by a known value.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The builder initializer exists, but its declaration alone does not establish that arbitrary ordinary views are compatible as children of a fragment-managed container or that the closure renders fragments. Keep ordinary layout views outside FragmentContainerView.

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text: Fragment is a reusable part of a screen with its own view. An activity can host several fragments, and a fragment can host another fragment when a screen needs nested sections.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use a fragment when a screen has sections that should be created, replaced, or reused independently—for example, a list beside a detail pane or a settings area inside a larger flow.

Use a child fragment when one part of a screen needs its own fragment content area. Keep the container and the fragment manager in the same parent fragment so nested content stays within that screen section.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Override buildUI() and set the fragment's view with body { ... }. Droid calls buildUI() while creating the view returned from onCreateView. If the body produces several sibling views, Droid wraps them in a FrameLayout; use an explicit layout such as LinearLayout when the children need a particular arrangement. Without a body, the current implementation displays a centered “Empty Fragment Content” placeholder.

Each fragment has a parentFragmentManager() for the manager associated with its host. A nested fragment can use childFragmentManager() to manage its own children. The host activity exposes its manager through FragmentActivity, and FragmentContainerView provides a fragment-specific content area.

At the current Droid source pin, the Swift wrappers expose only their implemented methods. The AndroidX FragmentManager and FragmentTransaction references explain those concepts; they do not describe the complete Swift API available through Droid.

docs.title: Build a fragment view
docs.text:
This fragment displays two lines of account information in a vertical layout.

import Droid

final class AccountSummaryFragment: Fragment {
    override func buildUI() {
        body {
            LinearLayout {
                TextView("Account")
                TextView("Plan: Standard")
            }
            .orientation(.vertical)
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Show nested details
docs.text:
The parent owns a FragmentContainerView, then uses its child manager to replace the content after the parent view has been created.

import Droid

final class AccountHostFragment: Fragment {
    private let detailsContainerID: Int32 = 41

    override func buildUI() {
        let containerID = detailsContainerID
        body {
            FragmentContainerView(id: containerID)
        }
    }

    func showDetails(_ details: Fragment) {
        guard
            !isStateSaved(),
            let manager = childFragmentManager(),
            let transaction = manager.beginTransaction()
        else { return }

        transaction
            .replace(containerViewId: detailsContainerID, fragment: details)?
            .commit()
    }
}

Use the same detailsContainerID for FragmentContainerView and replace; it identifies the target container. Do not begin or commit the transaction after the host has saved its state.

docs.title: Build the view
docs.text:
buildUI() is the hook Droid calls while creating the fragment's view. Use body { ... } to provide one root view; put multiple arranged children inside a layout.

override func buildUI() {
    body {
        TextView("Profile")
    }
}

docs.title: Choose the fragment manager
docs.text:
Use parentFragmentManager() to work with the manager that owns this fragment. Use childFragmentManager() for content nested inside it. Both return the manager used to begin a FragmentTransaction; the example above shows a focused replace flow rather than a full transaction catalog.

Use the parent manager when this fragment should be replaced in its host's container:

func replaceThisSection(with next: Fragment, in containerID: Int32) {
    guard
        !isStateSaved(),
        let transaction = parentFragmentManager()?.beginTransaction()
    else { return }

    transaction.replace(containerViewId: containerID, fragment: next)?.commit()
}

docs.title: Check the host and view state
docs.text:
activity(), context(), view(), arguments(), host(), and parentFragment() return optional values. The corresponding requireActivity(), requireContext(), requireView(), requireArguments(), requireHost(), and requireParentFragment() methods use implicitly unwrapped optionals at the Swift boundary. Use the optional accessors while detachment or missing arguments are possible.

The state queries include isAdded(), isDetached(), isHidden(), isInLayout(), isRemoving(), isResumed(), isStateSaved(), and isVisible(). Check isStateSaved() before changing fragment state.

docs.title: Supply arguments
docs.text:
Call arguments(_:) before the fragment is added, or before its manager has saved state. The bundle is retained across fragment destruction and recreation; arguments() reads it back as an optional value.

func configureBeforeAdding(_ bundle: Bundle) {
    arguments(bundle)
}

docs.title: Coordinate transitions
docs.text:
postponeEnterTransition() delays an entering fragment transition. Call it before adding the fragment, or during onCreate, onAttach, or onCreateView; call startPostponedEnterTransition() when the content is ready.

func beginLoadingContent() {
    postponeEnterTransition()
}

func contentDidLoad() {
    startPostponedEnterTransition()
}

The wrapper also exposes enter/return overlap controls and transition getters and setters. For example, allowEnterTransitionOverlap(false) waits for the exit transition to finish before starting the enter transition.

docs.title: Start an activity
docs.text:
startActivity(_:) starts an intent from the fragment. The overload with options: accepts a Bundle of launch options.

func open(_ intent: Intent, options: Bundle) {
    guard isAdded(), activity() != nil else { return }
    startActivity(intent, options: options)
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(permission:) returns true from its default implementation at this source pin. Do not use that default to infer whether Android has previously denied a permission.
  • FragmentManager.beginTransaction() must be used before the host saves its state. isStateSaved() is available for a guard; commitAllowingStateLoss() exists but its source documentation warns that the transaction may be lost and the UI may change unexpectedly.

docs.title: RecyclerView
docs.text: RecyclerView shows a scrollable collection of item views. A layout manager selects their arrangement; an adapter supplies the item count, creates views, and binds each view to its data.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use it for a list or grid whose rows come from a collection, such as a catalogue, message list, or search results. Choose a layout manager for the arrangement and keep the adapter's data consistent with the changes you report.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
RecyclerView.adapter(...) builds a RecyclerViewAdapter behind the scenes. Its item views conform to Viewable; View already conforms, so a TextView can be used directly. createView supplies a view and bindView receives that view and an item position. The item-data overload also passes the item itself.

The nested RecyclerView.Adapter is the underlying adapter slot/type used when attaching this generic Swift adapter. Use the generic route shown here.

An ordinary items: array expression is evaluated through an escaping autoclosure when the adapter reads its count or an item. Mutating that array does not emit notifications. Keep the data in storage that the closure can read, then notify the matching change.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
This list displays thirty numbered rows:

let recyclerView = RecyclerView()
    .layoutManager(.linear(orientation: .vertical))
    .adapter(
        count: 30,
        createView: TextView(),
        bindView: { view, index in
            view.textKeepState("Item \(index + 1)")
        }
    )

For mutable item data, keep both the array and the view on an owning object. These properties display the current destination names and support the notification examples below:

@MainActor
final class DestinationList {
    var items = ["Yerevan", "Gyumri", "Dilijan"]

    lazy var recyclerView = RecyclerView()
        .layoutManager(.linear(orientation: .vertical))
        .adapter(
            items: self.items,
            createView: TextView(),
            bindView: { view, item, _ in
                view.textKeepState(item)
            }
        )
}

docs.title: Adapter inputs
docs.text:
The count: overload binds by index. The ordinary items: array overload also passes each item to bindView. Both forms accept a view expression or a zero-argument creation closure:

RecyclerView()
    .layoutManager(.linear(orientation: .vertical))
    .adapter(
        count: 10,
        createView: { TextView() },
        bindView: { view, index in
            view.textKeepState("Result \(index + 1)")
        }
    )

docs.title: Layout managers
docs.text:
layoutManager(_:) accepts a LayoutManager. The base type exposes itemPrefetchEnabled(_:), which controls whether it is queried for views outside its viewport while the UI thread is idle between frames. Configure it on the selected manager:

RecyclerView().layoutManager(
    LinearLayoutManager(orientation: .vertical)
        .itemPrefetchEnabled(true)
)

LayoutManager.linear, .grid, and .staggeredGrid are convenience factories for the corresponding concrete managers. Specify .vertical or .horizontal explicitly when direction matters.

docs.title: LinearLayoutManager
docs.text:
Use a linear manager for a vertical or horizontal list. Pass direction to its initializer; reverseLayout(_:) reverses traversal and layout order, and stackFromEnd(_:) fills from the opposite end, such as the bottom of a vertical list.

RecyclerView().layoutManager(
    .linear(orientation: .vertical)
        .reverseLayout()
        .stackFromEnd(true)
)

recycleChildrenOnDetach(_:) controls whether children are recycled when the manager detaches. initialPrefetchItemCount(_:) sets the number of inner items to prefetch when this list is nested in another RecyclerView. smoothScrollbarEnabled(false) avoids pixel-based scrollbar calculations that assume similarly sized items.

LinearLayoutManager(orientation: .horizontal)
    .recycleChildrenOnDetach(true)
    .initialPrefetchItemCount(4)
    .smoothScrollbarEnabled(false)

docs.title: GridLayoutManager
docs.text:
A grid manager takes a span count. For vertical orientation, spans are columns; for horizontal orientation, they are rows. It inherits the linear manager configuration methods.

let grid = GridLayoutManager(spanCount: 3, orientation: .vertical)
RecyclerView().layoutManager(grid.usingSpansToEstimateScrollbarDimensions(true))

usingSpansToEstimateScrollbarDimensions(_:) includes span information in scroll offset and range calculations.

docs.title: StaggeredGridLayoutManager
docs.text:
The staggered manager requires both span count and orientation. reverseLayout(_:) reverses traversal and layout order. gapStrategy(_:) selects how gaps are handled; changing the strategy requests layout.

RecyclerView().layoutManager(
    .staggeredGrid(spanCount: 2, orientation: .vertical)
        .gapStrategy(.moveItemsBetweenSpans)
        .reverseLayout()
)

.none leaves gaps alone. .moveItemsBetweenSpans checks for gaps when scrolling becomes idle and can move items to correct them. .lazy is marked deprecated and unsupported.

docs.title: FlexboxLayoutManager
docs.text:
Configure Flexbox direction and wrapping through the initializer, then set alignment with alignItems(_:):

RecyclerView().layoutManager(
    FlexboxLayoutManager(flexDirection: .row, flexWrap: .wrap)
        .alignItems(.flexStart)
)

flexDirection(_:) and flexWrap(_:) also expose those settings as methods. Direction cases are .row, .rowReverse, .column, and .columnReverse; wrapping cases are .noWrap, .wrap, and .wrapReverse. Alignment cases are .flexStart, .flexEnd, .center, .baseline, and .stretch.

RecyclerView().layoutManager(
    FlexboxLayoutManager()
        .flexDirection(.column)
        .flexWrap(.noWrap)
        .alignItems(.center)
)

docs.title: Fixed item size
docs.text:
Use hasFixedSize(true) only when all item views keep an identical fixed size in the scrolling direction: height for a vertical list or width for a horizontal list. For content-dependent sizes, keep it disabled:

recyclerView.hasFixedSize(false)

docs.title: Report item changes
docs.text:
For the ordinary array example, the following snippets are separate operations inside DestinationList methods. Mutate the data first, then report the same positions and counts. Use precise notifications when you know the change; these calls forward to the attached adapter and do not mutate your data.

Insert or remove one item with notifyItemInserted(at:) or notifyItemRemoved(at:):

items.insert("Vanadzor", at: 1)
recyclerView.notifyItemInserted(at: 1)

items.remove(at: 1)
recyclerView.notifyItemRemoved(at: 1)

Report a changed item with notifyItemChanged(at:), or a move with notifyItemMoved(fromPosition:toPosition:):

items[0] = "Yerevan centre"
recyclerView.notifyItemChanged(at: 0)

let moved = items.remove(at: 0)
items.insert(moved, at: 2)
recyclerView.notifyItemMoved(fromPosition: 0, toPosition: 2)

For contiguous changes, use the corresponding range notification:

items.insert(contentsOf: ["Sevan", "Goris"], at: 0)
recyclerView.notifyItemRangeInserted(startAt: 0, count: 2)

items[0] = "Lake Sevan"
items[1] = "Goris centre"
recyclerView.notifyItemRangeChanged(startAt: 0, count: 2)

items.removeSubrange(0..<2)
recyclerView.notifyItemRangeRemoved(startAt: 0, count: 2)

When replacing the entire collection without a precise change description, notifyDataSetChanged() reports a full refresh:

items = ["Kapan", "Meghri"]
recyclerView.notifyDataSetChanged()

docs.title: Paging helper
docs.text:
paginable() constructs a PagerSnapHelper and calls its attachToRecyclerView method:

recyclerView.paginable()

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Paging is unverified at this source revision: PagerSnapHelper.attachToRecyclerView signs the view argument as PagerSnapHelper.className. The exposed call therefore does not establish that page snapping works at runtime.

docs.title: SlidingPaneLayout
docs.text:
Use SlidingPaneLayout when a Swift view tree needs the AndroidX SlidingPaneLayout container with child views supplied inside it.

Droid lets you declare those children through a @BodyBuilder content initializer. This page covers construction of that view tree.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use the content initializer when you want to declare the container and its child views together in Swift.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text: The Swift API provides two construction forms: an optional Int32 ID alone, or an optional ID with a required @BodyBuilder closure. The closure can supply one or more child views. These signatures describe construction; they do not assign pane roles or specify how Android arranges or interacts with the children.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The first root view contains a text child labeled “No item selected.” The second contains two text children labeled “Choose a record” and “Record details.”

let emptyStateContent = FrameLayout(id: 100)
emptyStateContent.body {
    SlidingPaneLayout(id: 200) {
        TextView(id: 201, "No item selected")
    }
}

let recordContent = FrameLayout(id: 110)
recordContent.body {
    SlidingPaneLayout(id: 210) {
        TextView(id: 211, "Choose a record")
        TextView(id: 212, "Record details")
    }
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
The ID is optional. To create the container without passing child content, use the ID-only initializer:

let layout = SlidingPaneLayout(id: 300)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: At the inspected source pin, the Droid type declares no SlidingPaneLayout-specific interaction controls.

docs.title: ViewPager
docs.text: At Droid source pin ab7a20dca6b6173848ad25dfd1411399a7d7012c, Droid does not expose a live type-specific Swift view wrapper or callable view constructor for ViewPager, ViewPager2, PagerTabStrip, or PagerTitleStrip.

docs.title: AppCompatButton
docs.text:
AppCompatButton is an AppCompat button with controls for EmojiCompat fallback in its text. Use these controls when the button’s text may contain emoji that EmojiCompat should attempt to supply.

It inherits the text and view behavior of Button. The methods below let you enable or disable EmojiCompat fallback on an existing button and read back its enabled state.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use AppCompatButton when you need to choose whether an existing AppCompat button attempts EmojiCompat fallback for missing emoji in its label.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Calling emojiCompatEnabled() enables attempts to use EmojiCompat for missing emoji. Passing false prevents that fallback. The setting is applied to the underlying button or queued until its instance is available.

isEmojiCompatEnabled() returns the enabled state reported by the underlying button. It returns false if the Java instance or call result is unavailable. This Boolean is API readback, not proof that an emoji was rendered successfully.

docs.title: Enable fallback for missing emoji
docs.text:
This enables EmojiCompat fallback on an existing button. With correct device configuration, EmojiCompat can provide fallback for missing emoji.

@MainActor
func enableEmojiFallback(on button: AppCompatButton) {
    button.emojiCompatEnabled()
}

docs.title: Disable fallback and read the setting
docs.text:
This disables EmojiCompat fallback and returns the API’s enabled-state readback. The returned value does not verify the button’s visible text.

@MainActor
func disableEmojiFallback(on button: AppCompatButton) -> Bool {
    button.emojiCompatEnabled(false)
    return button.isEmojiCompatEnabled()
}

docs.title: emojiCompatEnabled
docs.text:
Enable or disable EmojiCompat fallback. This method is inherited from View and returns the button for chaining; you can also ignore the return value. Omitting the argument passes true, which does not establish the initial state of a newly constructed button.

@MainActor
func disableEmojiFallback(on button: AppCompatButton) {
    button.emojiCompatEnabled(false)
}

docs.title: isEmojiCompatEnabled
docs.text:
Read whether the underlying button reports EmojiCompat as enabled. An unavailable Java instance or call result produces false.

@MainActor
func emojiFallbackIsEnabled(on button: AppCompatButton) -> Bool {
    button.isEmojiCompatEnabled()
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: EmojiCompat must be correctly configured on the device for fallback to have a visible effect. This configuration is available by default when a correct downloadable-fonts provider is installed. If you initialize EmojiCompat manually after constructing the button, you may call emojiCompatEnabled() again to enable fallback.
