docs.title: Toolbar (AppCompat)
docs.text:
Toolbar is an app bar for use within application content. Its direct methods let you refresh an existing menu, inspect overflow and expanded action views, and forward events or direction-change callbacks.

Keep a reference to the toolbar when application state changes need a menu refresh or when you need to inspect its current menu state.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when your screen has an AppCompat toolbar and application events change which menu items should be displayed or enabled.

Use its state queries when you need to inspect overflow visibility, an expanded action view, or whether the toolbar will attempt back-callback registration in supported configurations. Event-forwarding methods are useful when you already have the corresponding event or direction callback to pass along.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Run these calls on the main actor. Each Boolean method forwards the Java result when an instance exists, or returns false when it does not. A pre-instantiation false therefore does not establish the toolbar's Android state. The two methods without a result, invalidateMenu() and onRtlPropertiesChanged(_:), skip forwarding when no instance exists.

Menu invalidation refreshes items supplied by menu providers after menu state changes. Manually inflated items remain manually managed. Overflow visibility is a current-state query and may not reflect a pending show operation.

docs.title: Refresh after application menu state changes
docs.text:
After your application changes existing menu state, such as disabling an item in response to a user action, request a refresh on its instantiated toolbar. This call returns no value.

@MainActor
func refreshMenu(afterAppMenuStateChange toolbar: Toolbar) {
    toolbar.invalidateMenu()
}

docs.title: Request that overflow items be hidden
docs.text:
When your application needs to dismiss overflow items on an instantiated toolbar, pass it to this helper. The helper returns the Boolean from hideOverflowMenu() as-is; the Swift method does not define it as success or as a change in visibility.

@MainActor
func hideOverflowItems(on toolbar: Toolbar) -> Bool {
    return toolbar.hideOverflowMenu()
}

docs.title: Menu refresh and overflow
docs.text:
invalidateMenu() requests that the displayed menu reflect its current state. Call it after an application menu-state change. Only items supplied by menu providers should be removed and repopulated; manually inflated items remain under your application's management.

@MainActor
func refreshChangedMenu(on toolbar: Toolbar) {
    toolbar.invalidateMenu()
}

isOverflowMenuShowing() queries whether the overflow menu is currently showing. A pending show operation may not yet appear in this result.

@MainActor
func inspectOverflow(on toolbar: Toolbar) -> Bool {
    let showing = toolbar.isOverflowMenuShowing()
    return showing
}

hideOverflowMenu() requests hiding the associated menu's overflow items. Its Boolean is forwarded without a success or state-change interpretation defined by this Swift method.

@MainActor
func requestOverflowHide(on toolbar: Toolbar) -> Bool {
    let hideResult = toolbar.hideOverflowMenu()
    return hideResult
}

docs.title: Expanded action views and back invocation
docs.text:
hasExpandedActionView() checks whether this toolbar currently hosts an expanded action view.

@MainActor
func inspectExpandedActionView(on toolbar: Toolbar) -> Bool {
    let expanded = toolbar.hasExpandedActionView()
    return expanded
}

isBackInvokedCallbackEnabled() reports whether the toolbar will attempt to register its own back-invocation callback in supported configurations to collapse expanded action items. The result does not establish support in every configuration.

@MainActor
func inspectBackCallback(on toolbar: Toolbar) -> Bool {
    let callbackEnabled = toolbar.isBackInvokedCallbackEnabled()
    return callbackEnabled
}

docs.title: Event and direction callbacks
docs.text:
onHoverEvent(_:) forwards an existing MotionEvent to the toolbar's Java hover-event method, identifying the argument as a MotionEvent. Return the forwarded Boolean to the caller without assigning additional event-consumption meaning to it.

@MainActor
func forwardHover(to toolbar: Toolbar, event: MotionEvent) -> Bool {
    let hoverResult = toolbar.onHoverEvent(event)
    return hoverResult
}

onTouchEvent(_:) forwards an existing MotionEvent to the corresponding Java touch-event method with the same argument type. This helper returns its Boolean result.

@MainActor
func forwardTouch(to toolbar: Toolbar, event: MotionEvent) -> Bool {
    let touchResult = toolbar.onTouchEvent(event)
    return touchResult
}

onRtlPropertiesChanged(_:) forwards a direction-change callback using the supplied LayoutDirection value's raw value. It returns no result. Use it to forward an existing callback; it is not a layout-direction setter and does not itself promise a visible layout change.

@MainActor
func forwardDirectionChange(to toolbar: Toolbar, direction: LayoutDirection) {
    toolbar.onRtlPropertiesChanged(direction)
}

docs.title: AppBarConfiguration
docs.text:
AppBarConfiguration holds the options that NavigationUI uses to configure app-bar behavior around top-level destinations. Choose which destinations should hide the Up button, then build a configuration to pass to NavigationUI.

NavigationUI consumes the configuration when it sets up an app bar or handles Up navigation. Creating a configuration alone does not connect or update a toolbar.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text:
Use it when your graph's start destination should be the app's only top-level screen, or when several destinations—such as Home, Search, and Library—should each hide the Up button.

Use the menu-based builder when a navigation menu already identifies those top-level destinations.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
A graph-based builder uses the graph's start destination as its only top-level destination. An ID-based builder uses the supplied destination IDs. A menu-based builder uses the menu item IDs; each item ID is expected to correspond to a destination in the navigation graph.

The Up button is not shown on those top-level destinations when NavigationUI applies the configuration. isTopLevelDestination(_:) lets you query whether a NavDestination was directly configured as top level.

Builder construction can fail, and build() returns AppBarConfiguration?. Handle the optional result before passing it to NavigationUI.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Build a configuration for a graph whose start destination should hide the Up button:

@MainActor
func makeAppBarConfiguration(for graph: NavGraph) -> AppBarConfiguration? {
    guard let builder = AppBarConfiguration.Builder(graph) else { return nil }
    return builder.build()
}

For several top-level screens, pass their actual destination IDs. This helper accepts the IDs assigned to Home, Search, and Library in your graph:

@MainActor
func makeTopLevelConfiguration(
    homeID: Int32,
    searchID: Int32,
    libraryID: Int32
) -> AppBarConfiguration? {
    AppBarConfiguration.Builder(homeID, searchID, libraryID)?.build()
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Choose AppBarConfiguration.Builder(graph) for a single top-level start destination, as in the first example. Choose the variadic ID initializer above or the array initializer when you supply the top-level destinations explicitly:

@MainActor
func makeTopLevelConfiguration(ids: [Int32]) -> AppBarConfiguration? {
    AppBarConfiguration.Builder(ids)?.build()
}

Choose AppBarConfiguration.Builder(menu) when the menu item IDs match the graph's top-level destination IDs:

@MainActor
func makeMenuConfiguration(menu: Menu) -> AppBarConfiguration? {
    AppBarConfiguration.Builder(menu)?.build()
}

docs.title: Build the configuration
docs.text:
Call build() on a successfully created builder to obtain an optional AppBarConfiguration:

@MainActor
func buildConfiguration(
    from builder: AppBarConfiguration.Builder
) -> AppBarConfiguration? {
    builder.build()
}

docs.title: Check top-level membership
docs.text:
Pass a NavDestination to isTopLevelDestination(_:) to check its configured membership. The result is a Bool:

@MainActor
func isTopLevel(
    _ destination: NavDestination,
    in configuration: AppBarConfiguration
) -> Bool {
    configuration.isTopLevelDestination(destination)
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Droid does not expose the fallback navigate-up listener, openable-layout getter, or top-level-destination getter. The Builder's fallback-listener and openable-layout setters are also not declared.

Use the nested Builder to construct a configuration for your app. AppBarConfiguration.init(_ object: JObject) wraps an existing JNI object.

docs.title: NavController
docs.text:
NavController manages navigation through an app's graph. Use an already-configured controller to inspect the current destination and graph, then navigate with directions supplied by your app.

For action-bar setup, Up handling, and menu selection, use NavigationUI. This guide focuses on inspecting navigation state and applying options to a direct navigation call.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use it when you need to read the graph's start destination or navigate to a detail screen with options that avoid another copy of the same destination at the top of the back stack.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Call these APIs from the main actor. currentDestination() returns NavDestination?, and graph() returns NavGraph?; handle their optional results before using them. A graph exposes its start destination ID as an Int32.

Inspecting the graph does not replace it. Replacing a controller's graph replaces its existing navigation data, including the back stack, so graph replacement should be a deliberate setup change.

NavOptions.Builder() can fail, and build() returns NavOptions?. With launchSingleTop(true), navigation requests single-top behavior: at most one copy of a given destination at the top of the back stack. This does not remove every earlier copy of that destination.

The directions-plus-options navigate call returns Void. It provides no Boolean result confirming that navigation succeeded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Both helpers receive a controller whose navigation setup is already complete. The navigation helper also requires existing NavDirections valid for that controller's graph and current destination.

Read the configured start destination ID without changing navigation state:

@MainActor
func currentDestination(in controller: NavController) -> NavDestination? {
    controller.currentDestination()
}

@MainActor
func startDestinationID(using controller: NavController) -> Int32? {
    guard let graph = controller.graph() else { return nil }
    return graph.startDestinationId()
}

Navigate to a detail destination using caller-provided directions and single-top options. If either construction step fails, the helper returns without making the navigation call:

@MainActor
func navigateToDetails(
    using controller: NavController,
    directions: NavDirections
) {
    guard let builder = NavOptions.Builder(),
          let options = builder.launchSingleTop(true).build()
    else { return }

    controller.navigate(directions, options)
}

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: The short calls below belong in a main-actor context, with the controller and directions supplied by the app's navigation setup.

docs.title: Inspect the current destination and graph
docs.text:
Use currentDestination() to retrieve the optional current destination. Use graph() to retrieve the optional graph associated with the controller, then read its start destination ID:

@MainActor
func currentDestination(in controller: NavController) -> NavDestination? {
    controller.currentDestination()
}

@MainActor
func startDestinationID(using controller: NavController) -> Int32? {
    guard let graph = controller.graph() else { return nil }
    return graph.startDestinationId()
}

docs.title: Build navigation options
docs.text:
Call launchSingleTop(_:) on a successfully created builder to request single-top behavior. It returns the same builder for chaining. Call build() to obtain optional options, then unwrap them before navigation:

@MainActor
func makeSingleTopOptions() -> NavOptions? {
    guard let builder = NavOptions.Builder() else { return nil }
    return builder.launchSingleTop(true).build()
}

docs.title: Navigate with directions and options
docs.text:
Pass the existing directions and built options to navigate(_:_:). Both arguments are required for this overload:

@MainActor
func navigateToDetails(
    using controller: NavController,
    directions: NavDirections,
    options: NavOptions
) {
    controller.navigate(directions, options)
}

docs.title: NavHostFragment
docs.text:
NavHostFragment gives one fragment area its own navigation graph. Place it in an existing FragmentContainerView, then use its controller to move between destinations in that graph.

Create the host with the graph resource ID and arguments for its start destination. Creating the fragment does not install it in the activity. A fragment transaction does that separately, and its commit is scheduled work rather than an immediate display guarantee.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use a NavHostFragment when part of a screen needs its own fragment navigation flow. It keeps that flow behind a fragment container while the rest of the activity can remain in place.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
The create factory returns an optional host and accepts a Contextable value along with the graph ID and start-destination Bundle. The container ID you pass to the transaction must already identify a FragmentContainerView in the activity layout.

supportFragmentManager(), beginTransaction(), replace(...), and commit() can each fail. Check their results before continuing. commit() schedules the transaction on the main thread; it does not mean the host is attached or visible yet. Commit before the activity saves its state, or the transaction can fail and its state may be lost.

The host's navController() can remain nil until onCreate has run and the host has had an opportunity to restore saved state. Keep controller use separate from host creation and call it only when the host is ready. These navigation APIs are main-actor isolated.

docs.title: Schedule a host in an existing container
docs.text:
@MainActor
func scheduleNavigationHost(
    in activity: FragmentActivity,
    containerViewId: Int32,
    graphResourceId: Int32,
    startArguments: Bundle,
    context: Contextable
) -> NavHostFragment? {
    guard let host = NavHostFragment.create(
        graphResourceId,
        startArguments,
        context
    ) else {
        return nil
    }

    guard
        let manager = activity.supportFragmentManager(),
        let transaction = manager.beginTransaction(),
        let replacement = transaction.replace(
            containerViewId: containerViewId,
            fragment: host
        ),
        let _ = replacement.commit()
    else {
        return nil
    }

    return host
}

The caller supplies the existing container ID and graph inputs. A returned host means the wrapper calls produced values and the commit was scheduled; it does not confirm attachment or display.

docs.title: Navigate after the host is ready
docs.text:
@MainActor
func showDestination(
    _ destinationId: Int32,
    in host: NavHostFragment
) {
    guard let controller = host.navController() else { return }
    controller.navigate(destinationId)
}

Pass an ID for an action or destination in the host's current graph. navigate(_:) returns no result, so this call does not report whether a destination appeared on screen.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Use create for a graph-backed application host. The required initializer takes an existing JObject. The no-argument IUO initializer and the environment/class-name initializer can fail and should be checked when used by low-level integration code.

The convenience initializer that accepts a JClassName ignores that argument and uses NavHostFragment's own native class name; it does not select a different fragment class. Application code should obtain controllers from a host or the Navigation lookup helpers rather than construct a NavHostController directly.

docs.title: Get a controller from a fragment
docs.text:
Use navController() when you already hold the host. It stays optional until the host has completed onCreate and had a chance to restore saved state:

@MainActor
func controller(for host: NavHostFragment) -> NavController? {
    host.navController()
}

For a destination fragment, the static lookup searches its parent-fragment chain and then its view hierarchy:

@MainActor
func controller(for fragment: Fragment) -> NavController? {
    NavHostFragment.findNavController(fragment)
}

docs.title: Find a controller from a view
docs.text:
Navigation is created from an ActivityContext with a failable initializer. Its view lookup is an instance method and returns an optional controller:

@MainActor
func controller(
    for view: View,
    in context: ActivityContext
) -> NavController? {
    guard let navigation = Navigation(context) else { return nil }
    return navigation.findNavController(view)
}

When you have the host view's ID instead, use the overload that also takes its containing activity context:

@MainActor
func controller(
    for viewId: Int32,
    in context: ActivityContext
) -> NavController? {
    guard let navigation = Navigation(context) else { return nil }
    return navigation.findNavController(context, viewId)
}

The view overload also returns nil if the supplied View has no Android instance. Both lookups return nil when they cannot obtain a controller. See NavController for the operations available after lookup.

docs.title: NavigationUI
docs.text:
NavigationUI keeps an AppCompat action bar aligned with a NavController and handles Up navigation and menu destination selection. Use the same AppBarConfiguration for action-bar setup and Up handling so both follow your top-level destination choices.

The helpers are static: you do not need to create a NavigationUI instance. Call them from the main actor.

docs.title: Use it when…
docs.text: Use it when an AppCompat activity's action-bar title and navigation button should follow the current destination, or when a menu selection should navigate using the item's ID.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
Action-bar setup updates the title when the destination has a valid label. The configuration controls the navigation button, and FloatingWindow destinations are ignored. Setup does not handle the Up action for you; delegate that action separately through navigateUp.

Menu selection requires an item ID that matches a valid action or destination ID. By default, selection pops the back stack to the graph's start destination. Items with android:menuCategory="secondary" do not pop the back stack.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
These functions accept the activity, controller, and configuration already used by your screen. Call the setup function when connecting the action bar, and the Up function when handling the Up action.

@MainActor
func configureActionBar(
    activity: AppCompatActivity,
    navController: NavController,
    configuration: AppBarConfiguration
) {
    NavigationUI.setupActionBarWithNavController(
        activity,
        navController,
        configuration
    )
}

@MainActor
func handleUp(
    navController: NavController,
    configuration: AppBarConfiguration
) -> Bool {
    return NavigationUI.navigateUp(navController, configuration)
}

For a menu-selection handler, pass the selected item and the controller that owns its destination:

@MainActor
func handleDestinationSelection(
    item: MenuItem,
    navController: NavController
) -> Bool {
    return NavigationUI.onNavDestinationSelected(item, navController)
}

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text: NavigationUI is an open, main-actor-isolated JObjectable class with an object: JObject property. If you need an instance, NavigationUI(existingObject) accepts an existing JObject, while NavigationUI(context) accepts a Contextable and can return nil if Java class loading or object creation fails. Neither initializer is required for the static calls above.

docs.title: Connect the action bar
docs.text:
setupActionBarWithNavController takes the hosting AppCompatActivity, its navigation controller, and the configuration that controls the navigation button:

NavigationUI.setupActionBarWithNavController(activity, navController, configuration)

This call returns no result. It returns without setting up the action bar if the activity context or Java class is unavailable.

docs.title: Handle Up
docs.text:
navigateUp uses the supplied configuration when delegating Up handling to the controller:

let handled = NavigationUI.navigateUp(navController, configuration)

The Boolean reports whether Up was handled. A false result also occurs if Java class loading fails or the Java call produces no Boolean result.

docs.title: Navigate from a menu item
docs.text:
onNavDestinationSelected attempts navigation for the selected item's ID and returns whether the navigation attempt succeeded:

let handled = NavigationUI.onNavDestinationSelected(item, navController)
let handledWithState = NavigationUI.onNavDestinationSelected(item, navController, true)

The optional third argument is saveState: Bool?, defaulting to nil. With nil, the Java call omits that argument; a supplied true or false is passed through. A false result can also indicate failed Java class loading or a missing Boolean result.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The Swift AppBarConfiguration.Builder does not expose fallback-listener configuration.

docs.title: JNIKit
docs.text:
It is a foundation library that provides best in class Swift layer for Java Native Interface with automatic memory management, convenient methods to work with Java objects, beautiful wrappers for Java types, and more.

Yeah nah it's not swift-java, it's an alternative foundation provided by the Swift Stream Family.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Open your Package.swift and add the following dependency:

// package dependencies
.package(url: "https://github.com/swifdroid/jni-kit.git", from: "2.10.0")

// target dependencies
.product(name: "JNIKit", package: "jni-kit")

Then head to the → basics

docs.title: 1D Arrays
docs.text:
Swift array wrappers for Java types:

Swift Type JNI Type Swift Array [Int8] jbyte[] JInt8Array or JByteArray [Int16] jshort[] JInt16Array or JShortArray [Int32] jint[] JInt32Array or JIntArray [Int64] jlong[] JInt64Array or JLongArray [UInt16] jchar[] JUInt16Array or JCharArray [Bool] jboolean[] JBoolArray [Float] jfloat[] JFloatArray [Double] jdouble[] JDoubleArray [Any] jobject[] JObjectArray

docs.title: Ways of initialization
docs.text:
With a Swift Array

JIntArray([1, 2, 3])

With a Swift InlineArray

let inlineArray: InlineArray<5, Int32> = [1, 2 ,3, 4, 5]
JIntArray(inlineArray)

Manually

let intArray = JIntArray(length: 3)!
#if os(Android)
var cArray: [Int32] = [1, 2, 3]
JEnv.current()?.setIntArrayRegion(intArray.object.ref.ref, start: 0, length: Int32(intArray.length), buffer: &cArray)
#endif

docs.title: Copy into a Swift Array
docs.text:
let intArray: JIntArray = ...
let swiftArray: [Int32] = intArray.toArray()

⚠️ Be careful with large arrays, copying them may consume a lot of memory.

docs.title: Iteration
docs.text:
Use this approach when working with large arrays:

let intArray: JIntArray = ...
for value in intArray {
    Log.d("value: \(value)")
}

docs.title: 2D Arrays
docs.text:
You can pass and receive not only [Int], but also [[Int]], [[Float]], and other similar types (listed above). This is a common pattern in Java and is often used in Android APIs, for instance, ColorStateList expects nested arrays for its state definitions.

The naming convention is the same, just add 2D in the end

Swift Type JNI Type Swift Array [[Int8]] jbyte[][] JInt8Array2D or JByteArray2D [[Int16]] jshort[][] JInt16Array2D or JShortArray2D [[Int32]] jint[][] JInt32Array2D or JIntArray2D [[Int64]] jlong[][] JInt64Array2D or JLongArray2D [[UInt16]] jchar[][] JUInt16Array2D or JCharArray2D [[Bool]] jboolean[][] JBoolArray2D [[Float]] jfloat[][] JFloatArray2D [[Double]] jdouble[][] JDoubleArray2D

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
Just as easy as with 1D arrays:

let intArray2d = JIntArray2D([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Equally straightforward:

let swiftArray: [[Int32]] = intArray2d.toArray()

docs.title: Iteration
docs.text:
Iteration is supported as well:

for array in intArray2d {
    Log.d("arrray: \(array)")
}

docs.title: Passing Arrays as Arguments
docs.text:
If a JNI method or constructor accepts a 1D or 2D array, you can simply pass it directly, no extra work needed:

object.callVoidMethod(name: "send1DArray", args: [1, 2, 3])
object.callVoidMethod(name: "send2DArray", args: [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])

docs.title: Basics of JNI in Swift
docs.text:
All communication between Swift and Java code happens via JNI – Java Native Interface.

It is low-level C-based API that allows calling Java methods, accessing fields, creating objects, and more. As well as allowing Java code to call Swift functions which are exposed via @_cdecl.

docs.title: JNI Environment
docs.text:
The main concept of JNI is the JNIEnv pointer, which represents the JNI environment. It is used to interact with the JVM (Java Virtual Machine) from native code.

Lifecycle looks like this:

  1. You initialize JNI connection from Java side by calling a Swift function exposed via @_cdecl.
  2. You receive JNIEnv pointer in that function as the first argument.
  3. You can use that pointer to create JEnv instance from JNIKit, which provides a beautiful Swift layer over JNI C API.
  4. Using JEnv instance, you can create Java objects, call methods, access fields, and more.

Since Swift is concurrent by design, each thread must attach itself to the JVM to obtain its own JNIEnv pointer. JNIKit handles this automatically when you call JEnv.current().

Read more about → environment.

docs.title: Local and Global References
docs.text:
The second concept of JNI is that it provides pointers to Java objects.

By JNI design, each Java object pointer passed to Swift as a local reference, meaning it can only be used within the current thread.

Original lifecycle looks like this:

  1. Java object pointer passed to Swift as a local reference.
  2. You use that local reference within the current thread.
  3. You convert it to a global reference manually.
  4. You release the local reference.
  5. When you no longer need the global reference, you release it manually.

JNIKit takes care of the heavy lifting for you. All local references are seamlessly converted into global references, ensuring smooth operation in concurrent scenarios. These global references are automatically managed and released when their corresponding Swift objects are deinitialized, so you can focus on writing Swift code without worrying about reference lifecycles.

With JNIKit lifecycle looks like this:

  1. Java object pointer passed to Swift as a local reference.
  2. JNIKit is wrapping it into JObject which automatically converts it into a global reference.
  3. When JObject is deinitialized, it automatically releases the global reference.

Important

JObject can be used across different threads safely.

docs.title: Naming convention
docs.text:
Let's talk about declaring JNI methods on the Swift side with @_cdecl.

@_cdecl naming convention is important as it follows JNI naming pattern Java_<package>_<class>_<method>, where: <package> is the fully qualified package name with underscores instead of dots <class> is the class name <method> is the method name

Let's say you have a package com.mylib.somecode which contains AwesomeCode class which contains exported hello method. @_cdecl for it will be:

@_cdecl("Java_com_mylib_somecode_AwesomeCode_hello")

Method arguments vary depending on your class and method declaration.

The first argument is required and is always a pointer to the JNI environment, which is used to interact with the JVM.

envPointer: UnsafeMutablePointer<JNIEnv?>

The second argument is required and depends on whether the method is static or not.

So it could be

thizRef: jobject

if the method is instance-based (non-static), in which case it will pass the instance from which it was called.

Or it could be

clazzRef: jobject

if method was static so it will pass just a reference to the Java class.

The next arguments are optional and directly represent the arguments declared in the Java method.

The return type can be empty (void) or can return a value (even an optional one).

The method can't be marked async, as it is not supported by @_cdecl. However, it is still possible to run asynchronous code in Swift if the original Java method was running on a non-UI thread.

docs.title: Wrapping up
docs.text:
First two arguments are required and passed into Swift automatically by JVM↔JNI mechanism, while third and subsequent arguments are actually arguments from your Java method.

Continue to → initialization to start coding.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
When working with JNI, it is important to minimize roundtrips to retrieve the same resources repeatedly. The JNICache implementation handles this by automatically storing jclass instances (by name), methodIDs, and fieldIDs for classes you have already used.

You don't need to do anything for this, it caches these things automatically under the hood.

And yes, it is thread-safe.

Beautiful, let's learn the → types.

docs.title: Casting
docs.text:
There are two situations where you need to cast an object from one class to another.

  1. When you want to treat an existing object as an instance of another class (usually a parent) to call a method or access a field.

This is done using the cast(to:) method of JObject. It creates a proxy JObject of the target class but retains the same underlying JNI reference:

let editText: EditText
let textView = editText.cast(to: TextView.className)
  1. When you need to pass an object to a method that expects a different class (also usually a parent).

This is done using the signed(as:) method of JObject:

let customView: CustomView
object.callVoidMethod(name: "setView", args: customView.signed(as: View.className))

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Loading a class is the first thing you will face.

There are a few ways to load it.

docs.title: Via env
docs.text:
let env = JEnv.current()!
let clazz: JClass = env.findClass("com/mylib/mypackage/MyClass")

This way you will use the system's class loader, which will fail loading your dynamically loaded class. It should be used only for fundamental classes like java/lang/Object.

docs.title: Via classLoader
docs.text:
The goal is to retrieve the application's class loader, which has access to dynamically loaded classes.

In pure Java you could retrieve a class loader from any jobject, as was shown above in the initialize method.

In Android the class loader is available in ApplicationContext or ActivityContext, as well as in any jobject of course, but there is a shorter convenience getter like context.getClassLoader().

The usage is as simple as

let clazz: JClass = classLoader.loadClass("com/mylib/mypackage/MyClass")

docs.title: Via cached instance
docs.text:
The preferred way is to use a convenience JClass method:

let clazz: JClass = JClass.load("com/mylib/mypackage/MyClass")

This way it tries to get it first from cache, then from the cached class loader, and if there is no cached class loader, then from the system's class loader.

Tip

You can call → static methods on the JClass type directly.

docs.title: Class names
docs.text:
As you can see above, the class name is represented as a String, but actually it is not. The JClassName object contains the class name in all possible forms: dotted, slashed, and even just its pure name.

You can predefine classnames as constants in the code for easy reuse and typo safety:

let class1 = JClassName("com/mylib/mypackage/MyClass1")
let class2 = JClassName("com/mylib/mypackage/MyClass2")

and then pass it like this:

JClass.load(class1)

or even put it into a JClassName extension:

extension JClassName {
    static let class1 = JClassName("com/mylib/mypackage/MyClass1")
    static let class2 = JClassName("com/mylib/mypackage/MyClass2")
}

and then use it anywhere like this:

JClass.load(.class1)

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Environment is the real bridge for any JNI call which in JNIKit's implementation is hidden under the hood but can also be used directly if needed.

The environment pointer is wrapped into convenient JEnv object.

Retrieve it this way:

let env = JEnv.current()

Warning

Each instance works only in the thread where it was retrieved, so call JEnv.current() again if you switched thread or moved into Task {}

The possibilities of JEnv are a huge topic to describe in detail. I would say if you know what you want from it you will get it.

All its methods are ergonomically wrapped for easy use with Swift types and convenience types like JClass, JClassName, JObject, JMethodId, and JFieldId.

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
/// Returns the version of the JNI environment provided by the JVM
///
/// This is typically used to verify compatibility
/// (e.g. `0x00010008` = JNI 1.8)
getVersion() -> Int32

/// Returns the JNI version as a human-readable string (e.g. `"1.8"`)
getVersionString() -> String

/// Returns the JNI version parsed into a `JNIVersion` struct
getVersionStruct() -> JNIVersion // { major: 1, minor: 8 }

docs.title: Class Definition
docs.text:
/// Defines a new Java class dynamically from raw bytecode
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - name: The fully qualified class name (e.g., `"com/example/MyClass"`)
///   - loader: A class loader object (or `nil` for bootstrap loader)
///   - buf: Pointer to the `.class` bytecode
///   - size: Size of the bytecode buffer
/// - Returns: A newly defined Java class, or `nil` if failed
defineClass(
    name: JClassName,
    loader: JObject?,
    buf: UnsafePointer<jbyte>,
    size: jint
) -> JClass?

/// Finds a class by name using the current class loader
///
/// - Parameter name: JNI slash-separated class path (e.g. `"java/lang/String"`)
/// - Returns: A wrapped class reference or `nil` if not found
findClass(name: JClassName) -> JClass?

docs.title: Class Hierarchy
docs.text:
/// Gets the superclass of a Java class
getSuperclass(of clazz: JClass) -> JClass?

/// Determines if `clazz2` is assignable to `clazz1`,
/// equivalent to `clazz1.isAssignableFrom(clazz2)` in Java
isAssignable(from clazz1: JClass, to clazz2: JClass) -> Bool

Read more about → classes

docs.title: Reflection Conversion
docs.text:
/// Converts a Java `Method` object to a native method ID
fromReflectedMethod(method: JObject) -> JMethodId?

/// Converts a Java `Field` object to a native field ID
fromReflectedField(field: JObject) -> JFieldId?

/// Converts a native method ID into a Java `Method` or `Constructor` object
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - clazz: The class that declares the method
///   - methodId: The native method ID
///   - isStatic: Whether the method is static
toReflectedMethod(clazz: JClass, methodId: JMethodId, isStatic: Bool) -> JObject?

/// Converts a native field ID into a Java `Field` object
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - clazz: The declaring class
///   - fieldId: Native field ID
///   - isStatic: Whether the field is static
toReflectedField(clazz: JClass, fieldId: JFieldId, isStatic: Bool) -> JObject?

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
/// Throws an existing exception object in the JVM
///
/// - Parameter throwable: A `jthrowable` object
/// - Returns: JNI status (`0` = OK, `-1` = error)
throwException(throwable: jthrowable) -> Int32

/// Throws a new exception given a class and error message
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - clazz: Exception class (e.g. `java/lang/IllegalArgumentException`)
///   - message: Error message
/// - Returns: JNI status
throwNew(clazz: JClass, message: String) -> Int32

/// Checks whether a Java exception has been thrown in the current thread
///
/// - Returns: A throwable object if an exception is pending, or `nil`
exceptionOccurred() -> JThrowable?

/// Describes the current exception (if any) to stderr (for debugging)
exceptionDescribe()

/// Clears the current exception from the JVM (if one is pending)
exceptionClear()

/// Triggers a fatal error in the JVM with a custom message
/// This terminates the VM
fatalError(message: String)

/// Throws a Java exception object that is a subclass of `Throwable`
throwObject(throwable: jobject) -> Int32

/// Throws a `JThrowable` instance and returns a typed JNI status
throwObject(throwable: JThrowable) -> JNIStatus
Example: Detecting and Handling Java Exceptions 
let env = JEnv.current()

// Call a Java method that might throw an exception
let result = env.callVoidMethod(...)

// Check if an exception occurred
if let exception = env.exceptionOccurred() {
    // Describe the exception (prints details to stderr)
    env.exceptionDescribe()

    // Clear the exception to allow further JNI operations
    env.exceptionClear()

    // Optionally, rethrow the exception or handle it in Swift
    print("Java exception: \(exception.getMessage())")
}
Example: Throwing a New Java Exception 
let env = JEnv.current()

// Define the exception class and message
if let exceptionClass = env.findClass(name: "java/lang/IllegalArgumentException") {
    let message = "Invalid argument provided"

    // Throw the exception
    let status = env.throwNew(clazz: exceptionClass, message: message)

    if status != 0 {
        print("Failed to throw Java exception")
    }
}
Example: Throwing an Existing Java Exception Object 
let env = JEnv.current()

// Create or retrieve a Java exception object
let exceptionObject: JObject = ... // Obtain a `JThrowable` or `JObject`

// Throw the exception
let status = env.throwObject(throwable: exceptionObject)

if status != 0 {
    print("Failed to throw Java exception object")
}
Example: Triggering a Fatal Error 
let env = JEnv.current()

// Terminate the JVM with a custom message
env.fatalError(message: "Critical error occurred in Swift")

docs.title: Reference Frames
docs.text:
/// Pushes a new local reference frame,
/// allowing scoped object reference tracking
///
/// - Parameter capacity: Number of local refs to allocate.
/// - Returns: JNI status code
pushLocalFrame(capacity: jint) -> Int32

/// Pops the current local frame, returning a single retained reference
///
/// - Parameter result: Optional object to retain from the popped frame
popLocalFrame(result: JObject?) -> JObject?

docs.title: Reference Management
docs.text:
/// Promotes a local reference to a global one (GC-safe)
newGlobalRef(obj: JObject) -> JObject?

/// Deletes a global reference previously promoted
deleteGlobalRef(globalRef: JObject)

/// Deletes a local reference to allow early GC
deleteLocalRef(localRef: JObject)

/// Returns whether two `jobject`s refer to the same underlying Java object
isSameObject(obj1: JObject, obj2: JObject) -> Bool

/// Creates a new local reference to the given object
newLocalRef(obj: JObject) -> JObject?

/// Ensures there's room for `capacity`
/// more local references in the current frame
///
/// - Returns: JNI status
ensureLocalCapacity(capacity: jint) -> Int32
Example: Promoting a Local Reference to a Global Reference 
let env = JEnv.current()

// `localRef` is a pointer to a Java object obtained from JNI
// which now needs to be converted to a global reference
if let globalRef = env.newGlobalRef(localRef) {
    print("Successfully promoted to a global reference")
    // Use `globalRef` safely across threads
    // Use `env.deleteGlobalRef(globalRef)` when done
} else {
    print("Failed to promote to a global reference")
}
Example: Deleting a Global Reference 
let env = JEnv.current()

env.deleteGlobalRef(globalRef)
print("Global reference deleted")
Example: Deleting a Local Reference 
let env = JEnv.current()

env.deleteLocalRef(localRef)
print("Local reference deleted")
Example: Checking if Two Java Objects are the Same 
let env = JEnv.current()

// Assume `obj1` and `obj2` are `JObject` instances
if env.isSameObject(obj1, obj2) {
    print("Both objects refer to the same Java object")
} else {
    print("Objects are different")
}
Example: Ensuring Local Reference Capacity 
let env = JEnv.current()

// Ensure there is room for 10 more local references
let status = env.ensureLocalCapacity(10)
if status == 0 {
    print("Successfully ensured local reference capacity")
} else {
    print("Failed to ensure local reference capacity")
}

docs.title: Object Allocation
docs.text:
/// Allocates an instance of a class without calling its constructor
allocObject(clazz: JClass) -> JObject?

docs.title: Object Creation
docs.text:
/// Creates a new Java object by calling its constructor
/// using a `jvalue[]` argument list
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - clazz: The class of the object to instantiate
///   - constructor: A `JMethodId` representing the `<init>` constructor method
///   - args: array of values for the constructor,
///           or `nil` if none
/// - Returns: A new `JObject` instance or `nil` if object creation failed
newObject(
    clazz: JClass,
    constructor: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> JObject?

Constructor methodID can be looked up using env.getMethodId(...) with name <init> and appropriate signature → read below

Read more about → JValuable

docs.title: Object Info
docs.text:
/// Checks whether a Java object is an instance of a given class
///
/// Equivalent to `clazz.isInstance(obj)` in Java
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - object: The Java object to check
///   - clazz: The class to compare against
/// - Returns: `true` if `object` is an instance of `clazz`
///             or its subclass; otherwise, `false`
isInstanceOf(object: JObject, clazz: JClass) -> Bool

docs.title: Method Lookup
docs.text:
/// Finds an instance method ID for a method declared in the given class
///
/// This wraps the JNI `GetMethodID` call and converts it into a `JMethodId`
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - clazz: The class in which the method is declared
///   - name: The method name (e.g., `"toString"`)
///   - sig: The method signature (e.g., `"()Ljava/lang/String;"`)
/// - Returns: A `JMethodId` if found,
///            or `nil` if the method doesn't exist or lookup fails
getMethodId(
    clazz: JClass,
    name: String,
    sig: JMethodSignature
) -> JMethodId?

Read more about → signatures

docs.title: Instance Method Calls
docs.text:
JNI provides a variety of methods to call instance methods on Java objects, depending on the return type of the method being called.

Supported return types include void, primitive types (like int, float, etc.), and object types.

Depending on the return type, you should choose different JNI method name.

If you want to call a method that returns an int, you would use callIntMethod. If the method returns an object, you would use callObjectMethod.

Let's break down the object method call process:

callObjectMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil,
    returningClass: JClass
) -> JObject?
  • object: the Java object on which you want to call the method
  • methodId: the method identifier obtained either using env.getMethodId(...) or clazz.methodId(...) → read more
  • args: an optional array of arguments to pass to the method → read more
  • returningClass: the JClass of the object that the method returns → read more

The method returns a JObject?, which is the result of the method call, or nil if the call failed.

The same pattern applies to primitive return types (void, int, float, etc.), but hese methods donot require the returningClass parameter since primitive types are known.

callBooleanMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> Bool
Full List of Methods 
/// Call a Java method returning `byte`.
callByteMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> Int8

/// Call a Java method returning `char`.
callCharMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> UInt16

/// Call a Java method returning `short`.
callShortMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> Int16

/// Call a Java method returning `int`.
callIntMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> Int32

/// Call a Java method returning `long`.
callLongMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> Int64

/// Call a Java method returning `float`.
callFloatMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> Float

/// Call a Java method returning `double`.
callDoubleMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> Double

/// Call a Java method returning `void`.
callVoidMethod(
    object: JObject,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
)

As you can see the principles are the same for all primitive types. Boolean method returns Bool, int method returns Int32, float method returns Float, void method returns nothing, and so on.

docs.title: Non-Virtual Method Calls
docs.text:
JNI also provides non-virtual method calls, which allow you to call a method as if it were a member of a specific class, bypassing any overridden implementations in subclasses.

It is the same as above but with NonVirtual in the method name, for example callNonvirtualObjectMethod or callNonvirtualBooleanMethod, and so on.

docs.title: Lookup
docs.text:
As well as methods you can access instance fields of Java objects.

First you have to find the field ID using getFieldId:

getFieldId(
    clazz: JClass,
    name: String,
    sig: JSignatureItem
) -> JFieldId?

And then you can get or set the field value using the appropriate JNI method based on the field type, same principles as with methods.

docs.title: Getters
docs.text:
getObjectField(
    object: JObject,
    fieldId: JFieldId,
    returningClass: JClass
) -> JObject?

With object fields you need to provide the returningClass parameter to specify the class of the object being retrieved.

For primitive fields, you would use methods like getBooleanField, getIntField, etc., which do not require the returningClass parameter.

getBooleanField(object: JObject, fieldId: JFieldId) -> Bool
Full List of Methods

docs.title: Setters
docs.text:
For setting object fields, you would use:

setObjectField(
    object: JObject,
    fieldId: JFieldId,
    value: JObject?
)

Here, value is the new object to set for the field, and object is the instance containing the field.

For primitive fields, you would use methods like setBooleanField, setIntField, etc.

setBooleanField(object: JObject, fieldId: JFieldId, value: jboolean)

docs.title: Static Method Lookup
docs.text:
Static methods are looked up similarly to instance methods, but on the class level and its lookup is done using getStaticMethodId:

getStaticMethodId(
    clazz: JClass,
    name: String,
    sig: JMethodSignature
) -> JMethodId?

docs.title: Static Method Calls
docs.text:
Static methods are called similarly to instance methods, but you provide the class instead of an object.

callStaticObjectMethod(
    clazz: JClass,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil,
    returningClass: JClass
) -> JObject?

The same applies to primitive return types like callStaticIntMethod, callStaticBooleanMethod, etc.

callStaticBooleanMethod(
    clazz: JClass,
    methodId: JMethodId,
    args: [any JValuable]? = nil
) -> Bool

docs.title: Java Strings
docs.text:
/// Create a new Java string from a UTF-16 buffer
///
/// This corresponds to the JNI `NewString` function.
/// It creates a `jstring` from the provided buffer of 16-bit characters
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - chars: Pointer to the UTF-16 characters (`jchar` array)
///   - length: Number of characters in the array (not bytes)
/// - Returns: A new `jstring`, or `nil` if creation fails
newString(chars: UnsafePointer<jchar>, length: jint) -> jstring?

/// Get the UTF-16 length of a Java string
///
/// Equivalent to `GetStringLength`.
/// This returns the number of UTF-16 code units, not bytes
///
/// - Parameter string: The Java string
/// - Returns: Number of UTF-16 characters in the string
getStringLength(string: jstring) -> Int32

/// Retrieve a pointer to the UTF-16 contents of a Java string
///
/// This returns a read-only buffer of `jchar` values
/// that represent the UTF-16 encoding of the string
///
/// - Important: After use, you **must** call `releaseStringChars`
///              to avoid memory leaks
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - string: Java `jstring` instance
///   - isCopy: Optional pointer that receives whether the data is a copy
/// - Returns: Pointer to UTF-16 characters or `nil`
getStringChars(
    string: jstring,
    isCopy: UnsafeMutablePointer<jboolean>? = nil
) -> UnsafePointer<jchar>?

/// Release the buffer obtained from `getStringChars`
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - string: The original Java string
///   - chars: Pointer returned from `getStringChars`
releaseStringChars(string: jstring, chars: UnsafePointer<jchar>)

/// Create a new Java UTF-8 string from a Swift `String`
///
/// This wraps `NewStringUTF`, which creates a Java string
/// from a C-style UTF-8 encoded string
///
/// - Parameter string: A Swift string (will be converted to C UTF-8)
/// - Returns: A new `jstring`, or `nil` if creation fails
newStringUTF(string: String) -> jstring?

/// Get the UTF-8 byte length of a Java string (not character count)
///
/// Equivalent to `GetStringUTFLength`, this returns the number of bytes
/// required to encode the Java string in UTF-8
///
/// - Parameter string: The Java string
/// - Returns: Number of bytes in UTF-8 encoding
getStringUTFLength(string: jstring) -> Int32

/// Retrieve a pointer to the UTF-8 encoded contents of a Java string
///
/// This pointer is valid until `releaseStringUTFChars` is called
///
/// - Important: After use, call `releaseStringUTFChars`
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - string: The Java `jstring`
///   - isCopy: Optional pointer to receive copy status
/// - Returns: Pointer to null-terminated UTF-8 C string
getStringUTFChars(
    string: jstring,
    isCopy: UnsafeMutablePointer<jboolean>? = nil
) -> UnsafePointer<CChar>?

/// Release a UTF-8 string buffer previously acquired from `getStringUTFChars`
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - string: The original Java string
///   - chars: Pointer obtained from `getStringUTFChars`
releaseStringUTFChars(
    string: jstring,
    chars: UnsafePointer<CChar>
)

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
/// Release memory returned by `getBooleanArrayElements`
///
/// - Parameters:
///   - array: The original `jbooleanArray`
///   - elems: Pointer previously returned
///   - mode: `0` to copy back,
///           `JNI_COMMIT` to copy without free,
///           `JNI_ABORT` to discard changes
releaseBooleanArrayElements(
    array: jbooleanArray,
    elems: UnsafeMutablePointer<jboolean>,
    mode: jint = 0
) {
    env.pointee!.pointee.ReleaseBooleanArrayElements!(env, array, elems, mode)
}
